articles.title: Poland is racing ahead with military spending – but will it help or damage its economic growth story?
articles.body:
A short distance north from Warsaw along the Vistula river, camouflaged missile launchers roll through the quiet village of Czosnów.
As recently as two years ago, their destination – a hi-tech weapons facility opened this month – had been a cornfield. Now, as Poland drives up defence investment at one of the fastest rates in the developed world, this rural spot has been transformed amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement.
“Everyone has had to move twice as fast to meet the Polish needs,” says Jim Price, the managing director of MBDA Polska, the local subsidiary of the European multinational arms group. Based in the UK, the former Royal Marine says Poland is shifting from importing its weapons to manufacturing them at home.
“When it became clear there is a need to defend Nato’s eastern flank, in the event of a war itself, they needed to be able to do things in the blink of an eye. So we decided to invest in-the country to create a facility. We had to build up our Polish subsidiary – and that means Polish jobs.”
Poland’s defence budget has grown at a blistering pace. Since Vladimir Putin ordered Russian troops into Ukraine almost five years ago, spending as a share of Polish gross domestic product (GDP) has more than doubled from 2.2% to 4.8% this year. In cash terms, this equates to $53bn (£39.8bn), the fourth-highest in the EU after Germany, France and Italy.
Attention in Warsaw is clearly focused on the risk of an imminent Russian test of Nato resolve. However, there is also another motive: growing the economy.
Inside the soundproofed, airlock-style doors enclosing his office in Warsaw, Marcin Bosacki, Poland’s deputy foreign minister, says Russian aggression is heavily influencing the Polish government’s plans for economic development and cooperation with EU and Nato allies.
“[It] is clearly benefiting Polish security; Polish defence, and the Polish economy as well,” he says.
Strengthening economic ties in the pursuit of military readiness would discourage Putin (“a traditional Russian imperialist”) from attacking Nato, Bosacki adds.
“The only thing which Putin understands is solidarity and power. And so the more we are united and strong, the less likely the outcome of more aggressive Russian provocations against Nato member states is.”
Hope remains for a diplomatic solution. This month, Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks in Moscow with Putin and in Kyiv with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Next month, further negotiations are scheduled in Abu Dhabi.
However, diplomatic sources believe Russia is unlikely to cede ground – rendering Nato’s demonstrations of military readiness critical.
History shows defence and economics are closely intertwined. Statisticians first devised GDP as a metric in response to the 1930s Great Depression and needs of wartime planning to gauge the capacity of an economy.
Poland has been through an economic miracle since the Solidarność (solidarity) movement that arose from the Gdańsk shipyard strikes paved the way for its transition from communism almost four decades ago. Living standards have shot up from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.
Joining the EU in 2004 and securing catch-up funds from Brussels – which was spent on new roads, railways, and other productivity-enhancing infrastructure – also helped. Annual output surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, with Poland among the fastest-growing EU countries at an annualised rate of 3.9% in the second quarter despite the global headwinds caused by the Iran war.
However, Poland’s defence boom is not cost-free. Nor has economic development helped it avoid political polarisation.
The rising military budget is among the reasons why Poland is predicted to run the biggest fiscal deficit in the EU next year, at 7.1% of GDP. Last week, Moody’s downgraded the country’s long-term sovereign credit rating to the lowest level since 2002, amid an apparent lack of willingness to rebuild fiscal buffers.
Leszek Kąsek, a Warsaw-based economist at ING Bank, said: “This path is not sustainable. You should ask people if Poland can maintain its growth story and whether politicians will be ready to adjust?”
Wedged between larger neighbours it has been subjugated twice within living memory, Poles are uneasy about national security. But despite its economic turnaround under EU membership, and as it secures billions of euros in defence funds from Brussels, support for Eurosceptic politics remains.
In the run-up to the general election next year, the defence of the country, support for Ukraine and EU relations will be highly politically charged.
Outside the foreign ministry in Warsaw, protesters wave placards in a “Poles for peace” nationalist rally, organised by rightwing politicians opposed to the EU and its support for Ukraine.
Inside the building’s marble halls, where the Polish flag appears to be positioned next to those of Nato and the EU at almost every opportunity, Bosacki says divisions over the benefits to Poland of membership to both institutions has emerged for the first time.
This year, Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who has backing from the rightwing Law and Justice party, attempted to block the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk’s liberal, pro-EU government from accessing €44bn (£38bn) of defence investment loans approved under the bloc’s security action for Europe (Safe) programme.
“I think our right is so eager to regain power they will use anything,” Bosacki says. “Here for the first time, the opposition was [against doing] something which, in my opinion – and the opinion of the majority of Poles – is clearly benefiting Polish security, Polish defence and the Polish economy as well.”
Through Safe, Warsaw secured the largest single disbursement in the loan programme. The government has pledged to channel almost 90% of it to domestic industry – led by Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa (PGZ), the state-owned defence conglomerate.
However, in the race to build up capacity, the tills are ringing for US-arms manufacturers supplying Patriot missiles, Abrams tanks and F-35 fighter jets.
In March, the International Monetary Fund cautioned that the positive economic spillovers from EU defence investment would not necessarily flow for the governments taking out their chequebooks.
However, Warsaw is doing defence deals with international partners, including the UK, to help develop its domestic manufacturing base at the same time as building military readiness.
The British defence group Babcock is working with PGZ to help build a fleet of new frigates. Known as the Miecznik, or swordfish, programme, the company has a shipyard at Gdynia on the Baltic coast. The first ship was launched this summer by Tusk.
“It’s a must for Poland, basically, to invest more. But they want to do it in a smart way,” says Andrzej Maciejewski, Babcock’s country director for Poland, who is based in Warsaw.
“We’re addressing this ambition – that these great investments in defence will bring greater value for money and, in the longer run, these capabilities.”
BAE Systems is partnering with the PGZ subsidiary Mesko, which makes ammunition and rockets, to build an artillery plant in Poland’s old southern industrial heartlands near Katowice.
By 2028, Poland plans three new munition factories. During a visit to the Mesko facility in August, Tusk said figures for 2023 showed Poland was capable of producing only 5,000 rounds of 155mm ammunition – a Nato-standard artillery shells. “More is used in one day on the Russian-Ukrainian front,” he said. This year, Poland will have increased production to 30,000 rounds, with a goal of 200,000 a year in the next two years.
This month, Luke Pollard, the UK minister for defence readiness, visited Czosnów for the opening of the MBDA facility. Pollard said it would help support jobs in both countries, including in Bristol, Stevenage and Bolton.
Despite this, Britain is increasing defence investment at a slower pace. The government has committed to increase spending from 2.3% of GDP last year to 3%, but has not spelled out precisely how or when this will be achieved.
In Poland, there are signs its investment spree is beginning to pay off for local contractors.
Maciej Klemm, the co-founder of Advanced Protection Systems (APS), which builds counter-drone systems in Gdynia, has increased its headcount from about 150 staff to 200 this year.
Amid growing Russian drone incursions into Polish airspace, APS is playing a role in the Warsaw’s $4bn San programme to build an “anti-drone wall” to protect the country’s eastern flank.
“We are spending a lot of money as a nation, and we are almost a poster child for it,” Klemm says. Splitting his time between Poland and the UK, where he still lives with his family after graduating from the University of Bristol in the 2000s, Klemm also sums up Poland’s recent economic history.
“I was moving to Britain at the time there was a big wave of Poles coming over here. Now after Brexit, that wave partly receded and went the other way. Now, companies like ourselves and others are showing we have technical talent; we can build on this, and grow companies in Poland.”

articles.title: Leaked Files Reveal Struck Russian Plant Was Feeding Kh-101, R-37M and Oreshnik Missile Programs
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Leaked Files Reveal Struck Russian Plant Was Feeding Kh-101, R-37M and Oreshnik Missile Programs
A Russian optical plant struck on September 26 was involved in the production chains of at least seven Russian missile programs, including the Kh-101 cruise missile, R-37M long-range air-to-air missile, and Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile, newly published internal documents indicate.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Dallas Analytics on September 26, records obtained from the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant, or AOMZ, show that the facility’s role extended well beyond its publicly known production of tank sights, rangefinders, and thermal imaging equipment.
The documents include internal correspondence, state contract records, and industrial cooperation schedules covering the period from April 2023 through March 2025. They involve AOMZ, Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation, the Michurinsk Plant Progress, and the Kurganpribor design bureau.
Dallas Analytics said the correspondence also shows direct oversight of production by Russian Defense Ministry military representatives stationed at enterprises participating in the state defense order system.
One document dated September 9, 2024, refers to seven state contracts connected to AOMZ’s 2025 production program. Five of those contracts were signed in 2022.
An attached two-page production schedule contains 71 component entries, identifying suppliers, required quantities, installation rates, and funding. The component budget for the 2025 program totaled 583.6 million rubles, with 497.6 million rubles already paid in advances, according to the documents.
The records also provide details on components used in several Russian cruise missiles.
For the Kh-101 air-launched cruise missile, Dallas Analytics identified AOMZ as the producer of two major assemblies: the Otblesk navigation lidar and a flight automation unit responsible for controlling missile systems and flight surfaces.
The Kh-101 is carried by Russian Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers and has been extensively used in strikes against Ukraine. The same records connect AOMZ to flight automation systems for the Kh-35U and Kh-59/Kh-69 missile families.
Dallas Analytics also identified 44 component suppliers in the plant’s documentation, including Russian manufacturers of capacitors, resistors, semiconductors, connectors, relays, and optoelectronic equipment.
Among them is TRV-Engineering, the procurement arm of the Tactical Missiles Corporation holding. The company is listed as supplying microcircuits for the Kh-101 navigation system. Dallas Analytics has previously identified TRV-Engineering as an intermediary involved in obtaining foreign electronic components.
Separate correspondence reviewed by Dallas Analytics names AOMZ as an assembler and supplier of components for the system designated 760K (L), described in the documents as a modification of the R-74 family of air-to-air missiles developed by Russia’s Vympel design bureau.
The R-74 family forms part of the weapons package developed for Russia’s Su-57 fighter aircraft. The documents also place AOMZ within the production chain for components used in the guidance system of the Oreshnik, Russia’s nuclear-capable intermediate-range ballistic missile.
Another document, dated March 4, 2025, details plans to increase production of components for the R-37M long-range air-to-air missile from 2026.
According to Dallas Analytics, Tactical Missiles Corporation informed AOMZ that the Russian Aerospace Forces were seeking higher delivery volumes and gave the plant three days to determine whether it could meet the requirement.
The requested annual production included 500 units each of several switching, power supply, battery activation, wiring, and circuit-board assemblies, together with 1,000 missile housings.
Based on the quantities listed in the correspondence, Dallas Analytics assessed that the request corresponded to components for as many as 500 R-37M missiles annually.
The R-37M is a long-range air-to-air missile with a reported engagement range of roughly 300 kilometers and is used by Russian aircraft against targets at extended distances.
The investigation also links AOMZ to the production of seeker components for the Kh-31P anti-radiation missile, which is designed to target radar systems.
AOMZ has been subject to international restrictions for several years. The plant was added to the US Entity List in April 2022 as a facility associated with Tactical Missiles Corporation and has also faced sanctions from the European Union, United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, Switzerland, Australia, New Zealand, and Ukraine.
Dallas Analytics argues that the documentation shows how Russian missile production continues to rely on broader networks of suppliers and procurement intermediaries despite restrictions placed directly on final manufacturers.
The group assessed that a prolonged disruption at AOMZ could affect production of navigation and flight-control systems for the Kh-101 and other cruise missiles, electrical assemblies for the R-37M, and components used in anti-radiation weapons.
However, Dallas Analytics noted that disruption at one production site would more likely delay output than permanently eliminate Russia’s ability to manufacture the systems, particularly if alternative supply chains and component procurement networks remain operational.
Earlier, in July 2025, Ukrainian strike drones targeted the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant in Russia’s Rostov region. Russian authorities said air defenses had repelled the attack, while eyewitness footage showed drones approaching the facility followed by explosions and smoke.

articles.title: Britain and Russia have been to war before. Ask the British fleet how that went
articles.body:
Britain and Russia have been to war before. Ask the British fleet how that went
On June 14, 1854, the allied Anglo-French fleet dropped anchor off Krasnaya Gorka, a village 20 km from Kronstadt and around 50 km from St. Petersburg. Dozens of screw-propelled frigates and steam and sail-powered ships – carrying 3,500 guns and over 30,000 sailors – formed an armada the likes of which had not been seen since the Battle of Trafalgar. They stood by, ready to attack the capital of the Russian Empire.
The press boasted that before setting sail, British Admiral Charles Napier reportedly promised to have breakfast in Kronstadt and dinner in St. Petersburg. Riding a wave of anti-Russian sentiment, the British public hoped to see the Union Jack on the spire of the Russian Admiralty.
The plans of the British were not destined to come to fruition, however. Why did the formidable Anglo-French squadron back down in the face of Russian military-technical power? Why did Britain demonstratively refuse to fight against Russia? And how is the legacy of this 19th-century war being utilized by militaries across the globe today? RT explores this little-known chapter of the Crimean War.
The unknown front of the Crimean War
The war of 1853-1856 – fought between Russia on one side and a coalition of Great Britain, France, Sardinia, and the Ottoman Empire on the other – is known as the Crimean War. Although the main events unfolded in Crimea, the war actually raged across a number of theaters: the Danube, the Caucasus Mountains, the icy waters of the White and Barents seas, distant Chukotka, and the Baltic.
The objective of the anti-Russian coalition was articulated with utmost clarity and candor by then-British Prime Minister John Palmerston, who demanded that Russia be stripped of its growing naval power. Achieving this required capturing and destroying Russian naval fortresses on all fronts, as well as annihilating the Russian military and merchant fleets.
In the Baltic, the British targeted Kronstadt – the naval fortress guarding St. Petersburg. The plan was to seize this maritime gateway to the Russian Empire and subsequently force Russia to capitulate by bombarding the capital. Other targets in the campaign included the Sveaborg sea fortress, which defended Helsingfors (Helsinki), as well as smaller fortresses in Finland and on the islands in the Baltic Sea.
The British were not merely interested in Russia’s surrender. Following their planned victory, they wanted to strip Russia of Crimea and the Caucasus and hand them over to Türkiye. They also planned to cede Moldavia and Wallachia to Austria; transfer parts of the Baltic region to Prussia; return Finland and the Aland Islands to Sweden; and re-establish an independent Poland on the territories of the Kingdom of Poland and Little Russia. In short, Britain aimed to inflict a devastating geopolitical defeat on Russia – one comparable to the events of 1917 and 1991.
These geopolitical ambitions should come as no surprise; the coalition comprising Britain, France, Sardinia, and the Ottoman Empire was, in itself, a formidable force. Moreover, Prussia and Austria – Russia’s recent allies from the Holy Alliance – each kept over 100,000 troops stationed near the border. While formally maintaining neutrality, they were in fact waiting for an opportune moment to share in the spoils should Russia suffer defeat.
One might blame imperial diplomacy for Russia’s lack of allies in the war; yet in other situations, it had no problem forging alliances with European powers. The crux of the matter was that, in the period immediately preceding the Crimean War, the Russian Empire’s power reached its zenith.
In the early 19th century, Russia stood as the undisputed leader of the anti-Napoleonic coalition and the Holy Alliance formed in the wake of the Napoleonic Wars. Furthermore, in 1849, shortly before the Crimean War, Russian troops suppressed the Hungarian uprising, effectively saving the Habsburg dynasty in Vienna. Russia was confidently emerging as a continental hegemon. This development deeply alarmed other European powers, prompting them to unite and join forces to crush – or at least weaken – Russia.
The war also had an ideological dimension. A dispute between Orthodox Christians and Catholics over the right to administer Christian holy sites in Jerusalem and Bethlehem rapidly escalated into a demand by the Archbishop of Paris Marie-Dominique-Auguste Sibour, to “put an end to the Orthodox heresy of the Russian people.”
‘Progressive West’ vs. ‘Backward Russia’
The Crimean War is frequently portrayed as a confrontation between ‘backward Tsarist Russia’ and the ‘progressive West’. From a strictly technical standpoint, the armed forces of Great Britain and France were indeed superior to the Russian Army of that era. They were already armed with rifled muskets having an effective range of 250-300 meters, compared to the 100-120 meter range of the smoothbore muskets with which the Russian forces were mostly equipped. Moreover, the British and French navies already had a significant number of steamships and screw-propelled frigates, whereas Russia’s transition to these new types of vessels proceeded more slowly.
Does this justify the claim that the Russian Army was weak and the Russian Empire backward? If so, we find that the losses suffered by the ‘weak and backward’ Russia in the war were actually lower than those of its progressive allies. Moreover, in Crimea, where the main battles took place, elite Anglo-French units were opposed by standard regular units of the Russian Army.
The true reason for Russia’s difficulties in the war was that the Russian Army was compelled to achieve several things at once: confront allied forces in the Crimea, maintain large and better-trained forces to counter the potential threats posed by Austria and Prussia, and keep its Imperial Guard Corps stationed near St. Petersburg to defend it from Anglo-French attacks. The allies, by contrast, could choose their points of attack and concentrate substantial forces.
St. Petersburg, as the capital of the Russian Empire, was naturally a tempting target for the allies. As British propagandist Friedrich Engels wrote in 1854, “The more sanguine portion of the British public expect shortly to hear of Kronstadt bombarded, the approaches to St. Petersburg forced, and who knows? perhaps even the Union Jack hoisted on the glittering spire of the Russian Admiralty.”
To this end, Britain assembled the largest fleet seen since the Napoleonic Wars, placing it under the command of Vice Admiral Charles Napier – a seasoned naval commander who received his ‘baptism of fire’ in the Napoleonic wars. Counting French forces, this armada comprised 11 steam-powered and 15 sailing ships of the line, along with 32 steam frigates and 7 sailing frigates; the fleet mounted over 3,500 guns and carried a combined crew and marine force of over 30,000 men.
The Russian Baltic Fleet was inevitably inferior to the allied Anglo-French forces in both the number of men and technical equipment. When Napier’s squadron approached the entrance to the Gulf of Finland on April 19, the Russian ships prudently avoided combat, withdrawing under the protection of the guns and forts of Kronstadt and Sveaborg.
It seemed that the Anglo-French fleet would ultimately break the resistance of Kronstadt’s defenders and proceed to bombard St. Petersburg. Yet, on approaching the fortress, Admiral Napier encountered a surprise prepared by Russian engineers.
‘I could do nothing with my powerful fleet’
“Kronstadt is the decisive point for any naval attack against Russia in the Baltic. Take Kronstadt, and St. Petersburg is at your feet, the Russian Navy exists no longer, and Russia is reduced to what she was before Peter the Great,” Engels wrote before Napier’s armada set sail. And he had ample reason to think so.
Established by Russia’s first emperor, Peter I, Kronstadt was a maritime fortress featuring a formidable system of forts, batteries, and fortifications that shielded the Russian Empire’s capital from the sea. The straight-line distance from Kronstadt to the center of St. Petersburg is around 30 km. The Russian command clearly understood the strategic importance of the fortress and had prepared in advance to repel Anglo-French attacks.
Before the war, Emperor Nicholas I personally inspected the Kronstadt fortifications, and they were further secured. Consequently, in spring 1854, the Anglo-French fleet was confronted by granite fortifications arranged in multiple lines, engineered to deliver artillery crossfire, and armed with over 700 cannons.
Despite these advantages, however, this was a classic fortification strategy. While Kronstadt’s forts were formidable, the Anglo-French squadron had superior artillery firepower, making the outcome of the confrontation by no means obvious. Recognizing this, Russian engineers went a step further and undertook an unprecedented feat.
Russian engineers established the world’s first naval minefield to protect Kronstadt. In total, more than 1,500 of these “infernal machines” guarded the fortress from the sea. They were developed by academician Boris Jacobi – who created galvanic mines (detonated from shore via wire) – and Immanuel Nobel, founder of the famous industrial dynasty, who developed contact mines. Placed at a depth of 3.5 meters, the five-row mine lines (and later, 13-row mine lines) were a technological marvel of the time and proved impassable for enemy ships. (Now would be a fitting moment to recall stories about the ‘technologically backward Russian Empire’.)
Napier was initially unaware of the mines. It was only upon approaching Kronstadt at close range on June 14, 1854 that the British admiral was able to gauge the scale and strength of the Russian defenses. As Napier said, “I could do nothing with my powerful fleet, since any attack on Kronstadt or Sveaborg would have meant certain death.” After spending several weeks in the waters near Kronstadt and realizing that there would be no breakfast, not to mention dinner in St. Petersburg, Napier was forced to turn back. The fleet also left Sveaborg.
However, returning to England without any victory was not an option. While Napier had managed to constrain elite units of the Russian Army near the capital and disrupted trade in the Baltic, the ambitions of British command spread far beyond that. They needed at least a semblance of military success to return home with.
Doomed fortresses
Realizing the futility of the attempts to capture Kronstadt, the British fleet decided to plunder coastal villages. However, this hardly justified the enormous resources the British had expended. Thus, the allies resolved to direct their full might against Bomarsund – an isolated, unfinished fortress on the Aland Islands.
The Aland Islands hold a critically strategic position in this part of the Baltic Sea, being just 22 km from Finland and 38 km from Sweden. Russia seized these islands during its war with Sweden in 1808-1809. At the time, in the midst of a very cold winter, General Bagration’s troops traversed the frozen waters of the Baltic Sea basin, moving from Finland to the Alands and then to Sweden, less than 100 km from Stockholm.
Understanding the strategic importance of the islands, Russia began constructing the Bomarsund fortress. Yet by the outbreak of the Crimean War, it was only partially complete and had only a quarter of the planned towers and weapons. The garrison comprised just 1,600 soldiers; their ammunition was extremely limited. Once a forward outpost of the Russian Empire, Bomarsund now found itself completely cut off as Napier’s fleet appeared in the Baltic.
The massive Anglo-French fleet approached the doomed fortress. Bombardment lasted several weeks before the Anglo-French coalition landed 11,000 troops, supported by dozens of heavy siege cannons. The Russian forces found themselves in a hopeless situation: Their artillery was far inferior to the long-range guns of the Anglo-French ships, and the invading force outnumbered the defenders six to one.
Despite these odds, the garrison fought fiercely. After another fortnight of intense fighting, on August 16, 1854, the Anglo-French troops finally breached the outer defense line of the fortress. By that point, the garrison had spent nearly all the ammunition, leaving Commander Yakov Bodisko with no choice but to surrender.
The British acknowledged the heroism of the defenders, and Bodisko was allowed to retain his sword while in captivity. Upon his return from imprisonment, a military tribunal deemed his actions at Bomarsund justified and commendable.
The garrison of another Russian fortress, Gangut (now the Finnish city of Hanko), did not wait for a similar fate to befall it, and blew up its own fortifications on imperial orders. Nevertheless, the success of the Anglo-French forces in the Baltic was mostly limited to these minor incidents. As British media noted, “English guns did not speak in the Baltic Sea. They whispered in Bomarsund, but the whole of Europe waited for them to resonate in Kronstadt and Sveaborg. One could not have dealt a heavier blow to Britain’s naval honor.”
Second attempt
British accounts of the Baltic campaign assess Napier’s actions in a rather flattering way, implying that though he didn’t secure any significant victories, his forces managed to tie down the Russian fleet and prevented reinforcements from reaching Crimea.
This theory is fundamentally flawed, since during wartime, Russia would have defended its capital no matter what. It’s hard to imagine the Baltic fleet abandoning St. Petersburg and making its way through the English Channel and Gibraltar, navigating hostile waters controlled by England and France, on the way to the Black Sea. Thus, the first year of the Crimean War in the Baltic was clearly a success for Russia: It distracted the Anglo-French fleet, which expended great resources without achieving significant military success.
The winter of 1854-1855 proved particularly harsh, particularly in the primary theater of war, Crimea; the allied forces got bogged down near Sevastopol. The military challenges and the inefficient use of resources, including during the Baltic campaign, were so severe that Aberdeen’s ministry was forced to resign. By the 1855 campaign, the allies urgently needed to turn their fortunes around.
For operations in the Baltic Sea that year, they again assembled a massive fleet of 67 ships. Just like the previous year, they set their sights on Kronstadt, hoping to lure out the Russian fleet stationed there. However, they only stumbled on underwater mines. Four British steamers became the first victims of these mines, leading the Anglo-French command to realize that capturing Kronstadt was out of the question.
Following this, light Anglo-French vessels began raiding the Finnish coast and plundering local fishermen. Meanwhile, the main forces of the allies aimed to capture Sveaborg – the second most significant Russian stronghold in the region, which defended Helsingfors.
In August, the Anglo-French squadron approached Sveaborg with plans to destroy the fortress and incinerate the strategically vital Russian shipyards. However, after a 45-hour bombardment and firing over 20,000 shells at the fortress, they failed to inflict any substantial damage on it. Russian military engineers had set up impressive defensive positions.
With no other options, the British and French had no choice but to leave the Baltic Sea by autumn 1855. This effectively marked the end of the Crimean War in the Baltic.
Lessons learned
Beyond the disastrous military operations, Britain also faced diplomatic setbacks in the Baltic.
After occupying the Aland Islands, Admiral Napier suggested that Sweden take them over. Following the resignation of Aberdeen’s ministry, the new British prime minister, Palmerston, spent all of 1855 actively working to draw Sweden and Norway – then united by a personal union – into the war against Russia. Britain frightened them with tales of ‘Russian imperialism’ while simultaneously hinting at the potential return of territories lost in previous wars with Russia.
In Sweden, revanchist sentiments were strong but pragmatism ultimately prevailed. The country declined to occupy the Aland Islands and did not sign a defensive alliance with Britain until the end of 1855. This was a disappointing outcome for London, which intended to open a second front against Russia.
Sweden’s pragmatic approach is understandable: Having suffered major defeats in past wars with Russia and lost the Baltics and Finland, it recognized the futility of engaging in another war with the Russian Empire on Britain’s behalf.
With its advanced military technology and strategic decisions in the Baltic, 19th-century Russia effectively anticipated the military strategy of the 21st century called ‘anti-access/area denial’. While the Anglo-French fleet formally surpassed the Baltic Fleet of the Russian Empire, it was paralyzed by Russia’s impregnable fortifications and minefields.
Today, various countries are implementing similar strategies. China has developed hypersonic anti-ship missiles known as ‘carrier killers’ to counter the US Navy, effectively closing off the Taiwan Strait and the South China Sea in the event of war. Another example is Iran. While it clearly pales in military strength compared to the US, its missiles and drones enable it to control the Strait of Hormuz, making any US naval operation in the region costly.
However, the most significant lessons from this conflict were undoubtedly learned by Russia. Although the Baltic campaign was successful for Russia and the powerful Anglo-French fleet didn’t achieve much, the war in general ended unsuccessfully for the empire. It exposed numerous areas of governance that required serious improvement. As a result of the Crimean War, Russia undertook crucial reforms in military affairs, finance, economics, law, and public life. This ushered in a new and more prosperous era.

articles.title: What Germany’s Wingcopter 262 Means for Ukraine’s Drone War
articles.body:
For years, the German startup Wingcopter built its reputation on civilian logistics. The company engineered autonomous aircraft to deliver life-saving vaccines and medical supplies to isolated communities in Africa and the Pacific. Today, it is making a direct jump into the military sector.
On Sept. 14 Wingcopter unveiled the Wingcopter 262, an all-electric tactical reconnaissance drone equipped with AI. Through a joint venture with Ukrainian manufacturer TAF Industries, these drones are headed straight to the front lines.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The move marks two critical developments in the war: commercial tech companies repurposing their civilian tools for military use, and European allies moving Ukrainian defense manufacturing into NATO territory to protect factories from Russian airstrikes.
Hybrid design
The Wingcopter 262 fills a vital tactical gap for Ukrainian forces. It uses a tilt-rotor design, meaning it can take off and land vertically in tight spaces just like a helicopter, but once airborne, it tilts its motors to fly fast and efficiently like a traditional airplane.
This design gets rid of the need for long runways or heavy catapult launchers. A single soldier can carry the 10-kilogram drone into rugged terrain and launch it in just a few minutes.
Zelensky Says Putin Keeps Finding Excuses to Continue the War
Once in the air, the drone can cover a tactical range of 150 kilometers and stay aloft for up to six hours. It carries high-resolution visual and thermal cameras backed by built-in AI, which helps operators spot targets, track movements and process imagery instantly.
Beating signal jamming
One of the drone’s biggest selling points for the front line is its ability to operate when GPS signals are completely cut off.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Russian electronic warfare units continuously flood the front lines with heavy jamming signals. Standard commercial drones that rely entirely on satellite navigation often lose control, drift off course, or crash the moment they hit a jammed sector. Wingcopter built the 262’s navigation system to stay on course even when GPS is blocked, using software fixes shaped directly by feedback from combat operations in Ukraine.
The German-Ukrainian deal
The partnership behind the drone represents a new approach to European defense. Wingcopter and TAF Industries, Ukraine’s largest drone producer, launched a joint venture under the “Build with Ukraine” initiative.
This arrangement fixes a major security issue for Kyiv. Domestic military factories inside Ukraine face constant threats from Russian long-range missile and drone attacks. By partnering with Wingcopter, TAF Industries can mass-produce its battle-tested designs inside secure facilities in Germany. In return, Ukrainian troops get priority access to the new Wingcopter 262 platform.
This partnership creates a shared defense pipeline, which is Ukrainian battle experience combined with German manufacturing power and funding.
Commercial tech reshaping defense
The Wingcopter 262 shows how fast commercial technology can adapt to battlefield realities. The engineering needed to deliver emergency medical packages in harsh weather over long distances turns out to be almost identical to what a military drone needs, with long battery life, reliable navigation and tough airframes that resist signal interference.
As European countries increase their defense spending, military procurement teams are turning away from slow-moving traditional defense contractors. Building a new military aircraft from scratch often takes years. Commercial startups like Wingcopter, which have spent a decade perfecting light electric flight and autonomous software, can deliver proven systems in a fraction of that time.
A high-stakes test for NATO’s future
The deployment of the Wingcopter 262 in Ukraine will act as a real-world stress test. If the aircraft holds up against Russian air defenses and electronic warfare, it will likely capture the attention of other NATO militaries looking to upgrade their tactical reconnaissance gear.
More importantly, the partnership between Wingcopter and TAF Industries proves that it is by moving past one-off weapon donations and fully linking Ukrainian tech into the broader European defense industry, that Western nations can sustain Ukraine over the long haul.

articles.title: German foreign minister sees no readiness for peace during first meeting with Russian counterpart since 2022
articles.body:
German foreign minister sees no readiness for peace during first meeting with Russian counterpart since 2022
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said that during a meeting with his Russian counterpart Sergei Lavrov, he saw no willingness on the part of the Russian delegation to refrain from further escalation.
Source: Deutsche Welle, citing Wadephul speaking on German TV channel ZDF; Tagesschau
Details: The officials met on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York. Wadephul said he had used the conversation to urge Russia to abandon its path of escalation.
He said he had made it clear to the Russian delegation that actions such as the attempted sabotage involving drones at Leipzig/Halle Airport were unacceptable.
Wadephul said he had made it clear to Lavrov that "a line had been crossed, we expect this not to happen again, and we are ready to respond at any time".
Meanwhile, Wadephul stressed that he had not conducted any negotiations with Lavrov concerning Ukraine's future. The minister emphasised that such negotiations were a matter solely for the Ukrainians themselves.
Quote from Wadephul: "There are indeed fundamental differences between the positions of our governments, and these also need to be discussed. During the Cold War, exchanges of views and contacts between the two sides never ceased. And I thought it was right, particularly now, to try to find an initial opportunity for such dialogue."
Details: The German foreign minister warned the Russian representative that Berlin would continue its comprehensive support for Ukraine and maintain economic pressure on Russia.
"This support is absolutely unwavering, and Russia must now come to the negotiating table. There is no justification whatsoever for this war, which is claiming countless lives, including Russian lives, but above all those of Ukrainian civilians," Wadephul said.
However, the minister acknowledged that he had seen no willingness on the part of the Russian delegation to heed his call to begin negotiations on ending the war.
"To all those who keep saying that Germany needs to negotiate, that Germany needs to talk to Russia, I say now: we are doing so. And unfortunately, Russia is currently showing no willingness to adopt a constructive negotiating position," the foreign minister said.
According to Russian state propaganda agency TASS, the meeting lasted "just over 20 minutes" and covered "bilateral relations and the situation surrounding Ukraine". Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the meeting had taken place at the request of the German side.
The foreign ministers of Germany and Russia last met in Moscow on 18 January 2022. At the time, Annalena Baerbock travelled to the Russian capital amid Russia's rapid military build-up near Ukraine's borders and warnings from Western intelligence agencies that Moscow was preparing for a full-scale invasion.
Background:
- The resumption of diplomatic contacts at this level was preceded by a series of Russian nuclear threats against European countries.
- On 10 September, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev threatened to wipe Lithuania "off the map" if nuclear weapons were deployed on its territory, and claimed that its NATO allies would not dare invoke Article 5 on collective defence.
- On 11 September, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov threatened Vilnius, saying that if nuclear weapons were deployed in Lithuania, the country would come under the sights of Russian nuclear weapons.
- On 21 September, it was reported that intelligence officials from three EU countries believed Moscow was planning to step up provocations against NATO in the coming months.
- On 25 September, Russian state news agency RIA Novosti published a column headlined "Russia is in for another SVO. It will be very short", which threatened Lithuania with a nuclear strike. The article was subsequently deleted.
- On the same day, political scientist Sergei Karaganov, an adviser to Russian leader Vladimir Putin, called on television for preparations to use weapons of mass destruction.
- "Europe is the source of humanity's greatest troubles and Russia's greatest troubles. A nuclear war in Europe can easily be won... We would rather it did not come to that. But we must be prepared for it, and they must know that," Karaganov said.

articles.title: Poland offers to host Patriot system production site for Ukraine after Kyiv secures license from US
articles.body:
Poland offers to host Patriot system production site for Ukraine after Kyiv secures license from US
Polish officials proposed on Sept. 27 that Ukraine use Polish land to manufacture Patriot systems after securing U.S. manufacturing licenses. 
The offer follows President Volodymyr Zelensky's announcement on Sept. 25  that U.S. President Donald Trump granted Kyiv permission to produce its own Patriot air defense missiles.
"We'll see if that happens," Poland's Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told Polish media. "We proposed that if such a factory is planned to be built in Ukraine, we propose building it in Poland, so that it would be in so-called 'safe territory.'"
The announcements come as Kyiv faces a critical shortage of air defense munitions, particularly of Patriots — the only weapons capable of reliably intercepting Russian ballistic missiles that continue to batter cities across the nation.
During overnight strikes across Ukraine, Russian forces killed 14 Ukrainians on Sept. 26-27.
On Sept. 24, Zelensky announced he had struck a 'very important' deal regarding a new batch of Patriot missiles while attending the U.N. General Assembly in New York City. Zelensky said that more Patriot interceptors would be heading to Kyiv soon, though he did not disclose which country would provide the missiles.
The Polish offer comes as Warsaw seeks to further U.S. military cooperation amid heightened risks emerging from Moscow.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said Polish lawmakers are pushing to accelerate the construction of a new U.S. military base in western Poland. The base would be intended to house at least 5,000 U.S. troops and their families.
"We need to prepare a special act…on faster construction of the base, defining the competences of specific ministries, because building the base is in fact building a small town," Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said she expects U.S. officials to decide where the new base will be located by December of this year.
Russian missiles and drones have violated Poland's airspace numerous times throughout the war, including striking a locomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw passenger train just 2 kilometers from the Polish border on Sept. 13.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russian attacks kill 14, injure 57 across Ukraine in 'mass strike'
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russian attacks kill 14, injure 57 across Ukraine in 'mass strike'
Key developments on Sept. 26-27:
- Russian attacks kill 14, injure 57 across Ukraine, with Odesa Oblast targeted in 'mass strike'
- Russia launches third consecutive attack on Kyiv, killing 1, injuring at least 4, setting off fires
- Zelensky says over 10,000 Russian troops killed or wounded this week as Ukrainian military advances in Lyman sector
- Ukrainian military delivers 4 tons of food to occupied Oleshky by drones, according to regional authorities
- Russia plans to spend $12 billion on jet-powered drones, loitering munitions next year, Zelensky says
At least 14 people were killed and 57 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day as Odesa Oblast in particular came under mass attack, local authorities said on Sept. 26-27.
In southern Odesa Oblast, Russia launched "a mass strike," damaging a residential building, a medical facility, a hotel, a shop and a grain storage facility, local governor Oleh Kiper said. One person was killed while two others were injured, he added.
Overall, overnight on Sept. 27, Russian forces launched 170 Shahed-type attack drones, including 76 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 147 drones, while strikes were recorded at 18 locations. Debris from downed drones fell at eight locations, the Air Force said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 27 that residential buildings, energy infrastructure, and other civilian infrastructure were attacked in Odesa, Kharkiv, Sumy, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Zhytomyr, and Kyiv oblasts overnight.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, four people were killed, and five were injured in Russian attacks across the region, local authorities said. Over the past day, Russia carried out 989 attacks on 59 settlements of the region.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed, and five were injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In the northeastern city of Sumy, a Russian glide bomb attack hit a residential area, killing two people and injuring 28 others, including four children, regional authorities said.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed two people and injured six others over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Sept. 26 and Sept. 27.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and the surrounding regions, killing two people and injuring three others, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Kyiv, Russian drones injured five people over the past day, damaging residential buildings and warehouses, local authorities reported.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian attacks over the past day damaged 23 facilities, injuring two people, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks in the region injured one person, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. He added that, as a result of the attacks, a high-rise apartment building, nine houses, a shop, and vehicles were damaged.
In Poltava Oblast, power lines have been damaged following the crash of a Russian drone, local governor Vitalii Diakivnych said. Around 500 customers were temporarily left without power while power company staff worked to restore the electricity supply, he added.
Zelensky said that over the past week, Russian forces launched more than 2,200 attack drones against Ukraine, as well as around 1,650 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types.
read also
Russia launches third consecutive attack on Kyiv, killing 1, injuring at least 4, setting off fires
Russia launched another drone attack on Kyiv on the night of Sept. 26-27, marking the third consecutive day of attacks on the Ukrainian capital, according to authorities.
"Just today, and only in Kyiv, Russian kamikaze drones 'defeated' two kindergartens and two schools, a residential building, a car repair shop, several warehouses, and communication facilities," Zelensky said. "Everywhere in the world, such a choice of targets would be called one word: terrorism."
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office said on Sept. 27 that a pre-trial investigation was launched into the commission of a war crime by the Russian military, which resulted in the death of a man.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at 5:17 p.m. local time that a drone struck a nine-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district of Kyiv.
Klitschko also said at 4:09 p.m. local time that an administrative building in the Holosiivskyi district was hit, according to preliminary reports.
In the morning of Sept. 27, Russia struck a non-residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district, Klitschko said at 9:26 a.m. local time. At least three people, a woman and two 16-year-old children, were injured in the area.
Air defense units were operating over the city, Klitschko said in an evening update. Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground also heard air defenses operating in the city.
In the Shevchenkivskyi district, a Russian drone struck an uninhabited residential building at around 10 p.m. local time on Sept. 26, according to Klitschko.
A fire at the building was later brought under control, while emergency crews continued working at the site.
In the Solomianskyi district, a drone fell in an open area overnight. The resulting blast wave damaged a five-story residential building, breaking windows and damaging its facade, Klitschko said.
A fire also broke out at a warehouse in the district after the site was struck by a Russian drone, he added. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said that a car service center was on fire as a result of the attack.
A woman was injured in the attack and handed over to medics, and a man was killed, the State Emergency Service said.
Zelensky said that on the morning of Sept. 27, Russian forces struck a data center in Kyiv twice.
Ukraine's largest mobile operator Kyivstar said that its headquarters was damaged during the drone attack on Sept. 27, as reported by the Ukrainian media outlet Suspilne.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured three others, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said.
In Vyshneve, five cars were damaged, and a fire broke out after a drone struck the area. In Brovary, the attack caused fires in a warehouse and an office building, according to Tkachenko.
The latest attack follows a series of Russian drone strikes on Kyiv that began overnight on Sept. 24.
Russian drones continued targeting Kyiv during the day on Sept. 26, with further damage and casualties reported. By the evening, Ukrainian officials said five people had been injured in attacks on the capital during the day.
In recent months, Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones, placing additional strain on Ukraine's air defenses.
One of Russia's newer jet-powered drone models, the Geran-5, can reportedly reach speeds of up to 600 km/h (373 mph), has an estimated range of up to 950 kilometers (590 miles), and can fly at altitudes of up to 6,000 meters (19,700 feet).
Ukraine is developing interceptor drones aimed at countering Russia's jet-powered drones, with some systems having undergone successful tests, according to Ukrainian officials. The government has not announced plans for mass production.

Zelensky says over 10,000 Russian troops killed or wounded this week as Ukrainian military advances in Lyman sector
Ukrainian forces have killed or wounded 10,660 Russian troops over the past week while making gains in the Lyman sector of Donetsk Oblast, Zelensky said on Sept. 27.
"The occupiers continue to be eliminated, and the designated objectives are being achieved," Zelensky wrote on X, citing a report by Ukraine's Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi.
According to Zelensky, Ukrainian forces have video evidence confirming every Russian loss included in the weekly figure. Russia does not routinely disclose its military losses, and the figures could not be independently verified.
Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 15 that Russian forces have lost more than 300,000 troops killed and wounded since the beginning of 2026. After the summer campaign on the battlefield in Ukraine ended, Russian losses exceeded 1.5 million since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Zelensky said the past week's results were achieved as part of Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman sector and another active defense operation involving Ukraine's Air Assault Forces.
Zelensky added that the heaviest fighting has been taking place in the Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka, and Lyman sectors, while Ukrainian forces are also carrying out operations in Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, and Sumy oblasts.
He did not provide further details on the territorial gains.
Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps offensive operation around Lyman in northern Donetsk Oblast, was only made public on Sept. 15, although Russian pro-war Telegram channels and independent open-source intelligence (OSINT) researchers on social media had been tracking Ukrainian attacks in the area since late spring 2026.
On Sept. 20, the 3rd Corps said it liberated a further 40 square kilometers (15.4 square miles) of territory in Donetsk Oblast and retook several villages during the ongoing offensive.

Ukrainian military delivers 4 tons of food to occupied Oleshky by drones, according to regional authorities
Ukrainian forces have delivered around four tons of food to residents of the occupied front-line town of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, distributing supplies to 100 locations across the city with the help of drones, the Kherson Oblast Military Administration head said on Sept. 27.
The operation was carried out in cooperation with several Ukrainian military and law enforcement units, according to Kherson Oblast Governor Oleksandr Prokudin.
Residents of Oleshky have reported that the town is running critically low on food due to a lack of supplies, while only a small number of residents have managed to evacuate.
The drone delivery is part of an effort that has been supplying food to Oleshky residents by drone since March 2026, according to the governor.
A local resident who left Oleshky in April told the Kyiv Independent that drones had previously delivered food.
"(Drones) dropped the packages in several places. (The packages) contained a little bit of medicine and food. I don't know whose drone it was, but I reckon it was Ukraine that dropped them for us," the resident said.
Prokudin said Russian forces have attempted to disrupt the deliveries, including by shooting down the drones carrying food. He also accused Russian forces of confiscating or reselling humanitarian supplies and detaining residents who receive aid.
"The occupiers are detaining residents of Oleshky for receiving humanitarian aid parcels, throwing them 'into the cellar', beating them brutally and resorting to violence," Prokudin said.
Volunteers who used to organize the evacuation from Oleshky raised concerns about such deliveries in local Telegram groups, saying they feared this might lead to checks from the Russian side and a "nightmare for people".
The last successful food delivery to the city by vehicles was on May 26. Further attempts to supply the city on June 2 and Sept. 1 were disrupted by Russian drone attacks that killed two and injured others.
Oleshky lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, less than 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the regional center of Kherson. The town has been under Russian occupation since Feb. 24, 2022.
Oleshky's population has fallen from around 24,000 to approximately 2,000 as of spring 2026, according to the Foreign Ministry.
While Russian troops occupy Oleshky and the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast, the Ukrainian military controls the western bank. Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Russian forces have placed guns, mortars, and mines in and around residential neighborhoods due to the city's proximity to Ukrainian-controlled territory, Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, told the Kyiv Independent.
Tolokonnikov said Russia shields its positions from Ukrainian strikes through the continued presence of civilians.
"Oleshky and its people are necessary for Russian troops so that Ukrainian troops cannot actively attack them in these settlements," he said.
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help people from Oleshky leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips. Now, they said, the high risk made evacuation impossible.
In recent weeks, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces.
Russian forces are preventing Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
On Sept. 25, the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, raised concerns about the worsening humanitarian situation in Oleshky. O'Flaherty said civilians, including children, were struggling to access adequate food, medicine, medical care, clean water, and electricity, warning that some could face a serious risk to their lives.
O'Flaherty said international humanitarian law requires occupying authorities to ensure civilians have access to food and medical supplies and to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid.
"The hardship and suffering of people caught along the frontlines of the war and in occupied territories demand international attention and action," O'Flaherty said.
read also
Russia plans to spend $12 billion on jet-powered drones, loitering munitions next year, Zelensky says
Russia plans to spend $12 billion next year on the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions, Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 26, citing Ukrainian military intelligence.
Zelensky said Ukrainian intelligence had obtained Russian internal documents showing the volumes of weapons Russia is preparing to produce next year and the funding allocated for them.
In recent months, Russia has increasingly relied on jet-powered drones in attacks on Ukrainian cities. In some attacks on Kyiv, jet-powered drones have accounted for around two-thirds of all drones launched.
"Next year, just for the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions, Russia plans to spend $12 billion on this one category of weapons," Zelensky said.
Zelensky said Ukraine is scaling up production of interceptor drones to counter Russia's increasingly widespread use of jet-powered drones. Several interceptor prototypes are already being tested in combat, he said, with some identified as potential primary means of defense against the weapons.
"We are scaling up production and components. There will be a response," Zelensky said.
The remarks come as Russia has intensified its attacks against Ukraine in recent days, despite renewed international efforts to secure a ceasefire. U.S. President Donald Trump called for an end to the war during his address to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, while Zelensky said following their meeting that Ukraine was ready to accept a ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure if Russia agreed to the same terms.
Zelensky said Russia's planned spending on attack drones shows that Moscow is not preparing to halt the war "at least for now."
He also said Ukraine's partners need to increase pressure on Russia through sanctions and strengthen joint efforts to defend against drones.
Ukraine currently intercepts about 55% of Russia's jet-powered Shahed-type drones, according to Zelensky. More than 2,730 jet-powered Shaheds were launched against Ukraine in September, he said.
Zelensky said Ukraine aims to raise the interception rate to the level achieved against conventional Shahed drones, which he said is above 90%.
Ukraine has already signed 11 drone deals, according to Zelensky. The 11th, with Finland, was signed this week in New York on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
He said Ukraine is preparing a 12th agreement, which it expects to sign with another country in the coming weeks.
"For Ukraine, this means more production capacity, more funding, and more technological advantages," Zelensky said.
Zelensky also said Russia is conducting a campaign targeting Ukrainian data centers, infrastructure, and communications. He said the goal is to leave Ukrainians without internet access, communications, and digital services.
Earlier, Russia's attacks on Kyiv on Sept. 26 caused internet outages across the capital and disrupted access to some online services.

articles.title: Iran insists on diplomatic solution after Trump rejects peace plan
articles.body:
Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the United States and Israel after U.S. President Donald Trump said he rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on social media. "Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock."
Iran announced a peace proposal last week at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators. Trump said on Saturday he rejected the plan and argued that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway.
"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters at the White House.
Despite Trump's public statements, mediators facilitating Iran's talks with the United States have not officially relayed a U.S. rejection of the plan, according to Araghchi.
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Araghchi posted.
The U.S. has imposed an economic blockade on Iran to put pressure on Tehran to stop Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, which have drastically reduced shipping through the area even as Trump repeatedly asserts that the U.S. controls the waterway.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected the Iranian proposal, citing unnamed U.S. officials.
It said Trump was privately skeptical that Iran would meet his demands and had told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November U.S. midterm elections.
A U.S. official had said earlier that discussions with Iran through mediators were "positive and constructive."
Conflict has disrupted oil flows, harmed global economy
The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the Strait of Hormuz, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through a critical shipping lane and taken a toll on the global economy.
Araghchi told reporters at the United Nations on Friday the proposed deal would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.
"If there is seriousness on the U.S. side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," Araghchi said. If the U.S. were to agree, the warring parties could start wider talks "on mutually agreed subjects."
That could potentially include discussions of Iran's nuclear program. Trump has said Tehran must never acquire a nuclear bomb, while a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran would show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the U.S. accepted its peace deal.
Iran would grant no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, the official said.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show "Face the Nation", said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues, but would not accept "bullying or coercion."
"Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that "we're not supposed to develop nuclear weapons."
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed to end the war, which began on February 28 with U.S. and Israeli attacks.
Since then, the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading the conventional forces of Iran and damaging its already ailing economy.
Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck U.S. allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests.
Yemen's Saudi-led coalition said early on Saturday it had intercepted two ballistic missiles and two drones launched by the Houthis toward the kingdom.

articles.title: Russian drone strikes on Kyiv kill at least 3, injure more than 10
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Russian drone strikes on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv killed at least three people and injured more than 10, local authorities said Sunday.
A drone struck a market in the village of Sofiivska Borshchahivka, according to the Kyiv regional prosecutor’s office.
The strikes also damaged vehicles and sparked fires at a warehouse and an office building across the region.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy earlier accused Russia of launching 277 attack drones of various types since Saturday, saying the strikes damaged civilian and public facilities across Ukraine, including a building used as the residence of the Saudi Arabian ambassador.
In the statement on the US social media platform X, he said the Russian drone attack on Kyiv “vanquished” kindergartens, schools, a residential building, an auto repair shop, warehouses and communications facilities.
“Russia has no military objective whatsoever in doing this – it is purely an attempt to break people and inflict as much harm as possible on our society,” he said,
He said the strikes also damaged a sports school in Dnipro and a children’s home in the Sumy region.
Zelenskyy said Russia knows how to send diplomatic signals that the world wants to hear in order to delay tougher international measures in response to the war.
“If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps toward de-escalation – as it claims, particularly to American negotiators – this wave of ‘shahed’ terror would not be happening,” he stressed, urging Ukraine's partners to increase pressure on Moscow.
New sanctions packages are being prepared, he said, targeting financial networks, supply chains for components and equipment used to produce Russian weapons, and companies and individuals involved primarily in producing Russian ballistic missiles.
“The new sanctions must take effect as early as October to provide a stronger foundation for changing the situation and pushing Russia toward real diplomacy,” he said.
Russia has repeatedly denied that its armed forces intentionally attack civilian targets in Ukraine, saying they only target military infrastructure or other military targets.
Earlier, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Telegram that its forces struck communications and logistics facilities as well as a cargo ship allegedly carrying military and dual-use supplies for Ukrainian forces in Kyiv and Odesa.
Independent verification of claims from both sides remains difficult due to the ongoing war.

articles.title: Iran captures another US spy drone in Hormuz (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Iran captures another US spy drone in Hormuz (VIDEO)
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has captured a US autonomous underwater vehicle in the Strait of Hormuz, the second such incident reported this month.
According to an IRGC Navy statement carried by Iranian media, the military UROV was conducting espionage in the strategic waterway.
The IRGC identified the vessel as a Remus 600, an advanced autonomous underwater vehicle used by the US Navy for mine detection, surveillance, and reconnaissance. It released footage of the vehicle being lifted from the water and said specialists are now working to recover its data.
The IRGC also warned that the Strait of Hormuz remains “closed,” saying it will continue confronting what it described as “dangerous movements and unauthorized” vessel activity. The US has not yet commented on the incident.
First Footage
Iran has captured a second US unmanned underwater vehicle intact in the Strait of Hormuz. pic.twitter.com/XP343uFzoU
The claim follows a series of drone incidents in the Strait of Hormuz this month.
In early September, Iran said it had seized a US underwater drone, with IRGC footage appearing to show an Anduril-built Dive-LD. The Pentagon acknowledged losing the submersible but said it was an older, damaged model carrying no sensitive data or classified equipment. Days later, the IRGC said it had destroyed a US Saildrone Explorer near the entrance to the strait, releasing footage of the craft burning in the water. In mid-September, the US military said it had thwarted an IRGC attempt to seize another Saildrone, striking two Iranian boats allegedly involved.
The incidents come amid an escalating maritime standoff between Washington and Tehran. The US has destroyed several Iranian oil tankers after accusing the IRGC of firing ballistic missiles at US warships. Iran, meanwhile, has targeted US vessels and commercial tankers it accused of violating restrictions around the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier this week, reports claimed that Washington had increased military activity around the waterway, with reconnaissance aircraft spotted near Iranian territory and additional fighter jets reportedly deployed to the region.
Meanwhile, this week’s diplomatic efforts to break the Iran-US deadlock appear to have failed. At the UN General Assembly, Iran presented what Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called a “concrete seven-day plan,” offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks if Washington lifted its naval blockade, eased restrictions on Iranian oil exports, released frozen assets, and observed a ceasefire, including an end to Israel’s operations in Lebanon. US President Donald Trump rejected the proposal as “unacceptable.”
“I reject their proposal,” he told reporters outside the White House on Saturday, claiming Tehran wants a deal “because they’re losing so badly.” At the UN gathering, he also said he faced a “big decision” over whether to “annihilate” Iran if negotiations failed.
Iran’s top army commander, Major General Amir Hatami, on Sunday argued that the “war is not over,” insisting Tehran had won the initial phase of the conflict but now needs to “consolidate its victory.”

articles.title: Zelensky Urges China, India to Pressure Russia as Weekly Strikes Top 2,200 Drones
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky called on China, India and other major non-Western powers to take a stronger stance on Russia, saying Moscow had launched more than 2,200 attack drones, about 1,650 guided aerial bombs (KABs) and 38 missiles at Ukraine this week alone.
In a statement posted to Telegram on Sunday, Sept. 27, Zelensky said overnight Russian strikes killed three people in Zaporizhzhia region and a man in Kyiv, while Russian forces struck a data center twice in the morning of that same day.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Unfortunately, there is a lack of a consistently strong position from China and India, Brazil and South Africa, the G20 countries and the Global South,” Zelensky said, adding that “each of these countries has influence over Russia and can help make peace a reality.”
Ukraine continues working with its partners, including the US, EU, Canada, Japan and Australia, to strengthen its defense and pursue diplomacy.
“Building guaranteed, dignified security here in Ukraine means adding to security and stability globally,” he said.
Kyiv data center hit twice
According to Zelensky, a significant share of the 38 missiles Russia launched this week were ballistic.
Three people, including two children, were injured in the first of the two strikes on the Kyiv data center, he said, adding that overnight strikes also hit residential buildings, energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in the Odesa, Kharkiv, Sumy, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Zhytomyr and Kyiv regions.
Russian Attacks on Kyiv Kill 1, Injure at Least 10 Since Saturday
Earlier, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a woman and two 16-year-olds had been hospitalized after the strike in the capital’s Shevchenkivskyi district.
On Saturday, Russian forces struck Kyiv’s Cosmonova data centers, affecting local television broadcasts and overall civilian ability to receive critical information.
The attack followed an almost three-week campaign against data centers, with four already hit on Wednesday.
China’s leverage over Moscow
China and India are the two largest buyers of Russian crude oil globally, providing revenue that helps sustain Moscow’s war effort. Beijing also supplies Russia with weapons-making components, while India remains one of largest buyers of Russian arms.
Brazil and South Africa, along with China and India, are fellow members of the BRICS bloc with Russia, which is why they have largely avoided taking sides – at least publicly – in the war against Ukraine.
Although US President Donald Trump gained new legislative powers to target Russia’s major oil and gas buyers with tariffs of up to 100% after signing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18, it remains unclear whether he will use them against China. Imposing such tariffs could potentially undermine the trade stability Washington is seeking to preserve with Beijing, despite the fact that cutting out Russia’s oil revenue would prove significantly meaningful to Ukraine.
Zelensky has repeatedly called on Trump to exercise his new rights as Russia increases its strikes on civilian infrastructure across Ukraine.
His latest remarks came only two days after Russian PresidentVladimir Putin revived claims that Russian speakers’ rights were being violated in the Baltic states – the same rhetoric the Kremlin used to justify its invasion of Ukraine.
While Zelensky continues to appeal to countries with significant economic ties to Russia, NATO faces a growing wave of Russian hybrid attacks, with the line between sabotage and direct aggression increasingly blurred.
Meanwhile, Kyiv and Washington continue working jointly on brokering an end to the war.
On Wednesday, 51 countries backed a joint statement at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) urging the Kremlin to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations.
Washington has also invited Putin to the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami in December, with Trump urging him to “settle the war.”
Moscow, however, has shown no sign of backing down. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the Kremlin would not pause its “special military operation” even during negotiations, while Putin blamed Kyiv for stalled diplomacy and has so far rejected every proposal for a direct meeting.
“It has been the same with him for years – and all our partners feel it. He is looking for excuses to keep waging the war,” Zelensky said on Saturday, Sept. 26.
“It always sounds the same – and our recent meeting with the US President showed that.”
