articles.title: Zelensky Hails Gains in Lyman Axis Under Operation ‘Vivaldi’
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces have achieved important battlefield results in the Lyman axis in Donetsk region under Operation “Vivaldi,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday, adding that Ukrainian units have killed or wounded about 10,660 Russian military personnel across the front this week.
In a statement published on Telegram Sept. 27, Zelensky said he had received a report from the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), Mykhailo Drapatyi. He also pointed to results achieved by the Air Assault Forces grouping in another active defense operation, without giving further details.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The destruction of the occupier continues, and the set objectives are being achieved,” Zelensky said, adding that every Russian loss was backed by video confirmation.
Kyiv Post could not independently verify Russian casualty figures.
Fighting remains heaviest in Donetsk region
The Donetsk region is particularly critical because Russian President Vladimir Putin’s military objective is mainly to seize the rest of Donbas, which consists of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
The Kremlin has long demanded full control of the regions as preconditions for any possible settlement.
Ukraine, however, categorically rejects giving up its territory and sovereignty as a prerequisite for peace, although it frequently calls on Russia to agree to an unconditional ceasefire.
According to Zelensky’s latest statement, the currently most intense fighting is taking place in the Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka and Lyman axes, while Ukrainian troops are also carrying out combat operations in the Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv and Sumy regions.
Could Central and Eastern Europe Present Itself as One Economy?
The General Staff of the AFU earlier reported 221 combat clashes along the front, stating that Russian forces had launched 26 attacks in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka axes and 12 in the Lyman axis.
In the Lyman axis, Russian forces reportedly tried to advance toward Novoselivka, Drobysheve, Lyman, Dibrova, Stavky and Chernechshyna.
“Every such week at the front that becomes ours, Ukrainian… prevents Russia from launching greater offensive activity against Ukraine,” Zelensky said while expressing particular gratitude for this week’s results to soldiers of the 3rd Army Corps and the 68th Separate Airmobile Brigade named after Oleksa Dovbush of the 8th Corps of the Air Assault Forces.
Together with Drapatyi, he had agreed on further operational steps.
What Operation ‘Vivaldi’ really is
The 3rd Army Corps, commanded by Brigadier General Andriy Biletsky, publicly announced the operation on Sept. 15 after weeks of strict information silence.
Its stated aims include pushing back Russian forces, dismantling their infiltration tactics and disrupting their supply lines.
In its first phase, the Ukrainian military cleared Russian infiltration pockets around Novoselivka, Yarova, Koroviahyi Yar and Oleksandrivka and liberated the village of Serednie, which Biletsky described as a “shaping, preparatory phase.”
Biletsky has hinted that more is yet to come. “Vivaldi, as everyone knows, has four seasons. This is the first of them,” he said according to Ukrainska Pravda.
On Sept. 20, Ukrainian Defense Forces announced the results of the second phase by saying that they had liberated Shandryholove and Derylove and established full control over Drobysheve. Across both phases, the corps said it had recovered 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) of territory including 50 square kilometers (19 square miles) formally de-occupied.
Russian forces reportedly lost around 800 soldiers in the second phase and more than 3,000 across both phases combined.
Russia eyes new mobilization
The gains near Lyman come as Kyiv warns that Moscow is preparing to replenish its forces with a new wave of mobilization.
In August, Ukrainian intelligence said the Russian General Staff had drawn up plans to mobilize 600,000 people, with 300,000 in 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027.
According to Ukraine’s Presidential Office of Ukraine, Russia lost around 240,000 personnel between January and July, while only 232,000 people signed contracts with the Russian military during the same period.
Meanwhile, Putin has consistently denied that Russia is preparing another mobilization campaign.
Russia last announced a mobilization in September 2022, when Putin ordered a call-up of 300,000 reservists, triggering widespread protests and mass departure of draft-age men from the country.
Earlier on Sunday, Zelensky said Russia launched more than 2,200 drones, about 1,650 guided aerial bombs (KABs) and at least 38 missiles at Ukraine this week.
He also called on China, India and other major non-Western powers – which portray themselves as neutral in the war – to take a stronger stance on Russia and its war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Neptune Missiles Hammer Russian Plant Supplying Missile and Artillery Components
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Neptune Missiles Hammer Russian Plant Supplying Missile and Artillery Components
Ukraine struck the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant in Russia’s Rostov region overnight on September 26, damaging multiple production facilities at an enterprise that manufactures components for Russian missiles, artillery, and anti-tank weapons.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said the strike was carried out by its Alpha Special Operations Center together with the Ukrainian Navy using domestically produced Neptune cruise missiles and Ruta, Palianytsia, and Bars jet-powered drone missiles.
According to the SBU, preliminary assessments showed damage to the plant’s optical and foundry production facilities, an assembly area, an electroplating workshop, and a printed circuit board production facility.
Ukraine’s General Staff separately confirmed the strike on September 26, reporting a fire at the plant’s foundry and damage to equipment in five production buildings.
The Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant is part of Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation, a major state-owned weapons manufacturer. Ukrainian military intelligence lists the facility as a producer of electronic systems used in precision artillery, missile, and anti-tank weapons, as well as radar seekers for tactical guided missiles, thermal imaging equipment, and optoelectronic systems.
The plant has been subject to international sanctions. The European Union lists the facility as part of Tactical Missiles Corporation and has included it in restrictive measures against Russia since June 2022.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also confirmed the attack, saying Ukrainian long-range weapons had struck a plant in the Rostov region supplying Russian forces with components for missiles and artillery, as well as a Pantsir-S2 air defense system.
The Azov facility was one of several Russian military and energy-related targets hit during the overnight operation. Ukrainian forces also struck the Ilsky oil refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar region, while a Russian ammunition depot was targeted in temporarily occupied Sievierodonetsk in Ukraine’s Luhansk region.
Ukraine’s General Staff also reported a strike on a Russian P-18 Terek radar near Semenivske in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region. The mobile two-dimensional radar is used to detect and track aerial targets and provide targeting information to air defense units.

articles.title: Iran insists on Hormuz conditions, Gaza death toll over 74,000
articles.body:
The Israeli Supreme Court ruled on Sunday that the Israeli government is violating a judgment requiring it to let the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) visit Palestinian prisoners.
Breadcrumb
Iran stood firm Sunday on its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, despite US President Donald Trump's rejection of the proposal that had created some optimism for breaking the Mideast war stalemate.
Iran's plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and fulfilling conditions in the ceasefire deal that fell apart months ago.
That agreement, which dissolved during fighting over Hormuz, called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Araghchi said on Sunday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights."
In Gaza, the death toll from Israel's genocidal war on the enclave has surpassed 74,000, Gaza's Health Ministry said.
This includes 1,145 Palestinians killed by Israel since a 'ceasefire' came into force in October 2025.
Syria said on Sunday that its forces had arrested four leaders and several members of an Islamic State group cell that was planning attacks.
Security and intelligence forces "dismantled a cell affiliated with the Daesh (IS) terrorist organisation that was involved in carrying out kidnappings, planting explosive devices, and assassinations", state television reported the internal security forces as saying.
"Four leaders of the cell", the statement said, were arrested in north Syria's Raqa "alongside a number of its members in Aleppo, Idlib and Homs".
Ireland struck three times in the first half to cruise to a 3-0 Nations League victory over Israel on Sunday, after a fraught weekend for the team following goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu’s withdrawal from the squad amid a dispute over whether to play.
A few hundred Israeli supporters and a handful of Irish fans filled the ground, and the shouts of coaches and players could be heard throughout.
The Irish players wore black armbands in memory of all those killed in the conflict and bowed their heads during the Israeli national anthem. They exchanged no pennants or pre-match handshakes.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar accused Ireland of being "on the wrong side of history", after the Irish football team wore black armbands for their game against Israel over the war in Gaza.
Ireland's football association came under intense public pressure to boycott the Nations League match with Israel over the country's conduct of its war against Hamas in Gaza.
On Saturday, the squad held a vote over whether to play the match. They ultimately decided to go ahead, but wearing the black armbands "for all lives lost in the conflict".
In a lengthy post on X, Saar referenced the Irish team of 1939 giving the Nazi salute ahead of a match against Germany in Bremen.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Abu Dhabi and met with UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on Sunday, a senior Israeli official told Reuters.
Netanyahu's office and the UAE's foreign ministry made no immediate comment.
The visit comes after Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported this month that Sheikh Mohamed had warned Netanyahu a week and a half before 7 October 2023 that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel.
The warning was not passed to Israeli intelligence agencies or the military, Haaretz reported.
Saudi airstrikes on Taiz in southwest Yemen caused dozens of casualties in an area controlled by the Houthis, the Iran-backed group said on Sunday, as fighting escalated further after a truce broke down months ago.
The Houthi's military spokesman Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of launching two air raids that hit a market on the outskirts of the city, saying nearly 50 people were killed or wounded without specifying the exact breakdown.
The spokesman said blood was "unjustly and aggressively spilled" in a statement posted online, vowing there would be consequences for the attack.
Israel's foreign ministry said on Sunday that it revoked the diplomatic status of Dutch diplomats at the Netherlands' Representative Office in Ramallah in response to the Dutch government's ban on imports of products originating from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The diplomatic status of the Dutch diplomats would expire in seven days, it said.
Iran-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah said on Sunday it would contribute soon to a project aimed at housing thousands of people displaced due to the war with Israel.
Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem made the announcement during a speech commemorating the second anniversary of leader Hassan Nasrallah's killing by Israel in 2024
"The party (Hezbollah) is committed to providing shelter, restoration, and reconstruction with the available resources and donations. The details of a new housing project for residents of villages that were completely destroyed will be announced very soon," Qassem said
Israel's far-right finance minister Bezalel Smotrich called Sunday for the annexation of parts of south Lebanon and the Gaza Strip and for Israeli forces to "go to war" against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
"I would like us to annex at least as far as the yellow line in Gaza and as far as the Litani River in Lebanon... because if a war ends along the same lines where it began, what will deter the enemy from going to war again," Smotrich said in a podcast for Israeli news site Ynet.
"I think we need to go to war in Judea and Samaria, to dismantle the Palestinian Authority that supports terror," he added, using the biblical term for the West Bank.
Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said on Sunday that Israel had been unable to break his Iran-backed group, at a ceremony marking two years since Israel killed the movement's longtime leader Hassan Nasrallah.
Hezbollah has demonstrated that Israel and its soldiers "were unable to achieve their goals to break the resistance, end its existence, consolidate the Israeli occupation and establish settlements in Lebanon", Qassem said in an address televised at a gathering in Beirut's southern suburbs attended by thousands of the group's supporters.
A top US official on Sunday dismissed a proposal for reopening the Strait of Hormuz presented by Iran as "cynical" and indicated it was a non-starter for Washington.
Iran's truce plan, announced by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi at the United Nations earlier this week, calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade in order for the key waterway central to the world's energy supplies to be opened.
"This was, I think, a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable," US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said on Sunday in an interview with NBC. "To ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions, and access to billions in assets just to talk."
President Donald Trump said on Sunday that the five people arrested on terrorism-related charges in the United Kingdom were aiming to do significant damage to the UK base that houses US troops and aircraft.
"We had them under investigation. They, they were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great," Trump said while on a visit to Chicago. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them."
US President Donald Trump told Axios on Sunday that he expected American negotiators to engage in more talks with Iran this week.
At least seven people were killed and 40 wounded in a strike on a market in Yemen's Taiz, the health ministry in Houthi-controlled areas of the country has said.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Sunday that they seized an American submarine drone in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has blockaded in the months-long Middle East war.
"Through a coordinated, complex operation involving intelligence oversight and electronic warfare, IRGC naval forces' personnel successfully captured an advanced unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) belonging to the terrorist US military," the IRGC naval forces said in a statement, according to state TV.
They added that the drone was "operating in the Strait of Hormuz for espionage purposes", identifying the model as a Remus 600 autonomous underwater vehicle that was "now in the hands of the force's specialists for data recovery".
Police have evacuated homes near a U.S. air base in England and arrested several men over suspected explosives offenses.
The Gloucestershire Police force says “a number of properties” are being evacuated in Whelford, western England. That is close to RAF Fairford, a base used by American forces during the war with Iran.
Police say several men have been detained on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act, and army bomb-disposal experts are examining several vehicles.
Parents across Riyadh received emails from schools on Sunday announcing a last-minute plan to shift to remote learning for a week, according to messages seen by AFP.
"We have just been informed by Saudi authorities that schools must remain closed all week," read two separate messages seen by AFP.
There was no official reason given but the move comes amid heightened tensions in the Gulf and near-daily attacks aimed at Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi fighters in Yemen.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that he had sent envoys around the world to pressure countries to economically isolate Iran, hailing new restrictions targeting the country's airlines and banks.
"At my direction, teams were dispatched across the globe to engage with countries and demand action against the Iranian regime," he said on X. "These efforts are delivering results."
Bessent noted that Turkey and Oman have halted incoming flights from private carrier Mahan Air, while the United Arab Emirates has stopped all flights by Iranian airlines.
Dubai, the UAE's commercial hub, is a major destination for Iran's carriers, with multiple daily flights, a large Iranian community and close business links.
Iran's ISNA news agency, citing officials, reported that five countries had revoked the Islamic republic's flight permits: Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iraq, Oman and the UAE.
But it said flights were still operating to China -- which is refusing to yield to US pressure -- and Russia via the two main airlines, national carrier Iran Air and Mahan.
Mahan had announced that it would no longer serve Turkey at the request of the Turkish authorities, but flights continue several times a day in both directions, via Iran Air or smaller Iranian carriers, according to the Tehran and Istanbul airport websites.
ISNA said Afghanistan, Armenia, Belarus, Malaysia, Pakistan and Tajikistan were still also being served.
Bessent had said on Monday that all Iranian airlines "will be shut down around the world".

articles.title: NATO article 5 is not what you think it is
articles.body:
NATO article 5 is not what you think it is
There are few myths as captivating and durable as that of Article 5 of the 1949 Washington Treaty. Proponents of the myth are convinced that, thanks to this provision, NATO is like Alexandre Dumas’s Three Musketeers, in which an attack against one is an attack against all, and the US would automatically come in full force to the rescue of any of the allies under attack.
It’s debatable and essentially unknowable to what extent that would have worked in the situation of the Cold War, when the US genuinely feared the Soviet/Communist threat, because the bloc was never tested to that extent. But it certainly is utterly false under present conditions and likely future circumstances, and America’s allies and partners need to pay attention and be careful.
The wording of the article itself is deliberately ambiguous. Clearly, there’s no automaticity there in the use of force, and such careful formulation was a condition for the treaty’s ratification by the US Senate because American policymakers at the time abhorred entering into entangling alliances.
So much for the automatic use of US military force.
Later, after the Soviet Union developed intercontinental ballistic missiles in the mid-to-late 1950s, American military strategy sought to avoid a direct nuclear exchange. Nuclear war, if it were to be fought, was to stay limited, confined to Europe, east and west.
So much for the US nuclear umbrella.
During the Cold War, recurrent crises around West Berlin were considered in Washington as a likely casus belli, but West Berlin was formally an occupied territory, rather than an allied country. It was safeguarded by American, British, and French military garrisons, and a move against the city (which was never attempted) would have been an attack on US military personnel. The situation along the German-German, Czechoslovak-West German, or Norway’s and Türkiye’s borders with the Soviet Union, though tense, was invariably stable. Elsewhere, NATO and the Warsaw Pact were separated by wide swaths of neutral territory.
So much for the likelihood of military conflicts which would have triggered Article 5.
The current US National Defense Strategy doesn’t view Russia as a major threat, with the Trump administration busy shifting the focus of US forces to East Asia and the Pacific. President Donald Trump has shifted the burden of NATO’s defense onto the European members themselves. If his performance in the Ukraine conflict is a gauge, he has no wish and no inclination to commit US forces to defending America’s allies and clients. Selling arms to them and sharing intelligence is the limit.
Washington also probably takes seriously Moscow’s warning that a NATO-Russia war would be different from the Ukraine conflict, and that it “would be short.” This logically means, in plain English, that it would be nuclear. Americans who studiously avoided a nuclear war with the Soviet Union when they felt genuinely threatened cannot be expected now to allow themselves to be dragged, on behalf of their European allies, into a nuclear conflict with Russia – still the only country in the world that has the capability to annihilate the US.
In his time, President Joe Biden said the US would defend Taiwan if China tried to achieve national reunification by force, but Trump is far more circumspect. To contain China, as with Russia, his administration pushes its allies to the fore, and the Philippines and Japan are the top candidates. As for Taiwan, after its semiconductor industry is safely relocated to America, the island’s significance for America will greatly diminish.
US security guarantees, though admittedly not Article 5-type, have been exposed as less than hollow in the ongoing US war against Iran. Instead of protecting the Gulf Arab countries, the American bases in the region acted like magnets, drawing Iranian drones and missiles which damaged the host countries’ infrastructure. Those in Eastern and Northern Europe who think they will be better off hosting American (or French, for that matter) nuclear facilities should think again.
Ukraine lost its way and brought untold calamities upon itself when its leaders made NATO membership their goal. They didn’t realize that Washington never intended to give them even a symbolic guarantee of protection. Security in the 21st century world can’t be delegated to foreign powers, it can only rest on one’s own resources and stable relations with neighbors. This is the lesson not just for Ukraine and Europe, but also for the Gulf Arab states and East Asia.

articles.title: Russia ignores German de-escalation calls as strikes kill 2 in Kyiv
articles.body:
Hours after Moscow rejected German calls to ease its escalation toward NATO, Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least two people overnight into Sunday, officials said.
Russia’s top diplomat Saturday brushed off what’s believed to have been the first tete-a-tete with his German counterpart since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The meeting was held during the U.N. General Assembly’s annual gathering of world leaders, as an intensifying aerial war between Russia and Ukraine shows no sign of slowing.
Ties between Russia and Germany have soured in recent weeks, following an attempted drone attack last month at Leipzig airport that Berlin blamed on the Kremlin.
With front-line positions largely unchanged since last year, Moscow has hammered its neighbor with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones in recent months. Meanwhile, Kyiv’s long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries and businesses.
In Kyiv, a man was found dead after a Russian drone hit a non-residential building overnight, according to Ukraine’s emergency service.
Another drone struck a single-story vehicle repair shop, leaving firefighters battling the blaze into early Sunday, the emergency service said.
Russian forces also struck Ukraine’s southern Odesa region, which surrounds the country’s main Black Sea port, multiple times overnight into Sunday, killing one person and injuring two others, according to the head of the local military administration, Oleh Kiper.
In Russian-occupied Ukraine, a strike by Kyiv's forces Sunday killed a civilian woman in Enerhodar, the town housing Europe's largest nuclear plant, according to its Kremlin-installed mayor. Maxim Pukhov said the Ukrainian drones also injured two others.
Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly blamed each other for damaging power lines supplying Enerhodar's Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, which Moscow captured early in the war. The plant is not in service, but needs power to keep cooling systems running and maintain safety.
Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was dismissive after the meeting in New York, which was held at German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul’s request. Lavrov said that Wadephul "simply reiterated his official position condemning Russia.”
"You can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not,” he said.
Wadephul expressed openness to a better relationship but said it required a genuine willingness from Russia’s leadership to end the war in Ukraine, according to a German delegation official.
An overwhelming majority of U.N. member nations have repeatedly condemned Moscow’s invasion.
The Kremlin describes the war a "special military operation” intended to ensure Russia’s security and the rights of Russian speakers.

articles.title: UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war
articles.body:
The Trump administration’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejected Iran’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”.
Echoing comments by Donald Trump on Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks on vessels in the strait of Hormuz.
“They were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on State of the Union. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.”
Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s peace plan, proposed at the recent UN general assembly in New York, arguing that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said.
Trump said the US was “winning tremendously” and had “total control of the Hormuz strait”.
In comments to Axios on Sunday, Trump said he expected more talks with Iran during the upcoming week. “They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make,” the outlet quoted the president as saying. “It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand.”
Earlier, Waltz pointed to the failed US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in Pakistan in June that laid out a 14-point framework agreement for a negotiated peace.
Iran, he said, “immediately violated it by attacking international shipping, in violation of international law, and 146 nations have joined us in condemning Iran for those attacks”.
Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the US and Israel.
“Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.”
Araghchi also appeared on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, saying his country is prepared to resume fighting with the US but has not yet abandoned diplomacy after Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal.
“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed,” Araghchi said. “We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war.
“At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.”
The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said his country was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues – but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.
On CNN, Waltz also addressed recent reports that China had assisted Iran in missile targeting of shipping in the strait of Hormuz and on US military bases in the region.
Waltz did not confirm the leaked intelligence assessments but said Trump had raised the issue with China premier Xi Jinping during the latter’s recent state visit to the US capital Washington DC. Trump had also done so “multiple times” previously, including during his visit to China in May, according to Waltz.
“I think we have seen movement in a positive direction,” Waltz said. “President Trump has made it clear it’s unacceptable.”
Waltz pointed to readouts of the high-level meeting that said the US and China had “agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon”.
“They cannot and should not be tolling, much less attacking, international shipping in an international waterway,” Waltz said. “So I think that was incredibly important to hear from President Xi coming out of the summit.”
Waltz also rejected reporting in the Wall Street Journal that the US would resume bombing Iran after the federal midterm elections in November. He pointed to Trump’s comments that Iran was miscalculating.
“The president is looking to make not just this generation – but the next generation – safer by not allowing what is essentially a terrorist organization in [Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] that is controlling the levers of government and wants to march towards a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said. “We’re not going to let the IRGC have a nuclear weapon, much less hold the world hostage with one.”

articles.title: Another catch in Hormuz
articles.body:
Another catch in Hormuz
IRGC captures second US spy sub in Hormuz, exposing the limits of Washington’s undersea warfare
TEHRAN — In another humiliating blow to the US automated naval warfare doctrine, the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) Navy has intercepted and captured a state-of-the-art American autonomous underwater vehicle in the Strait of Hormuz, further cementing Iran’s control over the world’s most vital energy chokepoint.
The Sunday operation marks the second time in less than a month that an advanced Pentagon spy submersible has fallen intact into the hands of Iranian naval and intelligence units. Crucially, the vessel was neither neutralized nor destroyed; it was methodically tracked, electronically commandeered, and seized as operational war booty—delivering an invaluable intelligence bonanza straight to Iranian military labs.
In an official statement, the IRGC Navy confirmed the captured asset as a REMUS 600, a premier autonomous unmanned submersible manufactured for sensitive expeditionary warfare. The platform is currently in the custody of IRGC technical specialists to decode its onboard encrypted mission computers and extract critical mission logs.
“IRGC Navy forces intercepted an advanced underwater drone belonging to the terrorist US military, which was conducting clandestine espionage operations in the Strait of Hormuz, through a synchronized, multi-layered operation combining tactical intelligence and advanced electronic warfare,” the IRGC said in a statement.
Underscoring Iran’s uncompromising posture, the statement firmly warned: “The IRGC Navy declares that the Strait of Hormuz is closed to hostile entities, and we will take decisive, relentless action against any unauthorized passage or hostile regional movements.”
Developed by American defense contractors, the REMUS 600 is a modular, high-endurance autonomous system tailored for deep-water intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), seabed mapping, naval mine detection and classification, and clandestine environmental data collection.
Engineered to operate at depths reaching 600 meters (roughly 2,000 feet), the vessel relies on sophisticated inertial navigation systems (INS), Doppler Velocity Logs (DVL), acoustic transponders, and GPS fixes upon surfacing. These systems allow the platform to execute complex, long-range missions fully autonomously, devoid of real-time tethering or manual operator intervention. Armed with cutting-edge side-scan imaging sonars, environmental sensors, and multi-channel data-logging architectures, the platform represents the backbone of US clandestine littoral reconnaissance.
The strategic windfall goes far beyond the captured physical hull. The recovery of intact mission hard drives, pre-programmed transit corridors, high-resolution acoustic seabed imaging, search patterns, and firmware configurations provides Iranian specialists with an unfiltered, forensic blueprint of how the US Navy conducts undersea reconnaissance within Iranian territorial and adjacent waters. The treasure trove of data will allow Iranian countermeasures to systematically anticipate and neutralize future hostile uncrewed deployments.
From Dive-LD to REMUS 600
Sunday’s operation directly parallels the IRGC’s historic seizure on September 8 of another flagship American autonomous system: the Dive-LD. Manufactured by California-based defense tech firm Anduril Industries and delivered to the US Navy’s Unmanned Undersea Vehicle Group 1 in 2025, the 2.7-tonne, 5.8-meter Dive-LD was heralded by Washington as the pinnacle of deep-sea endurance, capable of reaching depths of 6,000 meters.
That capture—achieved through an audacious electronic warfare strike that pierced the vehicle’s encrypted command links and brought it safely ashore—unraveled the Pentagon’s narrative of invisible undersea superiority. When US Central Command scrambled an MQ-9 Reaper drone in a desperate bid to locate the stranded asset, Iranian air defense batteries promptly blasted the multi-million-dollar surveillance aircraft out of the sky.
Washington’s frantic attempts to downplay the September 8 capture by alleging mechanical failure or framing the platform as “attritable” were thoroughly ridiculed by regional observers.
The subsequent capture of the REMUS 600 confirms a definitive pattern: far from experiencing accidental drift, the US military’s most secretive autonomous systems are being methodically hunted down and netted by Iranian forces.
The latest capture comes amid the US-Israeli war against Iran launched on February 28, underscoring Tehran’s continued ability to counter advanced US surveillance systems.
Facing formidable Iranian Anti-Access/Area-Denial (A2/AD) envelopes that preclude manned US capital ships from operating safely in the Persian Gulf without catastrophic risk, the Pentagon wagered its strategic deterrence on an uncrewed, three-tiered hybrid architecture spanning aerial drones (UAVs), robotic surface vessels (USVs), and subsurface craft (UUVs). With the consecutive, intact seizures of the Dive-LD and the REMUS 600, alongside the regular downing of high-altitude spy aircraft, Iran has systematically shredded all three layers of Washington’s unmanned warfare concept.
An unbreakable maritime bastion
The capture of the REMUS 600 offers resounding proof that the Islamic Republic’s electronic and asymmetric warfare capabilities have outpaced the Pentagon’s technological hubris. By pulling the veil off Washington’s most secretive undersea assets twice in four weeks, the IRGC Navy has sent an unmistakable signal across the Persian Gulf and beyond: the strategic waters of the Strait of Hormuz belong entirely to regional nations, and every covert imperialist footprint beneath the surface will be severed and seized.
As Washington grapples with the fallout of its failed regional adventurism and dwindling asymmetric options, Iran’s indigenous defense apparatus continues to turn the enemy’s prized hardware into its own intellectual property. The Strait of Hormuz is no longer a permissive playground for American covert aggression, but a fortified bastion where imperial arrogance sinks and Iranian technological mastery reigns supreme.

articles.title: Zelensky: Russia has launched 277 attack drones at Ukraine since yesterday, including 155 jet-powered drones
articles.body:
Zelensky: Russia has launched 277 attack drones at Ukraine since yesterday, including 155 jet-powered drones
According to Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky reported this on Facebook.
“Just today, and in Kyiv alone, Russian jet-powered drones ‘struck’ two kindergartens and two schools, an ordinary residential building, a car repair shop, several warehouses, and communications facilities,” Zelensky noted.
According to him, anywhere else in the world, such a choice of targets would be described with one word: terrorism.
“Russia has no military objectives here whatsoever. This is solely an attempt to break people’s spirits and inflict as much harm as possible on our society. Unfortunately, there have been fatalities… My condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims. Dozens of people have been injured. In total, since yesterday, the Russians have deployed 277 attack drones of various types, 155 of which are jet-powered,” the head of state emphasized.
He also noted that among the damaged facilities is a building used as the residence of the Saudi Arabian ambassador.
In addition, in the Dnipropetrovsk region, a sports school was among the damaged facilities, and in the Sumy region, a regional children’s home was damaged.
“If Russia were truly preparing to take any real steps toward de-escalation, as it claims—particularly to American negotiators—this wave of ‘suicide’ terror would not have occurred. And we must view the situation soberly. Russia knows how to send such encouraging diplomatic signals—the very ones the world wants to hear. It knows how to send such signals to delay the world’s tough response to the war,” the President emphasized.
As Zelensky noted, Lindsey Graham’s important sanctions and tariff bill is currently in the implementation phase in the U.S., and it could bring about significant positive change if fully enforced.
“This law must be implemented, and everyone in the world can see that there are grounds for applying it and that it serves a purpose. We are counting on effective decisions from the international community and on increased pressure from our partners so that Russia sees that its manipulation of diplomatic signals will not allow it to keep buying more time for war and terror. It is important that our other partners in the G7 and G20 also stand firm,” he emphasized.
As Zelensky reported, new sanctions packages are being prepared, specifically targeting financial networks, supply chains for components and equipment used in the production of Russian weapons, and specific companies and individuals primarily involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles.
“The new sanctions are set to take effect as early as October to provide a stronger foundation for changing the situation and pushing Russia toward genuine diplomacy. Thank you to everyone who is helping Ukraine! Thank you to everyone who is working 24/7 to provide additional protection for Ukrainians and our country,” the head of state concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Air Defense Forces shot down 147 drones used by Russian invaders to attack Ukraine beginning on the evening of September 26.

articles.title: Saudi warplanes bomb Yemeni marketplace, killing and wounding civilians
articles.body:
Saudi warplanes bomb Yemeni marketplace, killing and wounding civilians
TEHRAN — Saudi fighter jets bombed a crowded civilian marketplace in southwestern Yemen on Sunday morning. According to preliminary reports, the attack killed at least seven people and wounded at least 43 others. Several children were among the casualties.
It happened at the Mawiyah junction in Taiz province, an area packed with shoppers and stalls. The massacre reflects a sharp escalation by Riyadh.
Military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree confirmed in a statement hours after the attack that a formation of Saudi F-15s left Khamis Mushait air base at 11:00 a.m.
By 11:29, they dropped their payloads on the Economic Corporation Market, the statement read. The jets cleared Taiz airspace eight minutes later, flying north to Al-Jawf province to execute four more bombing runs on the Khabb and Al-Sha'af districts.
The Saudi-backed mercenaries told a different story. They said the strikes targeted a military camp, vehicles, supply lines and weapons depots that Ansarallah had allegedly set up near the junction.
Saudi-backed sources told Reuters a camp had recently appeared near the market. None of those claims could be independently verified.
The strike hit a populated commercial area. Whether a military camp sat nearby or not, civilians bore the cost.
This was no isolated incident. Saudi aircraft hammered Yemeni civilian infrastructure relentlessly over the weekend.
Gen. Saree recorded 27 airstrikes within 24 hours. F-15 and Typhoon jets targeted bridges, roads, and civilian areas across Taiz, Marib, Saada, Amran, Ibb, and Hajjah.
Since the latest escalation began, Saudi forces have launched over 1,059 air and missile strikes.
Washington enables all of it. The United States supplies the intelligence, the logistics, and the targeting data guiding Saudi munitions into Yemeni markets.
Over 100 American military advisers operate inside the kingdom, staffing a joint command designed to counter Sanaa.
Yemen refuses to absorb the blows quietly. Retaliation is already reaching deep into Saudi territory.
Last week, Yemeni air defenses shot down a Saudi “Karayel” armed reconnaissance drone over Hajjah province, according to a statement by Yemen’s Armed Forces. Soon after, Yemeni missile and drone units launched coordinated strikes against a sensitive military target in Riyadh and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
Those long-range weapons bypassed multiple layers of American-supplied air defenses before striking their marks.
The psychological toll inside Saudi Arabia is mounting.
Across Riyadh, private schools abruptly suspended in-person classes from September 27 through October 1. Administrators shifted students to remote learning without offering an official explanation.
Saudi civil defense authorities have been issuing near-daily air raid alerts. Interceptors are firing into the skies over the capital and southern border areas like Abha and Jazan.
Sanaa is bringing the war to its origin. Every bomb dropped on a Taiz market guarantees a reciprocal strike on Saudi military and economic infrastructure.
“The blood that was unjustly and wrongfully shed at the Mawiyah market in Taiz Governorate will have grave consequences for the Saudi perpetrator,” Gen. Saree promised.

articles.title: A new flash point in the Iran war: The narrow strait called the 'Gate of Tears'
articles.body:
A new flash point in the Iran war: The narrow strait called the ‘Gate of Tears’
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Houthi rebels’ seizure of Yemen’s Red Sea coast gives them a strategic grip on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital route for global shipping.
- With the Strait of Hormuz mostly closed by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, Bab el-Mandeb has taken on even greater importance.
- Known as the ‘Gate of Tears’ for the dangers of navigating there, the straight links the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean.
BAB EL-MANDEB, Yemen — To visit Bab el-Mandeb is to understand that old adage about looks being deceiving. For this humble fishing village in Yemen, a tumbledown grouping of barely-there huts nestled between the water and an imposing mountain range, stands sentinel over one of the world’s most vital waterways.
The village shares its name with the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow passageway connecting the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea that’s become another flash point in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
“You hear so much about Bab el-Mandeb, you’d think we would be like New York, with skyscrapers and money,” said Saleh, a 58-year-old resident who, like all people interviewed here, refused to give their full name to avoid reprisals.
“So many ships pass near here. If the Yemeni government knew how to invest in it, we would be rich. We should be bringing in billions of dollars. Instead, look around you,” he said, pausing as his gaze took in the sorry-looking boats haphazardly laid on the beach.
“We have nothing.”
Saleh was interviewed in January, when Bab el-Mandeb was thrust into the power struggle between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, the friendly-but-occasionally-fractious backers of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
That war of wills ended with the Emirates ceding control of Bab el-Mandeb — along with the nearby island of Perim, where the Emirates had built a drone airbase — to Saudi Arabia.
But this month, control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait switched once more, when the Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran, ousted government forces from the waterway in a blitzkrieg in which they seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
The move grants the Houthis a valuable foothold in controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a ribbon of Red Sea — known as the “Gate of Tears” for the dangers involving its navigation — between Yemen’s coast and Djibouti and Eritrea.
About 7% of global energy supplies and around 12% to 15% of all global shipping transit the strait. And in taking Perim Island, which lies in the middle the Red Sea at the strait’s narrowest point (a mere 12½ miles), the Houthis could harass ships with ease.
“We don’t need a drone or a missile,” one Houthi commander bragged in a social media video posted from the island. Instead, he added, all they had to do was place a few artillery units on Perim’s coast and they would be able to strike any ship crossing the strait.
The impact of any movement disruption through Bab el-Mandeb wouldn’t be limited to already skittish energy markets: To enter the Suez Canal’s southern entrance, ships must first transit through Bab el-Mandeb, meaning any trouble in the passageway would force freighters to circumnavigate the African continent — adding anywhere from 12 to 21 days to voyages and spiking fuel costs.
A shipping disaster in 2021 shows how blocking the strait — and thus severing a link to the Mediterranean Sea — could harm global commerce. A container ship in the Suez Canal ran aground and blocked the waterway for six days, delaying the delivery of billions of dollars of goods.
More recently, the Houthis sealed off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in 2023 to coerce Israel into stopping its campaign in Gaza; that pushed the U.S. to attack the Houthis, before the Trump administration agreed to a ceasefire of its own with the group.
These days, the Houthi advance comes at a particularly fraught moment, one in which Bab el-Mandeb has taken on outsize importance. With the Israeli-U.S. war on Iran prompting Tehran to seal the Strait of Hormuz — cutting off the world’s most important energy passageway — Persian Gulf oil powerhouses have been forced to divert crude exports to alternatives, including Bab el-Mandeb.
That’s especially true for Saudi Arabia, which turned to its East-West pipeline and exports through the Red Sea to sidestep the trouble in Hormuz. But it’s also the most vulnerable to the Houthi threat.
The Houthis have a long-running animus against the Saudis, which began in 2015, months after the Houthis overran the Yemeni capital of Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia, spooked about the notion of an Iranian ally on its border, led a coalition — with U.S. backing — to dislodge them. It started a blockade and a devastating air campaign that persisted until a 2022 truce.
But in July, the ceasefire broke after the Houthis accused the Saudis of striking Sanaa‘s airport in what appeared to be an attempt to stop Iranian flights from landing there. The Houthis began attacking Saudi Arabian oil infrastructure and declared a naval blockade against the kingdom.
The rebels’ land grab this month stunned Saudi Arabia, which failed to launch airstrikes and stanch the rout of its allied forces from the coast. Saudi leaders reportedly reached out to President Trump to push the rebels back, but he appears disinclined to help.
Still, on Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, “We have a very strong defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, and we will live up to our commitments in that agreement.” He did not elaborate on what U.S. support that would entail.
On Thursday, Saudi Arabia said its defenses intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif, a manufacturing center, and Yanbu, a port on the Red Sea. It responded with hundreds of strikes on the Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen.
For their part, the Houthis insist they have no plans to attack shipping on the Red Sea and that their blockade applies only to Saudi Arabia — a move calculated to prevent the rise of an international effort to dislodge them.
“They don’t want to attract international military operations,” said Mohammad al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory.
“They realize that when you do things in the Red Sea, you create panic in the world.”
But leaders in the internationally recognized Yemeni government say the Houthis are not to be trusted.
“The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” Yemeni Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer said at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.
He added that protecting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is the responsibility of “every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation.”
Using tribal power and rigorous detective work, a family of an army officer in Yemen tries to find out how he was abducted in broad daylight, and what happened to him afterward.
In the meantime, the Houthis have been consolidating their gains on Yemen’s coast, Basha said, setting up checkpoints and bringing loyalists to administer the regions now under their control.
In taking the coastal areas around Bab el-Mandeb village, they reap the benefit of Emirati investment, manifested in kilometers of paved highways that stand in stark contrast to much of Yemen’s road network. They also gain control of several airbases in the area, most crucially on Perim, where the Emirates spent years ferrying construction supplies to build out a roughly 6,000-foot runway along with three hangars.
Although such a runway could not be used by larger bombers, it still can accommodate attack and surveillance aircraft. Another area of the island, which lies roughly two miles off of Yemen’s coast, has what appears to be a helicopter landing area.
The U.S.-Israel campaign against Iran was billed as the final blow to Tehran’s ‘Axis of Resistance,’ but the alliance though bloodied is unexpectedly resilient.
One resident in Bab el-Mandeb village said much of that construction was done by the Emirates, whose contractors would ferry Southeast Asian construction workers to the island and provide them with food. It also built roughly 100 structures for Perim’s residents.
Government forces have since overcome their initial disarray and stopped further Houthi advances. But Basha warned any attempt to push out the Houthis from the coast will be difficult, especially with the group’s advances in manufacturing and fielding drones and ballistic missiles, not to mention the divisions and competing loyalties plaguing Yemeni government forces.
“It’s an uphill battle,” he said.
“You have a divided command-and-control; a divided Yemen; a divided society; a divided geography; and these divisions empower the Houthis.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Moscow terrorising Ukrainians as fresh strikes kill eight
articles.body:
- 
  As Russian drones struck Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was showing no signs of de-escalating the war despite assurances to the US that it would. In a statement on X, Zelenskyy accused Russia of terrorising Ukrainians with its latest attacks, which he said included setting on fire a market outside Kyiv, and striking kindergartens, schools, homes and communications facilities. “Anywhere in the world, this choice of targets would be called by one word – terrorism. Russia has no military objective whatsoever in doing this – it is purely an attempt to break people and inflict as much harm as possible on our society,” Zelenskyy said. “If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps toward de-escalation – as it claims, particularly to American negotiators – this wave of … terror would not be happening,” he said, calling on the US to fully implement the Lindsey Graham Act, which enables sweeping sanctions on Russia aimed at pressing it into ending the war.
- 
  Zelenskyy’s comments came ahead of the conclusion of the UN general assembly in New York on Monday. On the weekend, the foreign ministers of Russia and Germany met in New York on the sidelines of the assembly to discuss the war but Russia’s top diplomat dismissed Germany’s calls to ease off its “dangerous path of escalation” towards Europe. Zelenskyy said on X that Ukraine was relying on “effective decisions” being made by other countries and stronger pressure from its partners in the G7 and G20, “so that Russia sees that manipulating diplomatic signals will not allow it to keep winning more and more time for war and terror”.
- 
  New sanctions packages targeting financial networks, supply chains and companies and individuals helping produce Russian weapons “must take effect as early as October” Zelenskyy said also, to provide a stronger foundation for changing the situation and “pushing Russia toward real diplomacy”.
- 
  Russian strikes killed eight people across Ukraine on Sunday, according to authorities while Zelenskyy said Russia had fired about 3,900 drones, aerial bombs and other missiles at Ukraine over the past week. Ukrainian prosecutors said a drone attack hit a market in Sofiiska Borshchahivka on the western outskirts of Kyiv, killing two and injuring about 10 people. Others died in strikes in different regions and Kyiv also came under attack, local officials said. In the capital, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said nine people were injured, including a child.
- 
  Russia hit also the headquarters of Kyivstar, Ukraine’s largest mobile service provider on Sunday, the company told local media, as Moscow continued a bombardment of Ukrainian datacentres and communications infrastructure. Kyivstar told Interfax Ukraine news agency that its head office in Kyiv had been hit, but there were no casualties.
- 
  Peter Beaumont and Artem Mazhulin have reported on the dire living conditions inside Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson. Life in the city – once home to 24,000 people but now with only 2,000 remaining – has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there.
- 
  South Korea has demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of disclosing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea and then falsely denying that the two sides had agreed to keep the move confidential, according to a report from Reuters. “The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement,” Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement on Sunday. According to the statement, President Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer in his address to the UN general assembly. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

articles.title: British drone-killer startup heads to Japan with cheap interceptors
articles.body:
- Britain's Cambridge Aerospace plans to produce low-cost drone interceptor missiles in Japan and offer them to Japan's Ministry of Defense.
- Each round would cost several million yen, and the company already supplies its Skyhammer interceptor to British forces.
British startup Cambridge Aerospace plans to build its low-cost drone interceptor missiles in Japan and offer them to Japan’s Ministry of Defense, with each round priced at several million yen, or tens of thousands of dollars, the Nikkei business daily reported.
The company’s interceptors cost tens of times less than conventional air defense missiles, and it already has a contract with the British military, the newspaper said. Cambridge Aerospace plans to set up production in Japan before pitching the weapon to the ministry.
The company’s first missile, Skyhammer, is built to shoot down Shahed-type attack drones and slower cruise missiles. It has a range of more than 30 km (19 miles) and a top speed of 700 km/h (435 mph). Cambridge Aerospace has said it uses an X-band radar seeker, and The Register reported that it carries a blast-fragmentation warhead that detonates near its target. The company began developing Skyhammer in January 2025 and flew it within six weeks.
A Skyhammer prototype that crashed and washed up on a British beach in August, and was collected by the company after Reddit users identified it, appeared to be built largely from off-the-shelf parts, according to UAV engineer Chris Wheat, who analyzed photos of the wreckage and called his conclusions educated guesses. He said it seemed to be powered by a JetCat P250-Pro, a commercially sold small jet turbine costing about 4,000 euros ($4,560), and built around two aluminum box-section spars inside a 3D-printed outer shell whose material he put at about £150 ($203). Wheat estimated the airframe at roughly 1.5 m (4.9 feet) long with a similar wingspan, and said he could not find hardware for the radar seeker, suggesting it may not have been fitted to that prototype.
British Defence Secretary John Healey announced on April 10, 2026, that the Ministry of Defence would buy a “significant number” of Skyhammer interceptors and launchers for British forces and Gulf partners facing Iranian-designed drones, with deliveries starting in May. In July, the company won an award under the five-nation LEAP program, and in August it raised $300 million at a $3.4 billion valuation.
Cambridge Aerospace was founded in 2024 by Steven Barrett, a former MIT aeronautics professor who now holds the Regius Professorship of Engineering at the University of Cambridge, and Chris Sylvan, who previously led business in Europe, the Middle East and Africa for U.S. defense company Anduril Industries. Former British Defence Secretary Grant Shapps chairs the company. It has also shown a second interceptor, Starhammer, and builds solid rocket motors in Britain.
Its Nightstar rocket motor is one of seven finalists in the low-cost solid rocket motor category of the U.S. Army’s xTech|Apex Intercept competition, which is looking for cheaper interceptors to work alongside the Patriot air defense system. Finalists will demonstrate their technology in October and November.

articles.title: Berlin’s ‘Russian House’ stayed open despite Russia’s war in Ukraine and EU sanctions, shielded by a reciprocal deal over Moscow’s Goethe-Institut. Germany’s sabotage accusation was the final straw.
articles.body:
Berlin’s ‘Russian House’ stayed open despite Russia’s war in Ukraine and EU sanctions, shielded by a reciprocal deal over Moscow’s Goethe-Institut. Germany’s sabotage accusation was the final straw.
In early September, Germany’s Foreign Ministry announced the closure of the Russian House in Berlin, Russia’s largest cultural center abroad. The center had operated in the heart of the German capital for more than 40 years. It remained open after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, even as similar institutions across Europe shut down. What finally brought it to an end was a drone attack on Leipzig Airport that German authorities described as Russian sabotage. Meduza tells the center’s story.
In early August, a DHL cargo plane approaching Leipzig Airport had to climb sharply when the airport unexpectedly closed. After the plane landed in Hanover, inspectors found minor damage caused by a collision with an unidentified flying object.
At Leipzig Airport, bomb disposal experts found and defused a drone fitted with explosives and a detonator near a Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane. Ten days later, another drone bearing traces of explosives was found near the airport.
German authorities investigated for nearly a month before blaming Russia for the attempted sabotage. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced Germany’s response: the closure of Russia’s consulate in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova criticized the decision. Speaking about the Russian House, she said:
The Russian House was obviously a thorn in their side. Why?.. Its first and foremost purpose is to teach Russian. Demand was enormous. […] That’s the Russian House’s main offense — the reason the German establishment disliked it so much.
There are more than 70 Russian Houses worldwide. The full-scale war has disrupted their work.
The worldwide network of Russian Houses took its present form in 2008, when President Dmitry Medvedev signed a decree creating Rossotrudnichestvo, a Russian federal agency for cultural outreach abroad. Officially overseen by the Foreign Ministry, the agency runs Russian language courses and promotes Russian culture, science, and education.
Before the war, Russian Houses operated in at least 77 countries. Their work became more difficult after the EU imposed sanctions on Rossotrudnichestvo following the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In July 2022, the EU added the agency to its sanctions list, accusing it of promoting the ideas of the “Russian World,” funding propaganda projects, and spreading “Kremlin narratives” and historical revisionism.
After the EU’s decision, Russian Houses suspended operations in six European countries: Slovenia, Slovakia, Croatia, North Macedonia, Montenegro, and Romania. The Russian House in Baku also suspended operations in 2025 after a passenger plane crashed near Aktau. In July 2026, the Russian House in Chișinău closed indefinitely. Moldovan authorities called it a “tool of the Kremlin’s hybrid influence.”
In Berlin, however, the Russian House kept operating after the sanctions against Rossotrudnichestvo. Its seven-story modernist building on Friedrichstraße, within walking distance of the Russian embassy, opened in 1984 as the House of Soviet Culture and Science. It was the Soviet Union’s largest cultural center abroad. Russia later took ownership of the building, and the center became the Russian House of Culture and Science.
The Russian House’s activities changed little over more than 40 years. At its 20th anniversary celebration in 2004, then-director Anatoly Bogushevsky said the center drew about 300,000 visitors a year. Its main aim, he said, was to give people in Germany “as comprehensive a picture as possible of a new, reformed Russia seeking to strengthen democracy.” Its activities centered on a Russian language center, a Russian college, a Pushkin Library with more than 40,000 books, small clubs and workshops, concerts, and film screenings.
Decades later, the 29,000-square-meter building, which occupies an entire Berlin block, still housed children’s clubs and workshops — some free, others paid — as well as a movie theater, concert halls, and exhibition spaces. Rossotrudnichestvo says more than three million people attended events there over the past 15 years. Some events, however, were difficult to describe as purely cultural. After 2022, the theater sometimes screened RT material that called Ukrainians Nazis, and the center held photo exhibitions on similar themes.
Two agreements signed in 2011 and 2013 governed the Russian House’s operations. The first established its status as a cultural and information center; the second gave Russia the right to lease the building for 99 years. Throughout that period, Germany paid about 70,000 euros a year in property tax on the land beneath it. In return, Germany received the right to lease the Goethe-Institut building on Baumanskaya Street in Moscow on the same terms.
Berlin long resisted politicians’ calls to close the Russian House because terminating those agreements could put the Goethe-Institut in Russia at risk.
Even so, sanctions severely hampered the Russian House’s work. All its assets in the EU were frozen, and it could use its bank account only under Bundesbank supervision. Its ability to receive money was tightly restricted: EU legal entities were barred from providing it with funds or economic resources, directly or indirectly, while it could accept only enough from third parties to maintain the building.
The Russian House nevertheless continued collecting rent on apartments and offices in the building. Tagesschau.de found that 115 people lived there in June 2023. In 2018, for example, the Russian House earned about $2 million from rent. Meduza asked Rossotrudnichestvo what would happen to the apartment residents after the closure but had received no response by publication.
The Russian House has drawn espionage allegations
Once the invasion of Ukraine began, German authorities increasingly suspected that the building could be used for spying and to skirt sanctions. In January 2023, Berlin prosecutors launched a probe into possible violations of the country’s foreign trade law. It led nowhere. Prosecutors closed the investigation after Germany froze the Russian House’s accounts, and Moscow hit back by freezing the Goethe-Institut’s accounts there.
The allegations gained renewed attention in the summer of 2026, when German outlets Süddeutsche Zeitung and WDR reported on a French Interior Ministry document. According to the document, Russian intelligence services use the Russian House as a front, and the center’s mission is to influence the diaspora to support Moscow’s policies.
Green Party Bundestag member Robin Wagener called the allegations plausible, saying, “The center’s activities are not limited to harmless language courses.” Christian Democratic Union lawmaker Roderich Kiesewetter called it a “disinformation center” and an extension of the Kremlin. An investigation by CORRECTIV also found that the organization running the Russian House maintains a branch in Dresden called the German-Russian Cultural Institute.
In August 2026, Green Party Bundestag member Sara Nanni, who works on defense issues, pointed to unusual mobile phone and GPS “signal activity” near the building. She said it could indicate that powerful equipment for intercepting signals or communicating covertly was operating inside. Kiesewetter also said that although 100 people lived in the complex, the building used a disproportionate amount of electricity. He and Free Democratic Party member of the European Parliament Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann said the building might serve as a hub for technical intelligence gathering and the coordination of cyberattacks.
Many of the building’s business tenants, however, had no connection to Rossotrudnichestvo. They included the Samowar Hof restaurant and Mnogo Knig, one of Berlin’s few Russian-language bookstores. Businesses there may also have faced pressure from Russian authorities. Journalist Ilya Barabanov said that in 2024, a complaint from Rossotrudnichestvo led the bookstore to remove his book “Nash biznes — smert” (“Our Business Is Death”), about the Wagner private military company, from sale. Meduza published the book.
Hi, I’m N.
I report for Meduza from inside Russia. I could go to prison for my work. To stay safe, I have to follow strict security protocols. I know my lawyer’s phone number by heart. And, of course, my articles are published anonymously.
Working for an independent news outlet while still living in Russia feels like something out of a spy film. My friends know me by one name. My colleagues and sources know me by another. But sometimes there’s a glitch. At a close friend’s birthday party, someone I don’t know reaches out to shake my hand. “Hi, I’m Lyosha.” It takes me a few seconds to decide how to introduce myself. Do I use my real name or my pseudonym? I’m trying to figure out whether this is someone I might one day end up writing about.
What I do is journalism in exile, even though I’m not in exile myself. I have the rare opportunity to do uncensored, on-the-ground reporting in Russia. Please support Meduza so I can continue this work.
The closure led to deportations and cost dozens of people their jobs
Staff assigned from Russia to the Russian House and Rossotrudnichestvo were ordered to leave Germany within seven days. On September 10, they arrived in Belarus along with diplomats from the closed consulate in Bonn. According to Ekho, only about seven Russian House employees were specialists assigned from Russia; they were the ones who had to leave Germany. The rest had been hired locally, and some were German citizens.
Sabine Gimaeva, who owns the Samowar Hof café that opened in the Russian House more than a decade ago, told Meduza that many cultural and educational projects stopped almost immediately after Germany’s Foreign Ministry announced the closure. Commercial tenants were given until December to leave. Gimaeva said the closure would affect more than Russians:
People of all different nationalities come here, with all kinds of passports — including a lot of Ukrainians. […] So to me, this is about much more than just our café closing. A whole network of services that very different people have used for years is disappearing from one building all at once.
In Gimaeva’s view, the German authorities’ decision hurts “ordinary workers and private businesses” rather than Russian state institutions. Businesses may struggle to relocate on short notice, she said, and some may close, costing people their jobs:
People who have worked and supported themselves for years may now end up relying on German welfare. I feel like very few people are talking about those consequences right now.
The Russian House closed just before the September 20 election to Berlin’s state parliament, and the decision quickly became a campaign issue. Even before the closure was announced, Social Democratic mayoral candidate Steffen Krach stood outside the building with a sign reading, “Here’s something we can expropriate, friends in the Left Party! Are you with us?” He did not clearly state his position on the Russian House’s status; his gesture appeared to invoke the Left Party’s plans to nationalize housing. Krach did not respond to Meduza’s request for comment.
On September 4, after the foreign minister’s official announcement, two protests took place outside the Russian House — one supporting the closure and one opposing it. Reforum Space Berlin, a space for antiwar Russians created by the Free Russia Foundation, helped organize the protest in favor. Its coordinator, Yulia Abdullaeva, who has lived in Berlin since 2011, told Meduza that alternatives to the Russian House already exist in the city:
The question isn’t whether individual classes held there were good or bad. It’s whether the Russian state should still have a venue of its own in central Berlin today, using culture as a tool of its foreign policy and propaganda. […] All the community activities people genuinely need — Russian lessons for children, cultural events, a library, films, educational programs — can exist (and already do!) in independent organizations, without Russian state control.
Supporters of keeping the Russian House open held their own protest that day. One organizer was the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, a party that advocates better relations with Russia. Alexander King, co-chair of its Berlin branch, told Meduza that closing the Russian House and the Bonn consulate amounted to “far-reaching measures that could bring us closer to a possible military conflict.” In the September 20 election, the party failed to clear the 5% threshold for seats in parliament.
Samowar Hof owner Sabine Gimaeva also attended the protest in support of the Russian House. “To me, that’s a perfectly normal way to stand up for what matters to me — if a decision directly affects my family, our business, the people who work here, and cultural projects that have been here for years, of course I’m not going to pretend it doesn’t concern me,” she said.
Die Welt estimated that several hundred people attended the protest against the closure. Deutsche Welle gave more precise figures: about 250 people attended the rally supporting the closure, and about 500 opposed it. Reforum Space Berlin coordinator Olga Galkina, however, told Ekho that the two sides were roughly equal in number. In her view, those who wanted to keep the center included ethnic German immigrants known as “late resettlers” and Putinverstehers, or Putin sympathizers. Abdullaeva made a similar distinction:
I wouldn’t apply the label ‘Putinverstehers’ to everyone who went to the Russian House. It was mainly about the politics of defending the Russian House. For many people, it really was, above all, a place where they could hear Russian, go to a concert, or take their child to a class. I used to go there fairly often myself, but since the full-scale war began, I haven’t gone back — because the war changed what this institution means to me.
The Left Party, which won the Berlin election, had not publicly commented on the Russian House’s closure during the campaign. Earlier, however, the party’s deputy federal chair, Maximilian Schirmer, had called the center “a propaganda institution.”
The parties that finished second and third — the Christian Democratic Union and Alternative for Germany, respectively — differed in their positions. The Christian Democrats, Berlin’s current governing party, had consistently called for the Russian House to close. Alternative for Germany had not stated a position directly, though its Bundestag member Karsten Hilse attended the protest in support of the center.
As the Russian House closed, Rossotrudnichestvo announced plans to expand the network. On September 8, agency head Igor Chaika signed agreements to open 11 new Russian Houses in Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, Senegal, Mali, Sierra Leone, São Tomé and Príncipe, Togo, Madagascar, Armenia, and Thailand. The agency’s deputy head also said a new Russian House in Germany “will definitely open” and that the search for new partners was already underway.

articles.title: Ukraine hits five workshops at a Russian military plant in Rostov Oblast – OSINT
articles.body:
Ukraine hits five workshops at a Russian military plant in Rostov Oblast – OSINT
At least five workshops have been damaged following an attack by the Ukrainian defence forces on the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant military facility in the Rostov Oblast in Russia.
Source: Absolutely Reliable Source OSINT project on Telegram
Details: Damaged buildings at the plant are used at various stages of production for components supplied to Russian weaponry. In particular, strikes were recorded at foundry workshop No. 022, which consists of two buildings.
Quote: "The lower building (the main one for the foundry workshop) experienced burning and significant damage in both its right section and its eastern side. The upper building was also affected, but only a portion of the roof and wall was torn down."
At workshop No. 008, which handles optics manufacturing, analysts recorded two strikes on the southwestern side along with a crumbling façade.
At least three strikes were registered at assembly workshop No. 009, with another hit recorded at electroplating workshop No. 010.
According to information from the Absolutely Reliable Source project, two more strikes were recorded at the machining workshop, one of which caused a roof collapse. In the images published by the analysts, it is located on the right.
Quote: "To its left is the frame-stamping workshop, next to which lies debris – a wall hit is likely there as well."
Details: Ukrainian defence forces attacked the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant on the night of 25-26 September. The strike was carried out by units of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Ukrainian Navy using Ukrainian Neptune cruise missiles, as well as Ruta, Palianytsia and Bars jet-powered drone missiles. Military officials previously reported damage to optical and foundry production facilities, an assembly section, an electroplating workshop and a printed circuit board manufacturing workshop.
For reference: The Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant is part of the Russian Tactical Missiles Corporation. The company manufactures electronic systems for high-precision artillery, missile and anti-tank weapons, radar homing heads for tactical guided missiles, on-board thermal imaging and thermal imaging equipment, as well as optical-mechanical and optoelectronic products, according to the "War&Sanctions" website by Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
The plant in Rostov Oblast is currently under sanctions imposed by the US, Canada, Switzerland, the EU, New Zealand, Japan and Ukraine.
Background:
- Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that on 25 September, Ukraine's defence forces struck three facilities in Russia's Ulyanovsk, Tula and Voronezh oblasts.
- Ukrainian forces also damaged five launch units for Shahed drones near Tsimbulova in Russia's Oryol Oblast.
