articles.title: Russian attacks kill eight in Ukraine after Moscow vows to continue war
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill eight in Ukraine after Moscow vows to continue war
Russian strikes killed eight people across Ukraine on Sunday, authorities said, a day after Moscow vowed to continue the war. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had launched about 3,900 drones, aerial bombs and missiles over the past week. Ukraine accused Moscow of deliberately targeting civilians as winter approaches.
Russian strikes killed eight people across Ukraine on Sunday, a day after Moscow vowed to pursue the war, authorities said Sunday.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia had fired about 3,900 drones, aerial bombs and other missiles at Ukraine over the past week.
Russia has stepped up attacks on Kyiv, with Ukraine charging that Moscow is deliberately hitting civilian targets as the country braces for another tough winter.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi announced that Russian strikes hit a children's centre in the northern city of Sumy, killing three people including a 16-year-old girl.
Zelensky said three people had been killed in night-time strikes on the southern Zaporizhzhia region and a Russian drone strike had killed one man in Kyiv.
Authorities in the Odesa region said a "massive strike" on the south of the Black Sea region had killed one more person.
Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitchko said a woman and two 16-year-olds had been wounded and hospitalised in the capital.
"The enemy continues to relentlessly attack the Kyiv region with strike drones," the city's administration said.
"Sixteen sites have been damaged," including 12 houses, a warehouse and production facility, it added.
Russian strikes in the Odesa region damaged housing, a shop, a hotel, a medical building and a grain warehouse, said regional head Oleg Kiper.
Read morePoland fears Ukraine war could spill over
Targeting 'civilian infrastructure'
"This past week, the Russians launched more than 2,200 attack drones against Ukraine, as well as around 1,650 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types, a significant number of them ballistic missiles," Zelensky posted on social media.
The latest strikes had targeted two kindergartens, two schools, housing "and other civilian infrastructure" in various parts of the country, he added.
"If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps toward de-escalation -- as it claims, particularly to American negotiators -- this wave of "shahed" terror would not be happening," Zelensky said in later comments.
In Moscow, Russia's defence ministry said it had bombed a Kyivstar data centre in Kyiv and another belonging to the Omega Telecom company, claiming that the firms were providing services to the Ukrainian army.
It also released an image of a drone bearing the ironic message "Digital Detox", confirming that the strikes were aimed at disrupting internet access in Ukraine.
On Saturday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov told the UN General Assembly his country intended to continue its military campaign "to the end".
Russia denies that it aims at civilian targets.
The defence ministry also said that Russian forces had seized the border village of Khrypuny in Ukraine's eastern Kharkiv region, where Russia controls pockets of land.
Russia does not claim the Kharkiv region as its own -- unlike the Donetsk, Lugansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson region. Throughout the war however, it has attacked the region and seized land there.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said it intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.
US-led talks to end the war have failed to produce a breakthrough and the UN has highlighted the growing civilian toll as the two sides become more entrenched.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Ukraine’s jet-drone kill rate just hit 55%. Russia’s answer: $12 billion to make more of them
articles.body:
Ukraine's defense forces intercepted 55% of Russia's jet-propelled drones in September—more than 1,500 out of over 2,730 launched—Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his 26 September evening address.
Russia's full-scale aerial campaign has shifted from propeller-driven Shaheds Ukraine learned to shoot down at over 90% to jet-propelled models that fly faster, resist jamming, and often slip past existing defenses.
55% and climbing
Zelenskyy said military intelligence had briefed him on Russian weapons production—not just jet Shaheds but other technological systems. The documents detail what Moscow is preparing for next year: the volumes and the financing. "We are preparing our countermeasures, and for every line item there must be a Ukrainian answer," he said.
Several effective interceptor prototypes are already in combat.
"Interceptors have been identified that can become the main tool of our defense. Production, components—all of this we are scaling up. There will be an answer," Zelenskyy said.
The goal is to match the interception rate for regular propeller-driven Shaheds, which exceeds 90%. At 55%, the jet-drone rate is climbing but still leaves nearly half reaching their targets.
$12 billion for one category
Russia plans to spend $12 billion in 2027 on jet drones and loitering munitions alone, Zelenskyy said. "This concerns not only Ukraine and not only us," he added, warning that multiple intelligence agencies have information Russia wants to expand its war to other countries and regions.
He said this is why Ukraine is pushing for stronger sanctions and the Drone Deal format. Ukraine has signed 11 such agreements, the latest with Finland at the UN General Assembly this week, and is preparing a 12th with what Zelenskyy called "a strong country."
The warning came as Russia struck a Kyiv data center twice on the morning of 27 September, injuring three people including two children, Zelenskyy wrote. Overnight strikes killed three people in Zaporizhzhia Oblast and one man in Kyiv.
In total this week, Russia launched more than 2,200 strike drones, roughly 1,650 aerial bombs, and 38 missiles—a significant share of them ballistic—at Ukraine, he said.
A $50 computer just flew Russia’s newest jet drone into a Ukrainian grain ship—and jamming couldn’t stop it
Jet drones are now Russia's main aerial weapon
Russia's jet-propelled Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones have become the dominant threat in Russia's aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities. By August, production of jet Geran-4/5 models exceeded that of propeller-driven Geran-2s, according to Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR). Russian factories produce roughly 3,000 jet models per month alongside about 2,800 of the older type. The Geran-5 is technically a drone but functions as a small cruise missile—faster, harder to jam, and increasingly guided by AI and mesh networking that complicate interception.
Ukraine's answer has been interceptor drones—cheap, fast enough to chase a Geran, and guided by machine vision. A Ukrainian interceptor recently scored its first kills against jet Gerans and is heading into mass production, though a presidential adviser warned that speed alone cannot catch them—machine vision and automatic guidance decide the chase.

articles.title: Satellite Imagery: Strike Damaged Five Workshops at Plant Involved in Kh-101 and Oreshnik Production
articles.body:
Satellite imagery shows damage to the Azov Optical and Mechanical Plant (AOMZ), which is involved in the production of Kh-101, Kh-35U, and Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles, as well as Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missiles.
The Absolutely Reliable Source Telegram channel published the satellite imagery.
Judging by the imagery, six buildings were hit. According to the channel, they house five production workshops.
Workshop 022, a foundry comprising two buildings, was hit. A fire and significant damage were recorded at the site.
Workshop 024, the machining workshop, also sustained significant damage, with part of its roof collapsing.
In addition, workshop 008, which produces optics; workshop 009, an assembly workshop; and workshop 010, an electroplating workshop, were damaged.
The Ukrainian Navy and the SSU’s Special Operations Center Alpha launched the strike on the night of September 26.
The attack involved Ukrainian Neptune cruise missiles as well as RUTA, Palianytsia, and Bars jet-powered drones.
The Azov Optical and Mechanical Plant joint-stock company is part of Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation and is one of its key optoelectronic production facilities.
The plant produces, among other things, radar and infrared seekers for guided missiles, thermal imaging devices, and electronic systems for precision-guided artillery.
The plant also supplies components for anti-tank weapons production, weapon stabilization systems for armored vehicles, navigation and laser equipment for aircraft and UAVs, and electronic warfare systems.
The enterprise also manufactures optomechanical and optoelectronic products and equipment for Russia’s aerospace industry.
Following a document leak, researchers found that AOMZ is involved in producing Kh-31P anti-radiation missiles, short-range R-74 and long-range R-37M air-to-air missiles, Kh-101 and Kh-35U cruise missiles, Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles, and Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missiles.
Open-source information also indicates that the enterprise is involved in producing KAB-250, KAB-500, and KAB-1500 guided aerial bombs and the Kh-38ML short-range air-to-surface missile.

articles.title: Swiss voters crush neutrality initiative that would have ended sanctions against Russia—70% say No
articles.body:
Swiss voters overwhelmingly rejected a neutrality initiative that would have banned Switzerland from adopting sanctions against warring states and blocked cooperation with NATO, Swiss public broadcaster SRF reported. The measure failed by 70.2% to 29.8%, with zero cantons voting in favor.
Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine has expanded beyond the battlefield into a campaign of sabotage, political influence, and pressure on European institutions. Every European country that has adopted sanctions or cooperated militarily with Ukraine faces some variant of the same push—to weaken the sanctions regime and fracture the coalition. Russia expressed sympathy for the initiative—which backfired. Opponents warned the measure would benefit Moscow.
What the initiative would have done
The initiative, formally titled "Safeguard Swiss Neutrality," sought to enshrine neutrality as "permanent, armed, and comprehensive," bar cooperation with military alliances unless Switzerland was under direct attack, and ban economic sanctions against warring states—with only UN-mandated measures exempted.
Switzerland currently adopts sanctions autonomously and has largely followed EU sanctions against Russia since the full-scale invasion in 2022. The Swiss government's own explanatory materials stated the initiative would affect sanctions against Russia, SRF reported.
Blocher's Russian connection
Former Federal Council member Christoph Blocher, 85, launched the initiative in autumn 2022—six months into the full-scale war and the same year his daughter Magdalena Martullo-Blocher, who controls Ems-Chemie, decided the two Russian plants would stay. He led the campaign through the organization Pro Schweiz.
Ems-Chemie produces plastics, adhesives, sealants, and technical fibers. Two subsidiaries, operating under the Eftec brand, continued working in Russia after the full-scale invasion, Swiss magazine Republik reported earlier this month. Company and government documents contain strong indications that Eftec products may have been purchased by KamAZ, UAZ, GAZ, and AvtoVAZ—sanctioned companies tied to military vehicle production and financial support for Russian soldiers deploying to Ukraine. Ems-Chemie denies supplying them.
The Federal Council and Parliament both recommended rejection. In the National Council, 124 members voted against and 65 in favor. In the Council of States, the vote was 29 to 10 against.
Politico: Fico is first in line for Orbán’s disruptor crown — but Brussels has four more leaders to worry about
Drones over Swiss military bases
Unidentified drones were spotted over Swiss military installations this year. In about 20% of sightings over military sites, authorities cannot identify who is responsible, army chief Benedikt Roos said earlier this month. Asked whether Switzerland is a target for Moscow, he said yes—the country holds critical infrastructure vital to Europe that anyone seeking to destabilize the continent could target.
Across Europe, pro-Russian forces continue to push back against sanctions. Germany's far-right AfD won 43.8% in the Saxony-Anhalt state election on 6 September—its strongest result ever, though every other party refuses coalition. In France, Marine Le Pen leads first-round polling for the 2027 presidential election at 36%. Slovakia's Robert Fico earlier demanded the EU lift Russian energy sanctions.
Russia has combined kinetic and political pressure across Europe—drone incursions into NATO airspace, arson at defense-linked sites, and sabotage of critical infrastructure—alongside support for political forces that oppose sanctions and military cooperation with Ukraine. Switzerland's own intelligence service assessed earlier this year that Russia is waging a long war against the West and escalating it.

articles.title: US and Russia Remove Requirement to Verify AI-Identified Targets From Draft UN Rules
articles.body:
The United States and Russia removed from a draft UN document on autonomous weapons requirements that systems operate “predictably” and “reliably,” as well as a mandatory human review of AI-identified targets before a strike.
The Washington Post reported this, citing its own sources and documents it obtained.
In early September, hundreds of diplomats gathered in a large UN conference room in Switzerland to work on an agreement that was intended to regulate the use of lethal autonomous weapons and become the first international agreement addressing AI-powered combat systems.
On the final day of negotiations, US and Russian diplomats removed several provisions from the document aimed at ensuring the safe use of artificial intelligence in weapons.
According to sources familiar with the discussions, the text no longer included requirements that systems operate “predictably” and “reliably,” or that ethical considerations be taken into account when using AI-enabled weapons.
The US and Russian delegations also removed a provision requiring human verification of AI-identified targets before a strike.
During a closed-door session, after UN cameras were switched off and observers from civil society organizations were asked to leave, the US and Russia each brought in about ten lawyers. That was nearly twice the number of lawyers on other delegations. According to three sources, the changes were being made so quickly that smaller delegations were unable to keep up with the process.
The negotiations are taking place amid an intense public debate over the threats AI development could pose to humanity’s existence. Leaders of technology companies are calling on world leaders to jointly establish limits on the technology. The UN has been trying for several years to regulate the use of AI-enabled weapons but so far has made only limited progress.
Meanwhile, efforts to introduce rules in the United States have stalled, with the Trump administration arguing that any regulation of AI would stifle innovation.
“The United States also categorically rejects any attempts to create a globalist scheme to control artificial intelligence, which is being discussed so much at present – it will henceforth officially be called ‘superintelligence,’” US President Donald Trump said.
As previously reported, during the active phase of military operations against Iran, the US came close to attacking a Chinese vessel that allegedly was carrying components for a nuclear weapons program. The incident reportedly stemmed from an erroneous intelligence report prepared with the help of AI.
Only shortly before the planned operation did officials more carefully review the report prepared by an analyst with the US Special Operations Command. They discovered that, in response to the analyst’s query, a chatbot had combined open-source intelligence with classified signals intelligence available to the government and reached an incorrect conclusion about the vessel’s cargo. The analyst then used AI again to format the findings as a standard intelligence report and circulated it.
According to one of CNN’s sources, the report was “completely false.” At the same time, the source emphasized that it “nearly started a war.” Any US operation against a Chinese vessel could have escalated into an armed conflict between the two countries.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Destroy Training Base of Russian GROM Kaskad Drone Brigade
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) have destroyed the training base of the Russian GROM Kaskad unmanned aviation brigade, which launches Geran-type strike drones, including jet-powered versions, against Ukraine.
The Exilenova+ community published satellite imagery.
Satellite imagery suggests the base was located on the grounds of the Viktoria boarding house in the village of Bilosarayska Kosa on the coast of the Sea of Azov, near Mariupol.
The attack took place on the night of September 15-16, 2026. According to reports, at least 15 explosions were heard at the site. Satellite imagery shows that four buildings containing hotel rooms were completely destroyed.
The GROM Kaskad Separate Unmanned Aviation Brigade is the first unmanned aviation formation within Russia’s Aerospace Forces. It was formed in October 2023 from the Kaskad BARS volunteer detachment, which had operated since 2022.
The brigade has at least two reconnaissance and strike battalions equipped with ZALA/Lancet, Orlan-30, SuperCam, and FPV drones, as well as one specialized reconnaissance battalion that is also involved in directing ballistic missile strikes.
In August 2025, the first reports emerged that the brigade had received Shahed-type strike UAVs. At the time, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence established that GROM Kaskad’s commander was Lt. Col. Ruslan Negrub.
According to intelligence estimates, the brigade also includes Russian officials and lawmakers who sign short-term contracts and receive combat veteran status.
Reports claim that the brigade has launch teams for various types of UAVs at the Tsimbulova droneport, as well as at the Donetsk and Hvardiiske airfields.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence established that on July 26, 2026, Combat Group No. 3 of the brigade launched a Geran-4 jet-powered drone at an ATB supermarket in Chernihiv. Two people were killed, and 25 others were wounded in the strike.

articles.title: Zelensky Says Putin Keeps Finding Excuses to Continue the War
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday that Russia shows no sign of preparing to end its war, accusing Russian President Vladimir Putin of repeatedly inventing reasons to avoid negotiations.
Zelensky made the remarks on Sept. 26, after a wave of Russian strikes that Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said had killed at least 10 people across Ukraine since Friday, including a child.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Putin always finds some lame excuse – not to meet, not to hold a trilateral, not to talk, not to end it, not to stop the killing,” Zelensky said, adding that Putin’s approach had not changed in years, and that Ukraine’s partners recognized the pattern as well.
“He is looking for excuses to keep waging the war,” he continued.
Throughout the five years of the war, Ukrainian authorities have repeatedly pushed for a direct meeting with Putin.
So far, the Kremlin has rebuffed every proposal.
Diplomacy repeatedly stalled
According to Zelensky, his recent meeting with US President Donald Trump confirmed that Washington shares Kyiv’s assessment.
“America sees the situation the same way,” he said, noting that the goal was to change Moscow’s calculations so that it chooses to stop fighting.
“Russia must develop a desire to spend money not on death, but on something else – they must develop a desire to end this war,” he said. He added that Ukraine was working toward that goal with the US, Europe, Canada, Japan and other partners.
Russian Attacks on Kharkiv Region Kill 2, Injure 7, Including 4 Children
In the upcoming days, Zelensky said he expects intense diplomatic activity aimed at changing the course of the war.
He also called for the Lindsey Graham Act, Russia sanctions legislation named after the US senator, and other pressure mechanisms to “work even harder.”
Speaking at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Tuesday, Sept. 22, before a scheduled meeting with Zelensky, Trump warned that Washington was prepared to use newly granted legislative powers to impose tariffs of up to 100% on Russian energy buyers.
When asked by a reporter what message he had for Putin, he simply said: “Settle the war.”
Zelensky also called for the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed into law on Sept. 18, to be used more forcefully.
Having the tool, however, does not guarantee Trump will use it.
Sanctioning China – the biggest buyer of Russian crude – could undermine the trade stability Washington has sought to preserve during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington this week.
Sybiha condemned the Russian barrage that continued throughout the day, killing and injuring civilians in several regions.
On Friday, Russian strikes killed at least four people and injured 47 in Kyiv.
On Saturday, at least two people were killed in Sumy, two in Zaporizhzhia, and two in the Dnipropetrovsk region, including a child, while dozens more were injured across Ukraine nationwide.
According to the FM, Russian forces struck a kindergarten in Kyiv, a lyceum in the Kyiv region and a university in Kharkiv over the past 24 hours. Residential buildings and energy infrastructure in the Poltava, Mykolaiv and Vinnytsia regions were also hit.
“There is a clear pattern – these are civilian sites. Places where people live, study, work, and bring their children,” Sybiha said.
He noted that air-raid alerts in Ukraine often barely end before the next attack begins, and urged Kyiv’s Western allies not to lose sight of what daily life under Russian bombardment looks like.
“Russia’s escalation is not something that happens occasionally between rounds of diplomacy. It is happening every day, with attacks becoming increasingly brutal and civilians paying the price,” he said.
Sybiha warned that the world must not grow numb to the attacks or treat images of destruction as routine news.
He called for every strike to be met with action and accountability, including more missile interceptors for Ukraine, tougher sanctions on those enabling Russia’s attacks and greater pressure on Moscow.
“Russia is testing how much violence the world will tolerate,” Sybiha said. “The answer must be clear: escalation will bring greater pressure, greater support for Ukraine, and a higher price for the aggressor.”
He said a firm response was the only way to keep Russia’s war from spreading further.
Fifty-one countries backed Ukraine in a joint statement on Wednesday, urging the Kremlin to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations on Wednesday, Sept. 23.
Around the same time, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that the Kremlin will not pause its “special military operation” even during negotiations.
His remarks came as Washington recently stepped up its efforts to broker an end to the war, while Ukraine’s Western allies are increasingly preparing for a possible Russian escalation on NATO territory.

articles.title: From the Cold War to post-Assad: 80 years of Syria-Turkey ties
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
From Cold War rivalry to post-Assad cordiality: 80 years of Turkey-Syria relations
In another sign of how swiftly relations have improved, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan will soon visit Syria, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on 14 September after a two-day visit.
This year marks the 80th anniversary of the two neighbours establishing diplomatic relations in 1946, the same year Syria became independent.
A brief look at the history of Turkey-Syria relations suggests that the present moment may mark the closest the two countries have ever been.
Disquieting developments
Syria and Lebanon were under French mandate from the collapse of the Ottoman Empire until the aftermath of the Second World War, when both countries became independent. Turkey immediately established diplomatic relations. At the time, it was viewed as “a Turkish step towards a closer union with the Arab world”.
From those early years of relations, the two neighbours joined rival alliances and forged close ties with the two superpowers. Turkey joined the NATO alliance in 1952. After Turkey concluded a mutual defence treaty with Iraq, then under the pro-Western monarchy, Syria in 1955 recalled its envoy to Turkey for consultations.
Tensions reached an unprecedented high point in 1957 when regional fears spread of a communist takeover in Damascus following the appointment of leftist officers to the Syrian Army in August. Ankara deployed thousands of troops along its border. Damascus charged that Turkey massed its troops in a “manner which presages imminent attack”.
The crisis reached a breaking point by that October, with Damascus additionally charging that Turkish soldiers fired at Syrian border residents and Turkish warplanes flew over Syrian territory.
It even risked drawing in the superpowers, with the US warning the Soviet Union that it would honour its commitments to Turkey’s defence and Moscow declaring it would “inevitably” intervene if Turkey went to war. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev wasn’t so subtle when he remarked that “if war breaks out, we are near Turkey and you are not”.
The crisis showed signs of thaw and ultimately ended that month. In early October 1957, Syria’s new minister to Turkey clarified that Syria only feared an attack by Israel, adding: “I hope Turkish-Syrian relations become better for both of our countries have close ties in language, history and custom.”
Khrushchev seized the opportunity presented by Turkey’s National Day on 29 October to “unexpectedly” show up at the Turkish Embassy in Moscow and toast “peace,” crediting Soviet diplomacy with “cooling off” Turkey.
Syria entered into a brief political union with Gamal Abdel Nasser’s Egypt, then known as the United Arab Republic, in 1958. In January of that year, Turkey again warned its southern neighbour of communist infiltration, arguing that such danger “has introduced in our region disquieting developments”.
Damascus seceded from the UAR in 1961 following a coup. Nasser broke off diplomatic relations with Turkey for recognising the new provisional government in Damascus on the day it was formed, citing a “hostile attitude” toward the UAR.
Any hopes for warmer relations between Ankara and Damascus were short-lived. The 1963 coup brought the Ba’ath Party to power, and Syria entered a closer, lasting relationship with Moscow, which became its leading arms supplier for the rest of the Cold War.
Still, the neighbours avoided another crisis like 1957 until the end of the century.
Insurgency, territorial disputes, and water-sharing
The rule of the Assads in Syria began in 1970 when Hafez al-Assad seized power in yet another coup, invariably justifying his family’s long and brutal reign by citing the endless coups that preceded them.
Assad’s first decade in power coincided with Turkey beginning its damming of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, both of which originate in Turkey and flow downstream to Syria and Iraq. Ankara’s move would create recurring tensions in the relationship over the decades to come.
Another dispute Assad would raise was over Turkey’s Hatay Province. During the French Mandate over Syria, it was known as the Sanjak of Alexandretta. France supported its transfer to Turkish sovereignty in 1939, hoping to convince Ankara to join the Allies against Nazi Germany. It didn’t work. Alexandretta became Hatay.
The Hatay and water-sharing disputes persisted for years. Assad would host the Kurdistan Workers’ Party group, well-known by its Kurdish PKK acronym, and its leader Abdullah Öcalan for years after it launched its armed rebellion against Turkey in 1984. While the two sides signed a border security agreement in 1985, relations between them were strained in this period by Syria’s support of the PKK and the Armenian Secret Army for the Liberation of Armenia.
In 1989, two Syrian MiG-21 fighter jets flew 12 miles into Turkish airspace and shot down a civilian Turkish plane, killing all five people aboard. Syria offered condolences and ordered an inquiry.
By 1990, Turkey’s massive Ataturk Dam on the Euphrates neared completion, again raising objections downstream, with Syria fearing it could lose 40 percent of water it could hitherto rely upon.
Turkey’s state minister said his country had “no international obligations” to provide other countries with water but added that Ankara would do its “best not to harm our neighbours”.
In 1992, Turkey promised to honour past water-sharing agreements. Turkish Foreign Minister Hikmet Cetin said Ankara would respect a 1987 pact on water-sharing under which Turkey would allow at least 500 cubic meters of Euphrates water a second into Syria. The two signed an accord committing to reach a “final solution” on Euphrates water allocation by the end of 1993.
From brink to thaw
Exactly forty-one years after the end of the 1957 crisis, 10,000 Turkish troops amassed along the Turkish-Syrian border in October 1998. Turkey’s military threatened “economic, political and military sanctions” on Damascus. Ankara finally had enough of Syria providing its PKK arch-enemy sanctuary.
“I am not only warning Syria, I am warning the world – this cannot continue,” declared Turkish President Suleyman Demirel. In addition to expelling the PKK, Turkey demanded that Syria drop territorial claims to Hatay.
The crisis lasted less than a month. On 20 October, they signed the Adana Agreement, under which Syria would end its support of the PKK. Damascus expelled Ocalan, who Turkey captured the following year, and restricted the group’s activities on its soil.
Hafez Al-Assad passed away in 2000. Under his son and successor Bashar, Turkey-Syria relations experienced a notable thaw.
Bashar Al-Assad became the first Syrian head of state to visit Turkey in 2004, declaring that his visit coincided “with a period when Syrian-Turkish relations are reaching a peak”.
The following year, Turkish President Ahmet Necdet Sezer visited Syria for two days. In April 2008, Erdogan flew to Damascus, where he discussed the possibility of direct Syria-Israel talks with Assad. The following August, they would meet again when Assad visited the Turkish resort of Bodrum, where he was also vacationing that month.
In 2009, Turkey and Syria reached a deal allowing their citizens to travel to each other’s countries without visas. As Turkey-Israel relations sharply deteriorated following the deadly May 2010 Israeli raid on the Mavi Marmara flotilla, Turkey-Syria ties briefly blossomed as tens of thousands of Syrians visited Turkey’s southeastern Gaziantep monthly.
In a far cry from the 1957 and 1998 crises, Turkey and Syria even held joint military exercises along their shared border in 2009 and 2010.
Little could anyone at the time know that the lowest point in relations was just around the corner.
Lowest point
Assad would ultimately initiate the worst of the regional crackdowns that followed the 2011 Arab Spring uprisings, killing and torturing what were initially peaceful civil demonstrators.
Turkey sought to preserve relations and urge restraint. By August, Turkish Foreign Minister Ahmet Davutoglu went to Damascus to deliver Erdogan’s message that Ankara had “run out of patience” with the Assad regime’s unrelenting violence, which at that point had killed more than 2,000 people. Assad remained unmoved.
The war grew increasingly violent with larger numbers of Syrian refugees pouring over the border into Turkey. The Syrian refugee population peaked at up to 3.7 million over the next decade, more than any other country hosting refugees from that bloody conflict, which eventually left more than 500,000 dead.
Turkey closed its embassy in Damascus in March 2012, hosted the anti-Assad opposition, and banned all Syrian flights from its airspace. Aleppo University even withdrew an honorary doctorate in international relations it had awarded Erdogan in 2009. In December 2015, both states cancelled their 2009 visa agreement.
Syria shot down a Turkish RF-4E reconnaissance jet after it briefly violated its airspace on 22 June 2012, killing both crew members.
Turkey would later intervene directly in Syria in August 2016 with its cross-border Euphrates Shield operation that targeted both the Islamic State and the Kurdish YPG. Ankara avoided fighting Assad’s forces, who were ferociously bombarding east Aleppo with Russian support at the time.
Instead, Turkey remained largely focused on combating the Kurdish forces in a series of cross-border incursions that followed in 2018 and 2019. At the same time, it established an on-the-ground military presence in Syria’s northwestern Idlib province, where the Islamist armed opposition Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) had come to control and govern.
The deadliest clash ever between Turkey and Syria occurred in Idlib in early 2020. After an airstrike killed at least 33 Turkish soldiers, Turkey launched Operation Spring Shield, devastating Assad’s forces with heavy air, artillery, and drone strikes.
New leader, new thaw
After the deadly February 2023 earthquake, which affected both sides of the Turkey-Syria border, regional states offered the Assad regime a second chance in return for reforms and ending the Captagon drug trade. Syria was readmitted into the Arab League but made little tangible effort to implement any reforms or even basic policy changes.
By June 2024, Erdogan offered to restore diplomatic relations for the first time in over a decade. In reference to the 2008 vacation, the Turkish leader said, “In the same way that we kept our relations with Syria alive in the past - we had these meetings with Mr Assad that included family meetings – we cannot say that it will not happen again”.
It did not. Not under Assad anyway. In his final days, the Syrian leader was detached from any semblance of reality, reportedly spending a lot of his time playing Candy Crush on his phone.
By December, a victorious HTS burst out of Idlib, swiftly captured Aleppo and marched on Damascus. Assad fled into exile in Moscow. HTS leader Ahmed al-Sharaa has succeeded Assad as interim president, ending a half-century of that family’s rule.
Sharaa quickly forged close relations with Turkey, making his first visit in February 2025. Turkey reopened its embassy in Damascus mere days after the transitional government seized power, and Turkish Airlines resumed flights to Damascus for the first time in 13 years.
Turkey even seems poised to replace Moscow’s traditional role as Syria’s main military client. However, Sharaa has shown signs that he wants to diversify Syria’s relations to avoid over-reliance on any one country.
The new leadership in Damascus has heralded a new era in Turkey-Syria relations, which may prove much more resilient and long-lasting than past thaws.
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs.
Follow him on Twitter: @pauliddon
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Most Companies Supplying Molniya Drones Remain Outside Western Sanctions
articles.body:
Most companies that supply components for Russian Molniya-series drones are not under Western sanctions. The manufacturer itself is currently not subject to U.S. or U.K. sanctions.
The Kyiv Independent reported this, citing a study by the Ukrainian think tank Center for Defense Reforms.
According to the media, Molniya has become one of the most widely used Russian strike UAVs. Its low cost, relatively simple production, and reported effectiveness have contributed to its widespread use.
In June alone, the Defense Forces shot down about 30,000 Russian Molniya drones. Depending on the modification, the UAVs are used for reconnaissance, air defense, strikes, or to carry FPV drones into the combat area.
The manufacturer, Atlant-Aero, is under sanctions imposed by the EU, Canada, and Ukraine, but is currently not subject to sanctions in the United Kingdom or United States. According to the study, Prominvest JSC, which controls Atlant-Aero, is not under sanctions in any jurisdiction.
Another 10 Russian companies that supply critical components and services for Molniya drone production are also not subject to Western sanctions.
Atlant-Aero’s ultimate beneficial owner, Viktor Grigoryev, and the company’s four other co-owners are also not under Western sanctions.
The study also identified 11 Chinese companies not under sanctions that supply critical components for Molniya drone production. They include Shenzhen Xingkai Technology Company, which supplies equipment for mesh networks. This allows Russian drones to fly deeper into Ukrainian territory. On its website, the company openly states that the technology has military applications.
Ukraine has repeatedly launched drone and missile strikes against Molniya production facilities in Taganrog. In particular, a drone attack on the night of September 12 destroyed three production and storage buildings, while in April, Neptune missiles hit two production halls and completely destroyed another workshop at the plant.

articles.title: The lesson America learned from the New York speech
articles.body:
The lesson America learned from the New York speech
Resalat highlighted the Iranian president’s forceful speech at the United Nations. The main message of the developments and speeches in New York can be summarized in one key proposition: the era of unipolar order and cost-free bullying has come to an end. Iran does not welcome war, but it will not compromise when it comes to defending its dignity and independence.
Iran has extended a hand of cooperation to the world and seeks an international order based on justice, equality among nations, and the rejection of double standards; a world in which nuclear weapons do not provide immunity to Israel's apartheid regime, while Iran's peaceful scientific and technological development is not met with sanctions and threats. If the United States wishes to escape this self-created quagmire, it has no choice but to recognize the new balance of power in West Asia and accept the legitimate rights of the Iranian nation.
Kayhan: Positive signals should not be sent to negotiations
In an interview with Foad Izadi, an expert on US affairs, Kayhan examined American hostile policies toward Iran and their impact on the region. There is a view in the United States that maritime and air blockades, along with its current policies, are effective tools. This is why, while the Iranian negotiating delegation was in New York, the United States initiated an air blockade before the delegation could return home. American assessments recognize the capability and resilience of Iran's military forces, believing they will not surrender. However, some US policymakers perceive certain Iranian political figures as having no option but negotiation. As long as this perception remains unchanged, the threat of war will persist, and American hostile policies will continue to escalate. Therefore, the best course of action for some Iranian officials is to avoid sending positive signals regarding negotiations, since the approach pursued by some political figures so far has produced the opposite of the intended results.
Ettelaat: Rejection of Iran's proposal or progress in negotiations?
Ettelaat discussed the decision by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his accompanying negotiating team to remain in New York until Wednesday. After the first meeting between Araghchi and Steve Witkoff, the US representative, Iranian technical experts joined the talks. During these negotiations, Iran proposed a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the maritime blockade were lifted. The paper suggested that, should negotiations advance further, meetings between Iranian and American officials could be held with mediation from Qatar or Oman. Nevertheless, it remains to be seen in which direction the New York discussions will move and which account of the negotiations more closely reflects reality, especially as the maritime blockade has been intensified by an air blockade and the economic consequences are rapidly becoming visible.
Arman-e-Melli: The efforts of mediators
Arman-e-Melli focused on efforts by mediators to revive negotiations between Iran and the United States. While many international media outlets and observers interpret recent developments as evidence of heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington, others believe that the positions and activities taking place on the sidelines of the UN gathering could mark the beginning of a renewed negotiating process and a way out of the current situation. The main mediators between Iran and the United States, namely Qatar and Pakistan, are seeking to use the opportunity provided by the UN General Assembly to help resolve the current dispute. In their view, the presence in New York of leaders and foreign ministers creates an opportunity for message exchanges and bilateral or multilateral consultations that could help steer the present deadlock toward negotiations. The outcome of Iran's proposed plan and the US response to it are issues whose implications may become clearer in the near future.
Shargh: Playing the oil card
In an explanation, Shargh addressed the uncertainty surrounding the prospects of war or negotiations. Oil prices have surpassed $100 per barrel, at a time when the outlook for conflict in the Persian Gulf remains uncertain. Meanwhile, the world's two largest economies, the United States and China, are paying particularly close attention to oil prices. According to forecasts by some oil-tanker tracking institutions, Iranian crude oil exports to China, its largest and nearly sole oil customer, had declined significantly by late September. Nevertheless, during the recent meeting between Trump and Xi Jinping, virtually no discussion reportedly took place regarding the Iran conflict or oil prices. At the same time, Iran has put forward a new seven-point proposal aimed at reviving negotiations, while reports suggest that China has urged Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and return to talks. Despite all these developments, the future of negotiations, the possibility of continued conflict, and the direction of the oil market remain more uncertain than ever.

“We can start winning the war if we start listening to our engineers,” she said. “When the country’s leadership has analysis and recommendations on the table, state resources can be directed toward acting ahead of the threat.”
She also called for greater reliance on private defense companies, saying the state should define future battlefield requirements, provide clear rules and financing, and allow private manufacturers to develop the necessary solutions.

articles.title: A humanitarian crisis is gripping Russian-occupied Oleshky as food deliveries stop and safe evacuation becomes nearly impossible
articles.body:
A humanitarian crisis is gripping Russian-occupied Oleshky as food deliveries stop and safe evacuation becomes nearly impossible
Oleshky (Alyoshki in Russian) is a city on the left bank of the Dnipro River, across from Kherson on the right bank. Only nine kilometers (about six miles) separate them in a straight line. People once crossed between them by bridge, but the bridge is now closed. The two cities are on opposite sides of the front: Ukraine controls Kherson, while Russia has controlled Oleshky since 2022. As in other cities near the front, life in Oleshky is difficult and dangerous. By September 2026, conditions had deteriorated so badly that people in both Ukraine and Russia were calling the situation critical. Those who remain are trying to survive without food, electricity, and adequate medical care. They cannot leave safely and often cannot even bury their loved ones. Here is what Meduza has been able to learn about conditions in the city.
The situation in Oleshky was already being called critical in Ukraine in the spring. By September, even the Kremlin agreed
“It’s a humanitarian catastrophe, people are driven to despair,” Tetiana Hasanenko, head of Oleshky’s evacuated Ukrainian administration, told The Kyiv Independent in April 2026. She tries to keep in touch with residents and tells Ukrainian media what is happening there.
“If the situation doesn’t improve, people will just die there from hunger. Because there’s no way out, no food supplies coming in,” Anna, an Oleshky resident who recently escaped to a Ukrainian-controlled area, told the outlet.
In the summer, the U.N. mission in Ukraine said Oleshky’s last store had closed in January 2026, and all food deliveries had stopped by late May. Medical care was available only for the most urgent cases. Ambulances no longer responded to calls, and patients with serious conditions could not be transferred to other hospitals. Anyone trying to enter or leave the city faced two dangers: drones overhead and mines on the ground.
In July, Human Rights Watch said shortages of food and medical care in Oleshky were compounded by the collapse of basic utilities. The city had no electricity or gas, and people had switched to wood-burning stoves. People who had managed to leave Oleshky said they were afraid even to go out for water because drones circled overhead and mines lay scattered along the streets. Human Rights Watch said it was impossible to say for certain whose weapons they were. Both Russian and Ukrainian forces had used drones and mines in the area during the war.
At the time, the Russian occupation authorities in the Kherson region still denied that there was a humanitarian catastrophe. By August, however, they acknowledged that Oleshky and nearby villages had no water or electricity, communications were unreliable, and utility crews could not make repairs because of shelling. On September 21, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the situation in the city critical. “The Kyiv regime is doing everything it can to obstruct deliveries [of food and medicine]. Russian troops are continuing to work to resolve the situation,” he said.
Oleshky is in its fifth year under occupation. Why is there talk of a humanitarian catastrophe now?
Continued fighting and the gradual deterioration of infrastructure appear to have made conditions worse.
In the fall of 2022, when Russian troops retreated from the right bank of the Dnipro and left Kherson, Oleshky became a frontline city. The destruction of the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant dam flooded Oleshky in the summer of 2023, badly damaging its infrastructure. The occupation administration says Ukrainian attacks have hampered repairs and deliveries of food and medicine.
As the use of FPV drones increased along the front, Oleshky — like Kherson across the Dnipro — became increasingly dangerous. Drone attacks killed civilians as well as soldiers. Mines added to the danger. The area around the city was so heavily mined that, by early 2026, getting in or out had become very difficult. That was when conditions in Oleshky began to deteriorate rapidly, Hasanenko said.
Gardens fed Oleshky’s residents through the summer. No one knows what winter will bring. Some are reportedly already eating dogs.
It is difficult to reach Oleshky’s residents now, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Some go months without making contact. Those who can charge a phone with a generator and occasionally call or send a message say food is scarce. “People have run out of food. They’re making soup with weeds, throwing in purslane, lamb’s quarters, and amaranth. I can’t even talk about the animals anymore — they have it worst of all. I just cry and don’t know what to do,” one Oleshky resident told Ukrainska Pravda.
Through the summer, residents survived mainly on what they grew in their gardens. Bartering is widespread in the city. “Anything you can still buy costs, say, a thousand rubles. A kilogram of sugar or salt is a thousand rubles; so is a pack of Citramon [painkillers]. But money is actually worth nothing, because no matter how much you have, no one is selling anything,” Hasanenko told Suspilne.
Some people risk traveling to Radensk for food. The village is 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) from Oleshky, farther from the front, and better supplied. But the trips are dangerous because of mines and drones. An Oleshky resident who recently returned from Radensk told Ukrainska Pravda that she brought back 85 kilograms (about 190 pounds) of food for three families. She rode a bicycle to Radensk but returned to Oleshky on foot.
Hasanenko told Ukrainska Pravda that people in the city had begun eating dogs: “A week ago, I was still denying the reports, but now someone there has confirmed it to me. There’s really nothing to eat. The situation isn’t just getting worse every day — it’s getting worse every hour.”
According to Ukrainian officials, Russian troops in Oleshky are also short of food, so they have been taking it from civilians. Some residents have begun putting signs on their fences saying things like “No food here” or “Elderly people live here.”
Oleshky’s hospital has been called the city’s last refuge. It stayed open after pharmacies and stores closed. But conditions there are dire, too.
Residents weakened by malnutrition used to be taken to the local hospital, where staff fed them as best they could. Recently, the hospital, already operating at limited capacity, has all but stopped functioning. Staff can still stop bleeding, but there are no medicines or equipment, and there is not enough fuel for the generator. According to Ukrainska Pravda’s sources, the hospital has begun turning away civilian patients.
“The hospital is asking local people to bring whatever grains or anything else they have, so it can at least give bedridden amputees breakfast. It’s the only place people can still come to spend the night, because it doesn’t get shelled, and get a hot meal if someone cooks it off the generator. But things are critical there,” said volunteer Kseniia Arkhypova, who is from Oleshky and remains in contact with people there.
According to Arkhypova, Russian troops do not allow residents to bury the dead themselves because they “want to take the bodies to Henichesk for examination and produce a report saying the Ukrainian Armed Forces shot them.” Bodies awaiting burial used to be taken to the morgue, but it has since been destroyed, so they are kept in the hospital basement. “Everything’s leaking, and it stinks,” Arkhypova said, and bodies have been piling up since May. Some people quietly bury loved ones in their yards or gardens.
“The occupiers won’t allow the bodies of people killed [in shelling] to be released. There are about 100 bodies in the hospital basements. […] We know of cases where bodies are simply left lying under the scorching sun and no one removes them. At best, if someone knew the person who died, they might cover the body with branches or a piece of cloth,” Hasanenko told Suspilne.
More than a thousand people remain in Oleshky, including dozens of children. Few manage to leave.
Ukrainian volunteers estimate that about 1,500 people, including 40 children, still live in Oleshky. Another 4,000 people, including 150 children, live in nearby villages. Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, these communities had a combined population of 40,000.
People remain in the city for different reasons. Some are elderly or have limited mobility. Others feel they have nowhere to go. Some have no documents. To leave through occupied territory, they need a Russian passport, but getting one in Oleshky is impossible because the city is cut off by land and air. Russia refuses to open a humanitarian corridor to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Some men of draft age fear they will be sent into the Russian army if stopped at checkpoints. Some people cannot leave relatives behind in Oleshky. Others have no money or are simply afraid of being killed on the way out.
There is no organized evacuation from the city. Ukrainian officials say the Russian army does not want civilians to leave because their presence deters Ukrainian strikes. Meduza found no comments from the occupation authorities explaining why they have not arranged an evacuation.
In any case, under the Geneva Conventions, the occupying power is responsible for civilians in occupied territory. It is obliged to provide the population with food and medicine “to the fullest extent of the means available to it.”

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: 9 injured as Russian drones, missiles continue to batter Kyiv for fourth consecutive night of strikes
articles.body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Multiple people were killed by a Russian strike on a food market in Kyiv on Sept. 27 amid a multi-day wave of attacks on the capital. 
A strike on the Stolichny market outside of Kyiv killed two and injured four, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Sept. 27. The strike caused a fire at the wholesale food market.
Eyewitness footage from the scene of the strike on the market shows multiple bodies and flames engulfing vehicles in the parking lot. Over central Kyiv, air defense systems were reported to be active, filling the city with sounds of blasts and explosions amid a nine-hour-long air raid alert. 
The attack comes amid a day of devastation in Kyiv with multiple attacks reported across the capital. An additional nine people sustained injuries in attacks on Kyiv throughout the day, said Klitschko. Six of the injured victims were hospitalized, including one child.
Amid the latest attack coinciding with the strike on the market, a Russian drone was shot down by the capital's air defenses and crashed in the Podil neighborhood, according to eyewitness reports by Kyiv Independent reporters.
"In the Podilskyi district, a fire broke out in the grass cover as a result of falling debris," said Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Emergency services were deployed to the scene.
Debris fell in an open area in the Dnipro district, as well as on a non-residential building, Klitschko said, with preliminary reports indicating that there are casualties.
In the Darnitsky district, debris fell in an open area near a store.
According to Kyiv Independent reporters, authorities halted trains set to depart during the attack, evacuating passengers to underground shelters.
The latest air raid alert was lifted just before 1 a.m. local time.
Unrelenting attacks on the capital occurred immediately prior on the night of Sept. 26-27, when Russian strikes on Kyiv killed one and injured at least five.
Across Ukraine on Sept. 26-27, attacks by Russian forces further killed 14 and injured at least 57.
"This past week, the Russians launched more than 2,200 attack drones against Ukraine, as well as around 1,650 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types, a significant number of them ballistic missiles," said President Volodymyr Zelensky.

articles.title: Turkish anti-drone guns put on show for 12 countries
articles.body:
- ASELSAN demonstrated its KORKUT 35 air defense gun system shooting down several types of drones before delegations from 12 countries.
- Mounted on an 8×8 wheeled vehicle, the system also hit a moving ground target while both were in motion.
Turkish defense company ASELSAN has shown its KORKUT 35 air defense gun system shooting down drones and hitting a moving target while driving, in a live-fire demonstration watched by military delegations from 12 countries.
The company released video of the firing.
The demonstration focused on drones, and KORKUT 35 engaged fixed-wing, delta-wing and small mini and micro drones, with particular attention to kamikaze drones built to dive into their targets, ASELSAN said. In a separate scenario, the system, mounted on an 8×8 wheeled armored vehicle, fired at a moving ground target while both were in motion, to show its accuracy and how tightly its rounds grouped.
ASELSAN says the system can also engage fighter jets, helicopters, cruise missiles and air-to-ground missiles, and describes it as a cheaper way to defend troops and key sites against low-cost aerial threats.
KORKUT carries twin 35 mm cannons that together fire about 1,100 rounds a minute, with an effective range of roughly 4 km (2.5 miles). It uses ASELSAN’s ATOM programmable ammunition, which bursts in the air near a target and scatters tungsten fragments, raising the chance of hitting small drones that are hard to strike directly. A typical battery pairs a command vehicle that searches for and tracks targets with gun vehicles that each follow and fire at an assigned target.
The system entered Turkish service in a tracked configuration and has been exported. ASELSAN unveiled the 8×8 wheeled version at the Eurosatory defense show in Paris in 2024, giving it higher road speed to keep up with moving units. In January 2026, the company released footage of the wheeled KORKUT 140/35 shooting down a first-person-view drone while on the move.
The system is also heading to Europe. In February, ASELSAN and Czech defense group CSG formed a joint venture to produce KORKUT in the Czech Republic for European and global customers, and unveiled a version mounted on a Tatra 6×6 truck. In September, KORKUT was identified among air defense systems in a public reveal by the Pakistan Air Force, though the variant supplied has not been disclosed.

articles.title: Japan races to fill its ammo stores after Ukraine lessons
articles.body:
- Japan will begin building at least 65 new ammunition depots from fiscal 2027 using a standardized design to speed up construction.
- Analysts say Japan's push to store more ammunition draws on lessons from the war in Ukraine.
Japan’s Ministry of Defense will start building at least 65 new ammunition depots for the Self-Defense Forces from fiscal 2027, using a single standardized design to get them into service faster, the Nikkei business daily reported Sept. 20. The push to store more ammunition follows lessons Tokyo has drawn from Russia’s war in Ukraine, where stockpiles, supply lines and the safety of military sites have shaped the fighting.
The ministry has so far designed each depot individually, and switching to a standard model is meant to shorten design work and speed up construction, the newspaper said. The Self-Defense Forces operate about 1,400 ammunition depots nationwide, and the ministry plans to add roughly 130 by fiscal 2032. Sites for 65 of those have been chosen, and three had been completed by August 2026. The Nikkei did not say where the next 65 will be built or what the program will cost.
Japan’s 2022 National Defense Strategy and Defense Buildup Program call for the Self-Defense Forces to secure the ammunition they need as early as possible so they can sustain a long fight. When those plans were drafted, Japan held only about 60% of the Patriot PAC-3 MSE and SM-3 interceptors it needed for missile defense, and its stocks of artillery shells and rockets would have lasted about two months in combat, Shephard reported. Then-Prime Minister Fumio Kishida said in October 2022 that the forces’ ability to keep fighting was inadequate.
A 2024 study by France’s Foundation for Strategic Research said Japan was trying to absorb lessons from the war in Ukraine on logistics, ammunition stocks, unmanned systems and the survivability of military bases. RAND researchers wrote in 2023 that Tokyo was increasing spending on munitions stocks and base hardening, and urged Japanese planners to prepare for a protracted conflict. Japan’s Ministry of Defense has not publicly linked the new depot design to any specific foreign example.
Czech police concluded in 2024 that officers from Russia’s GRU military intelligence carried out the 2014 explosions that destroyed ammunition warehouses at Vrbětice and killed two people, with the aim of stopping weapons from reaching Ukraine. In August 2026, explosions hit a Bulgarian plant run by EMCO, which makes 155 mm artillery ammunition for Ukraine, and a KNDS Ammo facility near Rome. Bulgarian and Italian officials have been reluctant to blame Russia, but Western intelligence officials have said the GRU now recruits criminal gangs to attack European arms sites while keeping Moscow’s hand hidden.
Kyodo News reported in 2023 that the ministry planned its first new depots at nine Ground Self-Defense Force sites in Hokkaido, Miyazaki, Kagoshima and Okinawa to store long-range missiles, including at Camp Ebino and the Okinawa Training Area. Japan is also buying 400 U.S.-made Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Japan spent about 48.2 billion yen ($308 million) on new depots from 2022 through March 2026, and its budget for the fiscal year that began in April includes about 56 billion yen ($358 million) more, Austrian magazine Militär Aktuell reported.

articles.title: Russia's finance ministry raises taxes to bolster Putin's military budget
articles.body:
More frequent long-range strikes by the Ukrainian armed forces on strategically important targets, as well as growing spending to counter these attacks, are further deepening Russia's budget deficit.
The Kremlin is seeking additional funds for the war in Ukraine by raising taxes, as the federal budget deficit reached 5.8479 trillion roubles (€60.4 billion) in the first half of the year, according to official data.
By the end of July, the budget deficit amounted to 2.8% of annual GDP, almost twice the initially planned annual figure.
The volume of funds in Russia's reserve fund has fallen to 1.6% of GDP, forcing the Kremlin to borrow from domestic banks.
At the same time, GDP growth has slowed compared with the peak rate of more than 4% year on year recorded in 2023–2024.
According to government forecasts, growth this year will be 0.6%, with the economy contracting in the first quarter and showing a modest rebound in the second.
Analysts cite a sharp increase in government spending as the main cause of the deficit – including massive outlays on the war and advance financing of state contracts – along with weaker revenues under sanctions pressure and volatile commodity markets.
More frequent and intensified long-range strikes by the Ukrainian armed forces on strategically important targets, above all oil refineries and depots, as well as growing spending to counter these attacks, are further deepening the deficit.
The still-low unemployment rate and generous state payments in poorer regions are helping to contain consumer discontent for now.
However, economists warn that long-term problems are eroding the foundations of the economy and could eventually trigger a crisis.
The Ministry of Finance has submitted a draft law to the Russian government on a new three-year budget with an annual deficit of around 2% of GDP, as well as a bill amending the Tax Code "to increase the resilience of the budget system."
The proposal states that "the strategic priority of the budget is the financial provision of defence and national security needs, and social support for participants in the special military operation (Russia's official term for the war against Ukraine) and their families."
Civilians and businesses will pay for the war
The Ministry of Finance has proposed taxing Russians' so‑called "passive" income at rates of 13%–22%. This includes interest on deposits, dividend income, securities transactions, property sales, as well as insurance and gift contracts. At present, passive income is taxed at 13%–15%.
Extending the progressive scale of personal income tax to income from deposits, dividends, investments and the sale of property could bring the budget an additional 500–700 billion roubles a year. That estimate was given by economist Dmitry Polevoy, quoted by the outlet Meduza.
Another initiative by the ministry is to introduce value added tax (VAT) on purchases from foreign online shops.
That would be applied immediately at the maximum rate of 22%, although there had previously been talk of a phased increase.
It is also proposed to introduce a fee of 100 roubles (about €1) for parcels from abroad worth up to €200, which are currently exempt from customs duty.
In parallel, Russian media say the Federation Council has proposed higher taxes for the self‑employed.
Andrei Yepishin, deputy chair of the committee on the budget and financial markets, said couriers and drivers who in practice work full time should pay tax at a rate starting from 13% instead of the 4%–6% self‑employment tax.
According to the ministry's estimates, the changes will affect about 4 million Russians, roughly 2.74% of the population. However, the Finance Ministry stressed in particular that the amendments should not affect the income of participants in the war.
For large businesses, a windfall tax is being introduced, according to the Finance Ministry's press release: for certain companies in the mining and metals sector the tax will be 30% of additional income. For gold producers the rate will be 20%.
The Russian Ministry of Finance openly states that "the resources envisaged will ensure that the armed forces are supplied with the necessary weapons and military equipment, the modernisation of defence‑industry enterprises, the payment of monetary allowances to servicemen and support for their families."
The ministry notes that priority funding will continue under the national projects "Machine tools" and "Unmanned aerial systems."
Their funding over three years will increase to 135.7 billion roubles (€1.4 billion) and 103.3 billion roubles respectively (€1.06 billion).
The Kremlin's forgotten promise
It is noteworthy that the Kremlin forgot its promise not to raise taxes on the fourth day after the State Duma elections.
"This is not under discussion," presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov said 10 days before the vote, according to the Interfax news agency.
Earlier this year, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov insisted that tax increases for Russian citizens were not being considered.
"These are fake leaks," he said at the time.
Judging by the proposed amendments to the Russian Tax Code, the authorities are having to seek additional revenue at home to sustain the war machine.
The measures being proposed show that the Kremlin intends to shift the rising cost of the war not only onto better‑off citizens with income from savings and investments and onto big business, but also onto ordinary consumers.
It is hardly surprising that consumer confidence has been gradually falling since its peak in 2024–2025, when higher military spending was fuelling economic growth and wage increases.
Recently consumers have been confronted with rising petrol prices and shortages due to Ukrainian drone attacks that have knocked out oil refineries. Many small businesses have also suffered losses of inventories and customers because of strikes targeting the online retailers Wildberries and Ozon.
The consumer sentiment index calculated by the Levada Centre, an independent Russian polling organisation, fell in the summer to 94 points, compared with 116 points in the spring and summer of 2025. Readings below 100 indicate that consumer sentiment is more negative than positive.
Against this backdrop, talk continues of VPN blocks and of a possible new wave of mobilisation, repeatedly denied officially.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russian P-18 Terek Early-Warning Radar Watching Skies for 250 Km
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russian P-18 Terek Early-Warning Radar Watching Skies for 250 Km
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian P-18 Terek early-warning radar in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region and an ammunition depot in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region during a series of attacks on Russian military targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s General Staff on September 26, the strikes were carried out throughout September 25 and overnight into September 26. The P-18 radar was hit near Semenivske in the Donetsk region, while a separate strike targeted an ammunition depot in Sievierodonetsk.
The military did not specify which weapons were used in the attacks or provide an assessment of the damage to either target.
The P-18, also designated 1RL131 Terek and known by the NATO reporting name Spoon Rest D, is a Soviet-designed mobile two-dimensional early-warning radar operating in the VHF band. The system entered service in 1970 and remains in operation, with several modernization packages developed over the decades.
According to the General Staff, the radar can detect airborne targets at ranges of around 250 kilometers and at altitudes of up to 35 kilometers. It is used to detect and determine the coordinates of aircraft and other aerial targets before passing radar information to other elements of an air-defense network.
Unlike fire-control radars that directly guide surface-to-air missiles, the P-18 primarily serves as an early-warning and surveillance sensor. Its VHF operating band and long detection range allow it to contribute to the broader air picture available to air-defense units.
Czech defense electronics company RETIA, which offers modernization packages for the P-18, also identifies its long range and ability to detect low-observable targets as key characteristics of the system.
On September 21, Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian Kasta-2E2 radar in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region. The mobile system, valued at an estimated $60 million, can detect low-flying aircraft, missiles, and drones at ranges of up to 150 kilometers.

articles.title: Iran will respond to any aggression with new weapons
articles.body:
Iran will respond to any aggression with new weapons
TEHRAN — Iran has warned the United States against any intervention in the Strait of Hormuz, while stressing that its Armed Forces have developed new military technologies and capabilities to respond to any potential aggression.
Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi, spokesman for Iran’s Armed Forces, issued the warning on Saturday night, saying that any U.S. attempt to interfere in the strategic waterway would face an Iranian response.
“If the United States intervenes in the Strait of Hormuz, it will get slapped,” Shekarchi said, using a colloquial expression to underline the consequences Washington would face in the event of direct intervention.
He also said that the United States had “no way out other than leaving West Asia,” arguing that the sooner American forces withdrew from the region, the lower the losses they would suffer.
Shekarchi described the Islamic Republic as a “global power” and said Iran would not allow the United States to return to its former position in a “new world order.”
Iran’s military doctrine and new technologies
The senior military spokesman said Iran’s Armed Forces had sought to strengthen their combat capabilities and incorporate advanced technologies since the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s, also known as the “imposed war.”
He cited the beginning of Iran’s indigenous missile production during the conflict with the former Ba’athist regime in Iraq as a tangible example of the country’s efforts to develop defense capabilities under wartime conditions.
According to Shekarchi, one of the most significant changes in Iran’s military doctrine following the Islamic Revolution was the shift from conventional warfare toward asymmetric warfare.
He said conventional military methods could be vulnerable when confronting an adversary equipped with costly and technologically sophisticated heavy weapons.
“Asymmetric warfare means standing up to the enemy’s expensive heavy weapons and achieving victory with lower costs and simpler but more effective and practical defense equipment,” Shekarchi said.
’A surprise in store for the enemy’
Shekarchi said Iran’s adversaries had miscalculated the country’s resilience and defensive capabilities.
He argued that if the enemy had properly assessed Iran’s capabilities, it would not have chosen to attack the country.
The general also emphasized information security as a key principle within the Armed Forces, saying that safeguarding military information was essential to preserving the element of surprise.
He said Iran possessed unique elements of national power and pointed to the participation of the Iranian people both on the streets and on the battlefield as a fundamental factor in the country’s ability to withstand attacks.
Referring to recent threats against Iran, Shekarchi said the Armed Forces would employ newly developed military technologies in responding to any future aggression.
“The powerful Iranian Armed Forces are many times stronger than they were at the outset of the second and third imposed wars,” he said, describing the current condition of the Armed Forces as “very good.”
He said Iran’s missile and drone capabilities had become more advanced and powerful and warned that Tehran had capabilities that had not necessarily been publicly disclosed.
“This time we have a surprise in store for the enemy,” Shekarchi said, adding that Iran would respond to any potential aggression with new military technologies.
Hormuz at the center of the dispute
Shekarchi also reiterated Iran’s position on the Strait of Hormuz, saying that the strategic waterway was under Iranian management.
“Management of the Strait of Hormuz is in Iran’s hands,” he said. “Any ship that wants to pass outside the Iranian route will not have security.”
The comments come as control and security arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz have emerged as a major point of contention between Tehran and Washington.
In recent indirect negotiations in New York, Iranian officials presented conditions under which Tehran said it could facilitate the reopening of the waterway and the resumption of nuclear talks. According to Axios, U.S. negotiators told their Iranian counterparts that Iran did not control the strait and therefore could not impose conditions concerning it.

articles.title: In Germany, intelligence services are searching for Russian “weapons caches”; there is a threat of sabotage at a defense company — media reports
articles.body:
In Germany, intelligence services are searching for Russian “weapons caches”; there is a threat of sabotage at a defense company — media reports
Kyiv • UNN
German intelligence services suspect that weapons for sabotage against a defense company have already been hidden in Bavaria. The investigation is classified.
According to German intelligence, Russian intelligence has created weapons caches in Germany. As BILD has learned, a search for these caches is currently under way, reports UNN.
Details
On the evening of June 11, 2026, Serbian police stopped two cars near Subotica that were heading toward the Hungarian border. In the Peugeot belonging to Danilo Bogdanović, a Serb with a Russian passport, they found drone components, while in the black Volvo belonging to Slobodan Dučić, they discovered a concealed compartment containing two tin cans packed with explosives. Investigators assessed that a flying bomb could have been assembled from these materials. Bogdanović and Dučić were arrested.
The next day, a friendly intelligence service passed information to its German counterparts about a suspicious truck traveling to Germany from Serbia. According to the Serbian authorities, the truck contained a compartment for smuggling weapons. However, Serbian police failed to intercept the vehicle.
On June 27, Bavarian border police detained the truck as it entered from Austria. The Serbian driver was detained, banned from entering Germany, and sent back to Austria. The truck was confiscated. Investigators did indeed find concealed compartments—but they were empty. The security authorities concluded that the delivery of the weapons about which the Serbs had warned may have reached its destination in Germany earlier. According to BILD, the weapons may have been intended for an attack on a defense company in Bavaria that is of major importance for military aid to Ukraine.
The search for the weapons is in full swing. According to the German government, several networks of saboteurs controlled by Russia are currently operating in Europe. They are believed to be coordinated by the GRU, which is apparently conducting covert operations in Europe with the help of a special-operations unit. German investigators suspect that the weapons from the truck are already in a cache in Germany and ready to be used for acts of sabotage.
In response to BILD's inquiry, all authorities involved in the case unanimously cited the need for secrecy. The pages of documents that BILD was able to see in connection with the investigation bear the words "officially classified" printed in red at the top.
