articles.title: Russian Forces Begin Using New Geran-5 Version With Autonomous Optical Navigation
articles.body:
Russian forces have begun using a new modification of the Geran-5 jet-powered UAV, which features an autonomous optical navigation system and a modified fuselage design.
The monitoring channel Colonel GSh reported this, referring to the new version as the Geran-5 K5.
According to the channel, the UAV is equipped with an electro-optical correction system that allows it to navigate using images of the ground surface.
Its operating principle is similar to that of OEKС (DSMAC) systems, which use terrain image matching for navigation and allow the flight path to be corrected without satellite navigation.
The new version also has a higher speed than the standard model. As a result, it may be mistakenly identified in flight as other jet-powered strike assets, including the Dan-T.
At the same time, the K5 designation and the installation of a DSMAC-class system have not been officially confirmed by Ukrainian sources.
An indirect indication that autonomous optical navigation has appeared on Russian Geran-series drones came from a statement by Russian military correspondent Andrei Filatov. He said that Russian drones of this series already use an autonomous optical navigation system called Susanin.
Filatov claims that the system navigates using images of the underlying terrain, allowing the UAV to continue along its route without radio beacons.
However, the Russian source does not specify which Geran modification is equipped with the system and does not identify it as DSMAC.
According to official data from Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, the baseline Geran-5 is 6.5 meters long, has a wingspan of 3.2 meters and a maximum takeoff weight of up to 850 kilograms.
It is equipped with a warhead weighing about 90 kilograms, has a cruising speed of 450–600 km/h, a range of about 950 kilometers and can reach an altitude of up to 6 kilometers.
The Geran-5 examined by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence was found to contain a Kometa-M12 jam-resistant satellite navigation system, an inertial navigation system, a tracker with cellular modems, a mesh modem and a Chinese TELEFLY TF-TJ2000A turbojet engine. The current public list of components maintained by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence does not include a separate DSMAC system.
Russia is known to have already modified the Geran-5’s design by moving the turbojet engine inside the fuselage from an external nacelle, reducing aerodynamic drag and potentially increasing the UAV’s speed and flight range.

articles.title: Trump expects new Iran talks despite rejecting deal offer
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump expects new Iran talks despite rejecting deal offer
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, despite his rejection of a truce proposal put forward by Tehran.
Iranian officials brought a plan to the UN General Assembly in New York for a seven-day truce, followed by the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz shipping channel.
Trump dismissed the plan and has mused on resuming full-scale air strikes on Iranian targets, but he told the news platform Axios that he expects negotiations to resume.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Trump told Axios. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."
"They overplayed their hand," Trump said, in the interview published Sunday.
Citing sources familiar with the matter, Axios reported that indirect talks between Washington and Tehran could take place as early as Monday.
On Sunday, Iran was still standing by its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the Gulf front of the Middle East war locked in a stalemate, while fighting rages in Yemen.
'We will not back down'
Hormuz is a key chokepoint for the world's energy supplies and is now central to the conflict between Washington and Tehran, which was started nearly seven months ago when the US and Israel launched a wave of strikes against Iran.
Iran's plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and a return to the conditions in an earlier ceasefire deal that fell apart.
That agreement, which collapsed during fighting over Hormuz, called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Araghchi said on Sunday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights."
Washington's ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, accused Tehran of demanding too much in exchange for a return to the negotiating table.
"This was, I think, a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable. To ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions and access to billions in assets, just to talk," he told NBC News in an interview broadcast Sunday.
"I think it's kind of common sense that the president doesn't have a lot of confidence this time after we just tried a few months ago."
Iran's Revolutionary Guards meanwhile said that they seized an American submersible drone on Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz.
It said the underwater vehicle was being used "for espionage purposes", adding that it was "now in the hands of the force's specialists for data recovery".
'Tool for pressure'
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at ending the war, reopening the strait and launching talks on Iran's nuclear programme.
But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.
Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.
Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.
Araghchi said at the UN that Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan, adding: "The choice now rests with the United States."
Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for Iran's Revolutionary Guards, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: "We will not cease punishing the US until Iran's seven conditions are met."
Mohebi had told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran's demands.

articles.title: UK: five arrested for on suspicion of preparing 'terrorist act'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK police arrest five on suspicion of preparing 'terrorist act' near air base
British counter-terrorism police were Sunday probing "a major" incident near a base used by the US air force after arresting five men on suspicion of "preparing a terrorist act", police said.
Armed officers detained the group in the early hours after a call to emergency services about three "suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the air base", London's Metropolitan Police said in a statement.
US President Donald Trump told reporters they had been "looking to do big damage" at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford air base in Gloucestershire, southwest England.
"We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he said, adding the US and UK had been working together on the incident.
A local resident who said it was known locally that the base was on lockdown due to a "terror threat" alerted emergency services after seeing three vans blocking the road and a large group of men wearing hoods and balaclavas.
She told the PA news agency she found it "astonishing" it had been effectively down to a "plucky amateur" spotting unusual activity to raise the alarm.
Some 85 households in the nearby village of Whelford were advised to evacuate and army bomb disposal experts called in to examine three large white vans stopped on a rural road.
Incident 'contained'
"Counter Terrorism Policing can now confirm they are leading an investigation into an incident which took place overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire," the Met statement added.
Broadcast aerial footage showed a bomb disposal robot moving around the vans, two of which had their rear doors open.
Police believed the incident had been "contained" and a 400 metre (1,300 feet) cordon had been put in place.
Armed officers could be seen guarding the entrance to the base.
In March, then prime minister Keir Starmer granted permission for "defensive" US action against Iranian missile sites from two UK bases including Fairford.
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham was being kept updated on the incident, a government spokesperson said.
Burnham, who was in the northwestern city of Liverpool along with other senior ministers for his Labour Party's annual conference, thanked the police, armed forces and residents who had been asked to leave their homes "while precautionary checks are carried out".
Defence Minister Wes Streeting said in Liverpool he had been in contact with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and the UK was "working closely with our American friends".
Asked if there was any Iranian involvement, he said it would be "irresponsible to speculate".
Gloucestershire police said earlier it had declared a "major incident" with several men arrested "on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act".
Villagers evacuated
Residents from Whelford were evacuated to a nearby leisure centre.
"My understanding is that the whole village was evacuated in the early hours of this morning," district councillor Tristan Wilkinson told AFP.
"Most people got in their cars, so when the police knocked on the doors and told them to go, most people were able to kind of drive away."
They were now waiting to see if the cordon would be relaxed later Sunday, as many were worried about pets which had to be left behind. "I'm hoping that the police will actually reduce the cordon quite quickly," Wilkinson said.
Villager Julian Tudsbery said it was his fellow villager who had alerted police first after they "phoned the airbase police who didn't answer the phone. It just rang out so she dialled 999".
Fairford is the UK base of the 501st Combat Support Wing, a US air force administrative support wing, which said in a statement that no US air force personnel had been involved in the incident.
"The 501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners," it said.
"We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities," it added.
The incident comes amid concerns about the actions of hostile foreign states.
Interior Minister Shabana Mahmood has accused Iran and Russia of using proxies to carry out criminal activities on their behalf on UK territory.
Earlier this month, reports said British military sites had been targeted by drones more than 300 times over the past year.

articles.body:
Two people were killed and at least seven injured, including four children, as Russian forces struck the city of Kharkiv and 21 settlements across the Kharkiv region over Saturday.
Oleh Synehubov, the head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration reported the casualties in the morning of Sunday, Sept. 27. He said Russia used a missile, three multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS) and 41 drones against the region.

Children among the injured
The village of Lebiazhe in the Prolisne community was among the hardest hit.

A 73-year-old woman was injured in the attack near Pytomnyk, while a 16-year-old boy was wounded in the strike between Shuby and Sinne.
In the village of Nyzhche Solone in the Borova community, a 60-year-old man was injured when an unidentified device exploded.

Russian forces attacked Kharkiv’s Shevchenkivskyi and Slobidskyi districts with drones, damaging an abandoned building and a stadium in the city.

Civilian infrastructure targeted again
Civilian infrastructure was damaged across six districts of the region, according to the regional military administration.
In Kupiansk district, Russian attacks damaged an ambulance in the village of Prosianka, a residential care facility and a garage in Shevchenkove, an outbuilding in Velykyi Burluk, a private house in Kotivka and a civilian enterprise in Novoselivka.
In Chuhuiv district, an apartment building and 15 private vehicles were damaged in Lebiazhe, while power lines were hit in the village of Zarichne.
In Bohodukhiv district, strikes damaged four private houses in Zolochiv, private homes in Riasne and Kalynove, and private vehicles in Skovorodynivka and Sinne.
In Lozova district, a private house and a civilian enterprise were damaged in Lozova, an administrative building and four cars in Zlatopil, and a private house in Dobropillia.
A residential building and a hangar were hit in the city of Izium.
In Kharkiv district, the attacks damaged cars in Pytomnyk and Ruska Lozova, a private house in Tsyrkuny and a shop in Derhachi.
Evacuations continue as Russian strikes persist
The transit evacuation center in Lozova received 185 people over the past day, Syniehubov said, adding that it has registered a total of 62,012 people since it opened.
Kyiv Post could not independently verify the figures.
Citing the General Staff of the AFU, Synehubov said Ukrainian units repelled four Russian attacks near the settlements of Ternova, Kozacha Lopan and Lyman in the Southern Slobozhanskyi axis.
In the Kupiansk axis, Russian forces made three attempts to improve their positions, launching assaults toward Kupiansk, Radkivka and Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi.

articles.title: Bill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulation
articles.body:
Bill Gates has called on the US’s federal legislators and law enforcers to regulate the development of artificial intelligence (AI), saying in an interview airing on Sunday that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths” and “no one thinks self-regulation is enough”.
“You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist said to Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.”
Using a term meant to describe an expense required to run a business, Gates continued: “It will be a little bit of overhead for the industry – but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.”
Another portion of the interview – excerpts of which NBC circulated in advance – saw Gates dramatically warn that AI in the wrong hands would be “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths”.
“There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” Gates added, echoing other recent similar warnings by a wide array of tech and political figures.
Gates also addressed the concept of a “kill switch” that could turn off AI if it became too potent, saying it was inadequate.
“It’s not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates remarked. “We’re not yet at the point where … they autonomously grab computers and, you know, can’t be shut down. So that discussion … just sort of shows how non-technical various people are.”
Gates otherwise is generally regarded as optimistic about humans’ future. Many reporting or commenting on his conversation with Welker noted that it occurred in the wake of a nearly 6,000-word essay that he published in late August warning about AI and the potentially lethal ills it poses to humanity on a large scale.
His fellow tech moguls including Sam Altman and Elon Musk have joined Gates in calling for a slowdown of the development of AI, which some experts theorize could precipitate the mass destruction of humans through bioweapons and nuclear war, among other methods.
Progressive US senator Bernie Sanders on 23 September proposed legislation that would temporarily pause advanced AI development while guardrails to the technology are put in place.
Meanwhile, Microsoft itself has been challenged for having a role in stoking some of the dystopian concerns surrounding AI.
Company employees and activists have organized a campaign aimed at getting Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military, which has used AI tools to kill in Gaza and – alongside US forces – in Iran, according to a Guardian essay published on Friday.
The essay’s authors, Mohamed Hussein and Granate Kim of the No Azure for Apartheid group, furthermore warned that “horrors wrought by AI” are also being seen in the US. For instance, the US Department of Homeland Security has used AI tools such as Microsoft’s Azure to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants en masse, Hussein and Kim wrote.
Gates’s essay in August and interview on Sunday were two of his first major forays into the public since becoming ensnared in the scandal surrounding Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier who pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a minor for prostitution before dying by suicide while incarcerated on sex-trafficking charges 11 years later.
An external review commissioned by Gates’s philanthropic foundation and released in July determined that he was among a number of organization staffers and leaders who had collectively held about 30 meetings with Epstein from 2011 to 2014.
Gates has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s admitted or alleged crimes. He has said he regretted “every minute” he spent with Epstein, and remains the chair of the $89bn (£65bn) Gates Foundation charity.
In a lighter moment during Welker’s interview with Gates, the host asked him: “Are there any ways in which you, professionally or personally, avoid AI and say that: ‘I’m not going to consult with it in this instance?’”
Gates, with a chuckle and a smile, replied: “Well, I’m not using it for my personal relationships. I’m not like: ‘Hey, do you like me? Hey, am I a nice guy?’
“So I just never went down that path, because I’m lucky in terms of my family, friends and everything. I don’t socialize with the AI. It knows I’m a very serious person.”

articles.title: Iran split screen: When US, Israeli interests reach a fork in the road - analysis
articles.body:
With the exception of a few years, for most of recent decades, US and Israeli interests regarding Iran’s nuclear program, as interpreted by their respective governments, have strongly converged.
Both countries want to prevent an Iranian nuclear weapon.
Israel because it could be an immediate existential danger.
The US because an Iranian nuclear weapon could make the ayatollahs (or the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which may have replaced them) the new hegemon of the region and eventually become a direct threat to the US mainland, like North Korea, which started with short-range atomic bombs and gained longer-range ones within only a few years.
One of the few exceptions was this summer, when US President Donald Trump’s administration cut a deal with Iran that was defined by both Israeli government and opposition officials as a “bad deal.”
Iran made a fateful error
They said it was bad because it reduced US military pressure on Iran, placed resolving the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz at the front of the sequencing of the deal, and pushed off resolving the nuclear issues to the end of the deal, conditionally on months of amorphous negotiations.
The Iranian ballistic-missile threat, which has devastated US military bases and harmed around a dozen countries throughout the region, was not even mentioned in the deal.
Had the deal gone forward as agreed upon, Israeli and American interests would have widely diverged on Iran.
But the Iranians made a potentially fateful error: They decided to rub Trump’s face in the deal and go for an even more humiliating deal, presuming that his readiness to make the concessions he had already made meant that they could push him further.
Trump has caved in stunning and rapid ways on a number of issues during his presidency, but he almost always does so quietly to avoid humiliation.
The Iranians’ insistence on humiliating Trump led him to walk away both from the new deal they wanted and from the concessions he had made under the old deal.
A new reality set in.
Iran had bet that he would continue to cave to try to save the Republican Party from major losses in the November 3 midterm elections.
They were right to a point, as this concern led him to cut the original “bad deal” (from Israel’s perspective).
Trump's bet to outlast the Iranians
To avoid humiliation, however, Trump shifted gears, choosing a third path. He would neither push to topple Iran’s regime with military force, nor cut a deal that would humiliate him; rather, he would try to beat it in a staring contest in which US military power would be used to harm Iran’s economy at a much worse rate than whatever harm the Islamic regime could inflict on America and its allies.
It took months for this strategy to play out, as the US had not really prepared in advance for such a scenario.
But sometime in August, Washington’s military power achieved a shift in which the harm to the West’s economy started to go down, while the harm to Iran’s economy escalated tremendously.
This time, Trump made a bet that Iran would be worn down before the US midterm elections, so he could claim victory leading into those elections and gain back some of the nuclear concessions he had negotiated away earlier.
In the constant miscalculations between the sides, however, Trump continued to project Western rationalism into how he expected Iran to act.
They had lost $200 billion to $300 billion. During the war in early 2026. Now they were losing more day by day. They would for sure finally crack under the ongoing pressure, he thought.
But the IRGC officers running Iran are a mix of religious fanatics who believe their regime is aided by messianic divine currents and are paranoid that the US will just try to topple them at some later date if they do not bring America to its knees.
They could care less when their people suffered in June 2025 and in early 2026, so they still do not care in late 2026 – not if it means giving up on their sense of victory and opens them to the possibility of another US-Israeli massive attack.
With five weeks to Election Day, there are no signs that Iran will change its tune anytime soon.
Meanwhile, Trump and his administration have alternated between saying they will immediately cut a deal with Iran after the midterms and saying they will immediately re-escalate into a full war with Iran after the midterms.
This means that the next fork in the road is set for five weeks from now.
Will Trump stick to his guns, thinking of protecting Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the region from Iranian hegemony and everyone, including the US, from an eventual Iranian nuclear weapon?
In that case, will there be a later point after the midterms when internal pressure on the IRGC forces it to return to nuclear concessions?
Or will Republican pressure from losing the midterms (almost accepted now as self-evident) compel Trump back into a bad deal with Iran to shore up short-term American interests, which will go against Israeli interests and long-term US security interests?
This monumental fork in the road is just over the horizon.

articles.title: UK Thwarts Suspected Terrorist Plot Against Base Used by US Bombers for Strikes on Iran
articles.body:
An air base in England where American bombers used to strike Iran are based was the target of a suspected bomb plot, U.K. officials said Sept. 27.
Five men were arrested on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses after being stopped close to RAF Fairford, police said, and explosive ordnance disposal technicians were dispatched to the scene. RAF Fairford is a British base currently hosting a dozen B-1B Lancer bombers, which have been stationed there for around seven months for strikes on Iran.
President Donald Trump said the suspects were “looking to do big damage” to the U.S. at RAF Fairford and called the arrests “fantastic” before boarding Air Force One on Sept. 27.
“We had them under view for a long time and we got them,” Trump added. “Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation.”
The base has been under increased security for days, which included the placement of vehicles around the perimeter, people familiar with the matter said. The threat level at the base was raised before the suspects were arrested. A U.S. Air Force spokesperson declined to discuss specific force protection measures, citing operational security.
Explosive ordnance teams from the British Army were called in to inspect the scene, and helicopter video footage aired by multiple U.K. news outlets showed a robot and personnel inspecting three white vans near the base fence, with B-1Bs parked on base nearby.
“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement.
Police said they were called by a local after receiving a report about three suspicious vehicles near RAF Fairford, which is located in Gloucestershire in southwest England.
“At around 12:45 a.m. today … police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be traveling towards the air base,” the Metropolitan Police, which investigates terrorism cases in the U.K., said in a Sept. 27 statement.
The U.K. government is still investigating the incident, counterterrorism officials said.
“We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said. “As you would expect, we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident.”
RAF Fairford does not have permanent U.S. Air Force aircraft assigned there, but it has a wing dedicated to supporting U.S. operations and is considered the main U.S. bomber site in Europe, having regularly hosted U.S. aircraft for years.
“The 501st Combat Support Wing and our other U.K.-based wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the Air Force spokesperson said. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people, and their families.”
Roadblocks, large machinery, and armed police have been seen around the base. Eighty-five homes in the nearby village of Whelford were evacuated.
“The emergency services have well-rehearsed plans for dealing with major incidents,” Gloucestershire Police assistant chief constable Richard Ocone said. “A cordon is in place as a precaution and the public can expect to see an emergency services presence in the area for some time.”
The B-1Bs at Fairford were heavily used during Operation Epic Fury, the large-scale air campaign against Iran in the spring, when the base housed some two dozen bombers including B-52 Stratofortresses.
Since a shaky ceasefire in April, most of the B-1Bs have remained while the U.S. carried out occasional strikes, including at least one involving a B-1 from Fairford. The bombers have regularly conducted training sorties out of the U.K.
The U.K. government gave permission for the base to be used in strikes on Iran in March under former Prime Minister Kier Starmer, for what the U.K. considers collective self-defense strikes. Burnham reaffirmed that decision in July, and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned the U.K. government that it considered Fairford a legitimate target for attack. The U.K. government said in July it was prepared to use the British armed forces to defend the base.
The U.S. Air Force said it would continue to cooperate with the U.K. government to ensure the safety of its bases in Britain. Another U.K. base with U.S. aircraft is RAF Lakenheath, which hosts F-35A Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters that have deployed to the Middle East for operations against Iran. Lakenheath is also used as a stopover location for fighters heading to the Middle East from the U.S.
“The safety and security of our Airmen, families, and surrounding communities remains our highest priority,” the Air Force spokesperson said. “We remain in close coordination with our U.K. partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities.”

articles.title: Why Iran's new push for a deal to end the war appears to be stalling - analysis
articles.body:
The perception is that Iran may be slowly losing the attrition blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran gambled on the idea that it could cut off shipping and hoped it would roil global markets. It wanted leverage that would pressure the US to end the war and the blockade. But the US has called Iran’s bluff for the most part.
The question is now why Iran has begun to talk up a seven-day relaxation of the blockade. That ceasefire plan has been floated for more than a week.
Tehran likely believed it could make this happen at the UN General Assembly. What happened, however, is that the US showed little interest. At least, most reports describe this cold shoulder as the US rejecting Iran’s push for a seven-day interim agreement.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reportedly said on Saturday that Tehran had yet to receive a formal response from Washington. While Iran had given a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the US has rejected this, Rudaw Media Network, a news channel in the autonomous Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq, reported.
Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz
Araghchi’s “remarks came hours after [US President Donald] Trump told Rudaw at the White House that he had ‘rejected’ Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days,” the report said.
Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting on Saturday quoted Araghchi as saying to journalists in New York: “We saw the first reaction from the US president, but nothing has yet been conveyed to us by the mediators.”
Rudaw Media Network quoted an Iranian diplomat as saying: “Reopening the Strait of Hormuz depends on these conditions being met; and we will make decisions based on a definitive response from the mediators.”
“Iran’s conditions for reopening the strategic waterway include the release of its frozen assets, an end to the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon, and the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iran,” the report said.
As such, it’s not clear whether the Trump administration would be willing to be seen as conceding to Iran. The US has invested a lot in this war since February. It will want something to show for it.
One of the main goals is preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. The focus of the war, however, has not actually been on the nuclear program.
This leaves a perplexing question, since Iran has shifted most of the talks to the Strait of Hormuz issue. Tehran has thus leveraged its proximity to the strategic waterway to make it the main issue of discussion.
“The Iranian initiative comes after Washington and Tehran resumed diplomatic contacts in New York this week on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly,” Rudaw Media Network reported. “Araghchi and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff held talks on Tuesday through Qatari mediators.”
The US is now waiting out Iran. The Trump administration appears to think time is on its side, and that it can wait until the midterms.
Even if it does go back into some kind of memorandum of understanding with Iran, or a deal, it will want something to show for six months of conflict, and that is the key.
So far, Tehran is not handing the US a “win.” Iran is talking about kicking the can down the road and doing more interim deals. It tried this in the summer as well.
Tehran also appears to be binding the hands of its negotiators so that it can’t get a deal anyway. The US no longer trusts this kind of Persian bazaar of negotiations.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before... or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly… with no chance of survival and no hope?”
Iran thinks it is winning
As long as the US believes the attrition is slowly going in its direction, there is no incentive to engage in another short-term deal in which Iran benefits. Tehran will need to come up with something more than its “seven days” concept, and it might have to adjust its demands for US concessions.
Iran thinks it is winning. The US also thinks it is winning. When both sides think they are winning, it is harder to get to an agreement.
Where Trump has excelled in the past is giving both sides the appearance of a win. The challenge today is that both sides believe time is on their side.

articles.title: Bundestag Approves Purchase of AIM-120, Meteor and Air Defense Systems for German Armed Forces
articles.body:
The Bundestag’s Budget Committee has approved a package of procurement and modernization programs for the Bundeswehr covering air-to-air missiles, air defense, armored vehicles, naval systems and strategic airlift.
The German Federal Ministry of Defence reported this following the Budget Committee’s meeting on September 23.
The Air Force will receive two additional batches of AIM-120 AMRAAM missiles for F-35A and Eurofighter fighters. The procurement will be carried out through the U.S. Foreign Military Sales program and financed from Germany’s defense budget.
The Bundeswehr will also receive two special batches of Meteor missiles for Eurofighters. They are intended to test tactics and technical solutions and to support integration work as part of the fighter’s radar modernization.
For the Navy, the committee approved a naval adaptation of the IRIS-T SLM system for F125-class frigates. The German Defense Ministry said this is intended to strengthen their self-defense capabilities against air threats.
Militarnyi previously reported that in October 2025, the naval version of IRIS-T SLM had already been tested aboard the Baden-Württemberg frigate during firing exercises off Norway. At the time, the system was installed on the ship’s deck as a separate module.
For the Army, the committee approved the integration of digital radios into Fennek 1A1 and 1A2 reconnaissance vehicles. Some surplus Fenneks will also be upgraded to the Joint Fire Support Team A5.1 standard as an interim solution until the arrival of corresponding vehicles based on the GTK Boxer.
The committee also approved the second amendment to the contract for the NNbS short- and very-short-range air defense system. Among other things, fire-control vehicle modules and air defense missile vehicle modules will be adapted to the standardized Boxer B0 chassis, while the air defense vehicle simulator will be built in a containerized configuration.
A separate procurement covers 70 mm rockets in combat and training configurations for Tiger attack helicopters and the Bundeswehr’s light combat helicopters. The committee also approved additional laser designators for Joint Fire Support Team dismounted teams.
For the Navy, one of two full-function NH90 simulators will be upgraded to integrate the NATO Frigate Helicopter German Navy Step 3 configuration. The Bundeswehr will also receive new multipurpose combat boats for the naval battalion, along with training, documentation and equipment.
In addition, a new contract under the Strategic Airlift International Solution was approved, guaranteeing the Bundeswehr access to strategic airlift aircraft for transporting oversized and heavy cargo.
As part of efforts to strengthen air defense, Germany is also increasing its procurement of IRIS-T systems.
As Militarnyi previously reported, in February 2026 the Bundeswehr ordered additional batches of IRIS-T missiles for SLS and SLM ground-based systems and combat aircraft.

articles.title: Iran to punish Trump, Netanyahu even after war ends
articles.body:
Iran's senior armed forces spokesman, General Abolfazl Shekarchi, said the Strait of Hormuz remains under Iranian control despite American provocations, warning that no vessel can guarantee safe passage without Tehran's approval.
Speaking in a televised interview, Shekarchi reviewed the history of the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, which he said was imposed on Iran under US leadership. He said the war, despite heavy losses, helped build the capabilities of Iran's armed forces from its early days, citing popular mobilization through the Basij as a key achievement.
Shekarchi said Iran's post-revolution military shifted its doctrine from conventional to asymmetric warfare, which he described as relying on lower-cost, simpler but effective equipment to counter the enemy's expensive heavy weaponry.
He said Iran had once been unable to buy basic medical supplies for wounded troops during the Iran-Iraq war, but has since become self-sufficient in producing modern defense equipment.
Shekarchi said Iran's armed forces are now significantly stronger than at the start of previous wars, adding that Iran's missiles and drones have become more advanced and that the country holds surprises for any future act of aggression using new military technology. He said Iran has not attacked the sovereignty of neighboring Muslim countries and that its responses have targeted American interests and facilities within those countries.
He warned neighboring Muslim states to reconsider their positions, saying reliance on the United States would not serve them, and said Iran would not make the slightest retreat in the face of the enemy.
On the Strait of Hormuz, Shekarchi said any vessel attempting passage outside Iran's designated routes would not be secure, and warned Washington against any interference in the strait, saying such a move would be met with force. He said Iran, as a global power, would never allow the United States to regain its former position in the international order, adding that American forces have no path to safety other than withdrawing from West Asia, and that the sooner they leave, the smaller their losses would be.
Referring to US President Donald Trump and Israeli regime’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Shekarchi said Iran would continue to pursue the killers of the country's martyred Leader and the Iranian people even after the end of the war, adding that they would be punished for their actions.

articles.title: Hezbollah marks second anniversary of Sayyed Nasrallah’s martyrdom with vows of continued resistance
articles.body:
Hezbollah marks second anniversary of Sayyed Nasrallah’s martyrdom with vows of continued resistance
Sheikh Qassem vows Hezbollah will not surrender weapons at massive Beirut commemoration
TEHRAN — The southern suburbs of Beirut transformed into a sprawling sea of black and yellow on Sunday. Tens of thousands of mourners converged on the shrine of Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah to mark two years since his assassination in an Israeli airstrike.
Crowds filled the streets surrounding the site in Bir al-Abed near the old airport road. Their chants of loyalty rose above the din of a city still bearing the physical scars of the U.S.-backed Israeli bombing campaign.
Many attendees carried portraits of Sayyed Nasrallah and his successor, Sayyed Hashem Safieddine, who was martyred in an Israeli strike mere days after his mentor.
Gathering in a neighborhood that Israeli warplanes systematically reduced to rubble was a deliberate statement of defiance. Mourners traveled from southern villages still under the threat of occupation.
Faithful to the pledge
Addressing the massive gathering in a televised broadcast, Hezbollah Secretary-General Sheikh Naim Sheikh Qassem delivered an uncompromising defense of the resistance. His speech served as both a tribute to the fallen commanders and a blunt indictment of Lebanon’s political establishment.
Sheikh Qassem spoke directly to the martyred leaders. He told Sayyed Nasrallah that while his physical body had departed, his teachings remain the driving force of the movement.
“You are the resistance and the resistance is you, and you have become its symbol for the free people of the world,” Sheikh Qassem declared. He praised Sayyed Safieddine as an indispensable pillar of the jihadist journey who never tired in his service to the cause.
The organizing theme of the memorial was “Inna Ala al-Ahd” (We remain faithful to the pledge). Sheikh Qassem defined this phrase as absolute operational continuity.
When leaders are martyred, new commanders immediately step forward to maintain the exact same trajectory, the Resistance leader explained. The pledge guarantees the continuation of the courageous, divine resistance against foreign aggression until every inch of occupied land is fully liberated.
The battlefield ledger
Sheikh Qassem then pivoted to the military realities on the ground, systematically dismantling the arguments of domestic opponents who question the utility of Hezbollah’s arms.
He turned the scrutiny back on the government. “Some, especially among our opponents, ask: what has the Resistance done?” he noted. “But it seems they forgot to ask: what has the state done?”
Hezbollah halted the Israeli aggression project, the Hezbollah leader explained.
Sheikh Qassem stated that the Israeli military deployed up to 90,000 soldiers and officers, backed by unlimited American capabilities, yet utterly failed to break the resistance. Israeli forces were physically prevented from establishing permanent occupation zones or settlements in Lebanon, he explained.
Fighters delivered legendary performances across the southern front. Sheikh Qassem listed the battlegrounds where Hezbollah forces entrenched themselves and bled the advancing brigades.
They held their ground in Bint Jbeil, Khiam, Aita al-Shaab, Naqoura, and al-Bayyada. At the Ali al-Taher ridge, resistance units maintained their defensive posture under heavy bombardment for three consecutive months, Sheikh Qassem stated.
He honored the 3,400 martyrs and 14,600 wounded from Operation People of Might. Sheikh Qassem directed special recognition to the survivors of the pager terror attacks, calling them living martyrs who transformed their wounds into active resistance.
Domestic betrayal and the disarmament illusion
The sharpest political warnings targeted Lebanon’s governing authority. Sheikh Qassem accused the state of acting as “an accessory” to the Israeli-American project by offering unforced concessions.
He argued that the current framework agreement handed Israel all of Lebanon’s negotiating leverage in a single session. Pointing to seven rounds of direct negotiations that yielded results “below zero,” he demanded an immediate freeze on direct talks.
The secretary-general ridiculed the persistent demands for Hezbollah to surrender its weapons. “You stayed two years trying to strip the weapons and you could not, so why do you ask the Lebanese Army?” he asked.
Asking the national army to serve as a disarmament tool for political factions is a delusion, the Resistance leader said.
Sheikh Qassem affirmed that Hezbollah will never forfeit a single inch of Lebanon’s 10,452 square kilometers.
Turning to the collapse of the Lebanese state, he asked where the government was regarding the ruined economy, hyperinflation, electricity blackouts, and stolen depositor funds.
Sheikh Qassem announced that Hezbollah, utilizing its own resources and donor funding, will shortly unveil a comprehensive housing and reconstruction project for displaced citizens, stepping in where the state has completely vanished.
Concluding his address, Sheikh Qassem reaffirmed that Palestine remains the absolute compass for the resistance.
He saluted the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Leader of the Islamic Revolution for their steadfast backing.
Pointing to Israel’s isolation at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, he noted that the regime has become an exposed global pariah.

The issues expected to be discussed include a possible end to the war, reducing strikes on energy infrastructure, and the safety of shipping, Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov said in a comment to Novyny.LIVE, as reported by UNN.
According to Budanov, the Ukrainian side is preparing for a meeting at which a number of security and technical issues are to be considered.
"First, we are planning such a meeting. Second, reducing strikes on the energy sector. Well, terrorism is abnormal in principle. Security, shipping, and so on. We have many technical issues," the Head of the Office of the President said.
He named next month—October—as the tentative timeframe for the talks. At the same time, Budanov did not specify the exact date, location of the meeting, or composition of the delegations.
The Head of the Office of the President had previously also spoken about preparations for the October round of talks. In particular, on September 12, on the sidelines of the Yalta European Strategy (YES) forum in Kyiv, he confirmed to the media that Ukraine was preparing for talks in October in a trilateral format. At the time, he did not comment on a potential location for the meeting.
The United States proposed a technical meeting in the UAE
On September 25, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the American side had proposed preparing a meeting of representatives of Ukraine, the United States, and Russia at the technical level. Washington proposed the United Arab Emirates as a possible venue. At the time of the statement, Kyiv was awaiting proposals from the United States regarding the date. According to the president, the Ukrainian and American negotiating groups had also agreed to hold consultations with the European side. After that, the United States was to establish contacts with Russia, and approximately ten days later the parties planned to return to discussing the results. This timeframe concerned the consultations, not an announced date for trilateral talks.
That same day, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that the possibility of such a meeting had been discussed during a phone call between Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. He allowed for it to take place in the near future, but did not provide any specific parameters.
What is being discussed regarding energy and shipping
The issue of a mutual cessation of strikes on energy infrastructure had already been raised during diplomatic contacts in September.
On September 14, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to support de-escalation if its American partners could ensure Russia's genuine and long-term readiness to stop the strikes. This position was voiced after Trump's statement that the parties had allegedly reached an agreement not to attack energy facilities. At the same time, as Reuters reported, neither Ukraine nor Russia confirmed that such an agreement had been concluded at the time.
A separate area is the safety of maritime transport. On September 23, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to do its part to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea, provided that Russia took genuine steps toward de-escalation.
According to the president, Egypt, India, and Turkey proposed their own options for ensuring maritime security. Ukraine supported measures capable of ensuring safe shipping and was awaiting a response from the Russian side.
Context
On September 6, American representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Zelenskyy in Kyiv after visiting Moscow. Following the meeting, the president confirmed Ukraine's readiness for trilateral talks. The parties also discussed the supply of air defense systems and support for Ukraine's energy sector ahead of winter.
We remind you
Earlier, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Russian leader Vladimir Putin was looking for excuses not to meet and not to end the war.

articles.title: Israel cannot secure the Red Sea without an African strategy - opinion
articles.body:
Israel has learned, at terrible cost, that dangers dismissed as distant do not remain distant. The same complacency that helped leave the country unprepared before October 7 now shapes its view of the Red Sea. Israel watches Yemen, intercepts Houthi missiles, and deploys naval power, yet it still lacks an African strategy for the waterway connecting Eilat to the world.
I write this as an Ethiopian-born Israeli-American who knows these societies. Africa is not a map I discovered in a security briefing. Ethiopia is where I was born. Israel is the homeland for which Ethiopian Jews prayed for centuries. America taught me how institutions, alliances, and public accountability can turn power into lasting influence. From that perspective, Israel’s approach is dangerously incomplete.
The problem is larger than the Houthis. Iranian-backed forces threaten ships near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Somali piracy is again rising in the Gulf of Aden. Eritrea remains a closed, militarized dictatorship, often called the North Korea of Africa, along a coastline. Meanwhile, Ethiopia, Africa’s second-most-populous nation and the headquarters of the African Union, depends on Djibouti for access to maritime trade.
This is not a collection of unrelated emergencies. It is one regional failure. The warning signs are no longer theoretical. Maritime authorities recorded two dozen attempted or completed incidents of piracy and armed robbery across the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden region in only three months this year.
Renewed Houthi advances along Yemen’s coast have increased anxiety around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, while conflict has displaced families toward Djibouti. Every government concerned with free navigation should understand what is at stake.
The Red Sea carries trade between Asia, Africa, and Europe. When terrorists fire missiles, pirates seize crews, or governments weaponize ports, the cost reaches American consumers, European industries, African families, and Israeli businesses.
Warships can escort vessels and aircraft can destroy launchers. But missiles cannot build legitimate institutions, create employment, or settle disputes among nations and communities.
The deeper analysis must confront an uncomfortable Ethiopian history. The leadership of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front and the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front emerged as allied guerrilla movements and later controlled Addis Ababa and Asmara.
I regard their leadership as a revolutionary political cartel that is secretive, ethnically divisive, and self-serving. My parents and I are living witnesses to the human consequences of that war. Their policies did not create democratic peace. They left authoritarianism, disputed borders, economic dependency, and unfinished tribal war and the Amhara ethnic cleansing.
Ethiopia’s Red Sea relationship is not a recent invention. The ancient Kingdom of Aksum reached the coast through Adulis, a port linking Africa to international trade. And Eritrea’s 1993 independence referendum cannot erase the reality. But neither should the international community pretend that one ballot settled every question fairly for every affected population.
The process did not adequately resolve the security of Afar communities whose historic homeland crosses Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Djibouti, and Ethiopia’s maritime future or long-term rights. Many Ethiopians believe the TPLF leadership accepted the loss of Assab and direct Red Sea access without securing a durable national arrangement.
Afar and other dissenting voices have long argued that decisions imposed by armed movements did not represent the full complexity of local loyalties. These grievances should be investigated and heard, not converted into propaganda for another war.
Ethiopia's need for dependable, diversified, and affordable sea access is real. But that need does not justify invading Eritrea or erasing internationally recognized borders. A nation of more than 130 million people should not be economically trapped; neither should smaller states live under threat. The answer is negotiated port access and enforceable regional guarantees.
Coordinating with African nations over the Red Sea
Israel should propose a Red Sea partnership led jointly with African states. Ethiopia, Djibouti, Kenya, Somalia, and willing regional partners should coordinate maritime intelligence, anti-piracy operations, port security, and emergency response. The African Union, United States, European Union, and responsible Arab governments should support it. Somaliland’s practical role in regional security should be discussed without casually dismissing Somalia’s sovereignty.
This partnership should establish a permanent regional secretariat, joint maritime exercises, a piracy prosecution framework, and an infrastructure fund connecting inland economies to multiple ports. It should guarantee commercial access without transferring sovereignty and require transparent contracts so ports do not become trophies for foreign powers.
Local Afar and coastal representatives must hold seats at the table. Peace negotiated only by presidents, generals, and financiers will remain fragile.
The partnership must also address conditions on land. Piracy and extremism flourish where young people see no work, governments offer no justice, and outside powers arrive only with weapons. Investment in ports, railways, education, water, agriculture, and coastal employment is security policy, not charity.
Israel also has a strategic resource it continues to overlook: Ethiopian Israelis. We understand African political culture, Jewish history, and Israel’s security concerns. Qualified Ethiopian Israelis should serve in diplomacy, national security, intelligence, and African missions. We should not be displayed as evidence of diversity while decisions are made elsewhere.
Our community also answers a lie spreading internationally: that Zionism is a white colonial project. Ethiopian Jews carried Jerusalem in our prayers across generations. We are a social capital and a living evidence that the Jewish people are not one color and that the bond between Africa and Zion is ancient. Yet our value is greater than public relations. We can help Israel build relationships based on dignity rather than emergency transactions.
Leadership renewal begins by abandoning the arrogance that military superiority alone creates security. Israel must listen before the crisis becomes a catastrophe, engage Africa as a partner, and include people who know the region from within.
The Red Sea can become a corridor of shared prosperity or a battlefield controlled by terrorists, pirates, and dictators. Israel may win engagements without an African strategy. It will still lose the larger struggle for secure trade, regional legitimacy, and lasting peace.
The writer is a former New York City Supreme Court detective, an investigator and educator in conflict resolution and restorative peace, and a moral diplomacy expert. His upcoming book, Moral Diplomacy for a Broken World, is inspired by the late Rabbi Jonathan Sacks.

articles.title: Zelensky says over 10,000 Russian troops killed or wounded this week as Ukrainian military advances in Lyman sector

Zelensky says over 10,000 Russian troops killed or wounded this week as Ukrainian military advances in Lyman sector
Ukrainian forces have killed or wounded 10,660 Russian troops over the past week while making gains in the Lyman sector of Donetsk Oblast, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 27.
"The occupiers continue to be eliminated, and the designated objectives are being achieved," Zelensky wrote on X, citing a report by Ukraine's Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi.
According to Zelensky, Ukrainian forces have video evidence confirming every Russian loss included in the weekly figure. Russia does not routinely disclose its military losses, and the figures could not be independently verified.
Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 15 that Russian forces have lost more than 300,000 troops killed and wounded since the beginning of 2026. After the summer campaign on the battlefield in Ukraine ended, Russian losses exceeded 1.5 million since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Zelensky said the past week's results were achieved as part of Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman sector and another active defense operation involving Ukraine's Air Assault Forces.
Zelensky added that the heaviest fighting has been taking place in the Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka, and Lyman sectors, while Ukrainian forces are also carrying out operations in Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, and Sumy oblasts.
He did not provide further details on the territorial gains.
Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps offensive operation around Lyman in northern Donetsk Oblast, was only made public on Sept. 15, although Russian pro-war Telegram channels and independent open-source intelligence (OSINT) researchers on social media had been tracking Ukrainian attacks in the area since late spring 2026.
On Sept. 20, the 3rd Corps said it liberated a further 40 square kilometers (15.4 square miles) of territory in Donetsk Oblast and retook several villages during the ongoing offensive.

articles.title: ‘Russian sleeper cell’: Can Germany’s far-right AfD be barred from sensitive intel?
articles.body:
‘Russian sleeper cell’: Can Germany’s far-right AfD be barred from sensitive intel?
The prospect of an AfD-led government in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt has exacerbated long-standing fears that the far-right Russia-friendly party may gain access to sensitive information of interest to the Kremlin, fuelling debate as to whether and how it can be barred from classified intelligence.
What happens when Germany’s domestic intelligence service is monitored by the very people it is meant to spy on?
The once speculative question has acquired sudden urgency – for both Germany and its allies – in the wake of a regional election that has put the German far right on the cusp of power for the first time since 1945.
The Alternative for Democracy (AfD) party scored a resounding election win in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month and is trying to form a coalition government in the small eastern state, one of 16 that enjoy broad powers under Germany’s federal system.
If it succeeds, the Moscow-friendly party could notably gain access to intelligence gathered by agencies tracking both domestic and external threats, a prospect that has spooked officials amid escalating tensions over the war in Ukraine and a surge in hybrid attacks attributed to Russia.
Watch moreOnly the beginning? German far right's breakthrough shakes Europe to its core
According to French investigative and satirical weekly Canard Enchaîné, such concerns were enough for France’s domestic intelligence agency to notify its German counterpart last week of its plans to withhold sensitive information about far-right extremists and Russia should the AfD govern in Saxony-Anhalt.
Unmasking spy cops
Germany’s domestic intelligence service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), has consistently ranked right-wing extremists as the greatest threat to German democracy. Its latest annual report, published in June, said their number had increased significantly to 58,700 last year, fuelled by a surge in support for the AfD.
The BfV stirred controversy last year when it designated the AfD as a right-wing “extremist group”, though the classification was suspended in February after a legal challenge from the party.
While the national party is now designated as “suspected extremist”, pending a court ruling, its local chapter in Saxony-Anhalt has a “confirmed extremist” label that means it is under surveillance by federal intelligence, including undercover agents.
German officials fear that an AfD government in the eastern state could use routine intelligence sharing to find those agents and scupper efforts to monitor it, said Jacob Ross, a Senior Research Fellow at the German Council on Foreign Relations.
“If the AfD gets hold of the interior minister job in charge of police forces and intelligence, they would potentially have access to files about their own surveillance,” Ross explained. “One of the big fears in the intelligence community, and more widely in German politics, is that they would then very rapidly try to find out who within their own ranks is spying on them.”
An asset for Russia
A greater concern for Germany and its allies is the possibility that sensitive information regarding German, European and NATO security arrangements might end up in Russian hands.
Before the election in Saxony-Anhalt, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius told German newspaper Bild that he opposed sharing classified information with AfD officials should they enter regional governments, stressing that their “close ties to (Russian President Vladimir) Putin are undeniable”.
The far-right party has repeatedly sparked alarm in Berlin by requesting information on vulnerabilities in German and NATO defences that would be of interest to Russia. In a heated debate at the Bundestag last November, a lawyer for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s ruling conservatives accused the AfD of harbouring a Russian “sleeper cell” intent on investigating Germany’s critical infrastructure.
Fears of sensitive information falling in Russian hands are well founded, according to Anton Shekhovtsov, director of the Austria-based Centre for Democratic Integrity and an expert on the European far right and its links to Russia.
With Hungary’s Viktor Orban out of power, “The AfD is now the largest and strongest pro-Russian party in the entire European Union,” Shekhovtsov argued, citing “extensive links with Russia that have been built over many years”. He added: “Obviously this is a weak spot for Germany and for the EU when it comes to dealing with Moscow and the political warfare that it is waging in Europe.”
Read moreFive takeaways from Germany's regional elections after far-right gains
According to a New York Times report published on Tuesday, the German federal government has moved swiftly to allay concerns among EU allies, drafting plans to block an AfD-led state government from reviewing sensitive intelligence.
One notable measure involves denying AfD officials access to a secret war plan drafted in 2024, a 1,000-page blueprint detailing how Germany and its allies would respond to a Russian attack similar to the invasion of Ukraine. Other possible steps include withholding intelligence concerning Russian subterfuge and investigations into far-right extremists.
The Austrian precedent
There are precedents for European countries restricting access to intelligence when dealing with far-right parties that are seen as cozying up to Russia. One notable example is Orban’s Hungary, which France accused of “betraying” the EU by leaking information to Moscow, just weeks before the longtime nationalist leader was voted out of power.
Austria also came under intense scrutiny after the far-right Freedom Party joined a coalition government in 2017 and secured the interior ministry portfolio, leading some European partners to place limits on intelligence sharing.
“The perception at the time was that Austrian security and intelligence services were deeply penetrated by Russia,” said Ross. “Those in Germany who argue in favour of excluding AfD from information flows often point to the Austrian case, warning that Germany could also lose its reputation as a trustworthy ally when it comes to intelligence-sharing mechanisms.”
Placing caveats on intelligence sharing is relatively commonplace, including between close allies, said Dan Lomas, an assistant professor in International Relations at the University of Nottingham specialising in intelligence and security-related issues.
“Intelligence services that cooperate on, say, counterterrorism might seek to limit the flow of other intel when they think it could be leaked,” he explained. “They might also seek to bypass specific figures in government, sharing information with other domestic services but with the caveat that it mustn’t be passed on to certain officials.”
Such limitations could pose logistical challenges should AfD continue its ascent at the regional level, warned Ross, pointing to the specificities of Germany’s federal system. Just days after triumphing in Saxony-Anhalt, the party also topped elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, underscoring its dominance in swaths of the country.
In the event of a major crisis, “keeping AfD-run states in the dark could create holes in operational plans”, he said. “Because while the army and the defence of German territory are within the purview of the federal government, the police forces needed to secure roads, convoys and power stations are the responsibility of individual states.”
Breach of trust
Another long-term problem, added Lomas, is that such limitations breed mistrust between security services, elected officials and the broader public, while also posing problems of democracy.
“Even if you find a practical way to work around the AfD, doing this is corrosive at a time when public trust in liberal Western democracies is already under threat,” he said.
Read moreHow far-right AfD breakthrough may ‘cause absolute chaos’ in Germany
Efforts to restrict far-right access to state secrets could lead to legal challenges from AfD, which argues that the country’s mainstream parties are undermining democracy by thwarting the will of voters.
Jork Herrmann, an AfD spokesman, told the New York Times, “It would be utterly undemocratic and impossible to justify to voters to withhold intelligence information from the party based on unsubstantiated and unprovable allegations.”
If the courts agree with Germany’s domestic intelligence agency and confirm AfD as an “extremist” organisation that poses a danger to the constitution, that would give the federal government “legitimate grounds not to share sensitive information”, said Shekhovtsov. But if they don’t, he added, “it’s hard to see on what grounds they could be kept in the dark.”
The conundrum facing German officials underscores the limitations of the “firewall” strategy aimed at keeping the far right out of power, argued Ross. He contrasted that approach with French President Emmanuel Macron’s decision last week to convene all major parties – including Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally party, which is polling well ahead of rivals ahead of elections next year – for an intelligence briefing on the threat of hybrid attacks from Russia.
“Macron seems to think it’s best to brief the National Rally rather than have pro-Russian experts do so,” he said. “In Germany, we’re counting on the firewall to hold firm. But if it doesn’t, then we have a huge problem.”

articles.title: Ukraine Now Neutralizes 55% of Russia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Drones, Zelenskyy Says
articles.body:
- Category

Ukraine Now Neutralizes 55% of Russia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Drones, Zelenskyy Says
Ukraine is currently neutralizing about 55% of the jet-powered Shahed-type drones launched by Russia, with more than 1,500 such UAVs shot down or suppressed since the beginning of September.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in his evening address on September 26, Russia launched more than 2,730 jet-powered Shahed drones during September. More than 1,500 were intercepted or electronically suppressed, putting Ukraine’s current neutralization rate at approximately 55%.
The rate remains below Ukraine’s interception performance against conventional Shahed-type drones, which Zelenskyy said now exceeds 90%. He said Ukraine aims to bring protection against the newer jet-powered variants to a comparable level.
Ukraine has already developed several effective prototype interceptors designed specifically to counter the faster drones, Zelenskyy said. Some are already being used by Ukrainian units under combat conditions, while several systems have been selected as potential primary tools for defending against the threat.
Ukraine is now working to expand production of those interceptors and the components required to manufacture them at scale, according to the president.
Zelenskyy also said Ukrainian military intelligence had obtained Russian internal documents detailing Moscow’s weapons-production plans for 2027, including planned volumes and financing.
According to the documents cited by Zelenskyy, Russia intends to spend about $12 billion next year on the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions alone.
The growing use of jet-powered Shahed variants has added another layer to Russia’s long-range drone campaign against Ukraine. Unlike conventional propeller-driven Shaheds, the newer systems travel at higher speeds, reducing the time available for Ukrainian air defenses to detect and intercept them.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine is developing dedicated countermeasures for the systems identified in Russia’s production plans, with interceptor drones expected to play a larger role in defending Ukrainian airspace as production expands.

articles.title: Iran ‘fully prepared’ for war to resume: ‘It is up to President Trump to choose,’ Araghchi says
articles.body:
Iran is prepared for renewed fighting with the United States but remains open to diplomacy, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday after U.S. President Donald Trump publicly rejected Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Speaking to NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” Araghchi said Iran had not yet received an official response through mediators despite Trump’s announcement that he had turned down the proposal.
“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed. We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war,” Araghchi said when asked about a Wall Street Journal report that Trump could seek to resume bombing after the U.S. midterm elections. “At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.”
Iran presented the proposal this week through mediator Qatar on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Under the plan, Tehran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restore normal maritime traffic through the critical global oil route within seven days, alongside a return to negotiations with Washington. Recent reporting has also described the proposal as tied to conditions similar to those contained in the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding reached in June. CNN Transcripts
Trump said Saturday that he had rejected the proposal. “I rejected their deal. They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly.”
Araghchi, however, told moderator Kristen Welker that Trump’s rejection had not yet been formally communicated to Tehran through the countries mediating between the two sides.
The Iranian foreign minister said Tehran remained prepared to reopen the strait as part of a broader agreement ending the conflict. In return, he said, “we want our monies, our assets, which are illegally frozen, to be released. We want to be able to sell our oil.”
Araghchi described those conditions as “not new,” saying Washington had previously committed to them under the memorandum of understanding signed by the two countries in June. The arrangement collapsed within days after the sides exchanged fresh strikes.
“If you ask us, there is no reason why we should go back to diplomacy,” Araghchi said. “But I am still trying diplomacy because I think we shouldn’t miss any chance for peace.”
He also dismissed suggestions that Tehran’s calculations were being shaped by the approaching U.S. midterm elections.
“We don’t care about U.S. midterm elections,” he said. “We care about our national interests.”
Before Araghchi’s appearance, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz also spoke to “Meet the Press,” saying Washington rejected Tehran’s proposal for “a number of reasons.” Waltz is serving as the U.S. ambassador to the UN.
“I think this was a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable, to ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions, and access to billions in assets,” Waltz said.
Waltz also questioned “who’s calling the shots in Iran right now,” and accused Tehran of violating the previous memorandum of understanding by attacking international shipping.
“I think it’s kind of common sense that the president doesn’t have a lot of confidence this time after we just tried a few months ago,” Waltz said. “What I can tell you is the president will leave all options on the table to ensure the world is safe from Iran holding the world hostage with a nuclear weapon.”
Asked what kind of agreement Trump would be prepared to accept, Waltz declined to lay out terms.
“I’m not going to negotiate for the president.”
“This is about keeping the next generation safe from Iran threatening the world with a nuclear weapon,” he added.
Trump earlier this week said he was still weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran or reach an agreement, while publicly linking the timing of a possible deal to the November midterm elections.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”
The confrontation with Iran has become an increasingly prominent issue in U.S. politics ahead of the November vote. Trump used his address to the UN General Assembly last week to defend his approach toward Iran and again said his administration would not allow Tehran to obtain a nuclear weapon.

articles.title: Trump left Saudi Arabia to face Houthis alone – Mearsheimer to RT (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Trump left Saudi Arabia to face Houthis alone – Mearsheimer to RT (VIDEO)
US President Donald Trump has effectively abandoned Saudi Arabia, a key ally in the Middle East, leaving it to face “almost a full-blown war” with Yemen’s Houthis, political scientist and University of Chicago Professor John Mearsheimer said in an interview with RT.
Hostilities between Riyadh and the Shiite militant group, officially known as Ansarullah, have flared up in recent weeks after several years of relative calm. The Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory, while Riyadh-backed government forces have tried to hold off the group’s advances inside Yemen.
Earlier this month, the Houthis seized control over Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a key waterway which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on for oil exports since navigation through the Strait of Hormuz was reduced to a trickle amid the US-Israeli war against Iran.
In an interview with New Order host Afshin Rattansi on Sunday, Mearsheimer said that because of its “foolish” decision to “attack the Houthis and pick a fight with them,” Saudi Arabia has found itself in “really deep trouble.” He added that the “Houthis are a formidable fighting force, and the Saudis are not.”
He went on to suggest, citing media reports, that Trump encouraged Riyadh to strike an airport in the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in mid-July. The attack, which was apparently meant to prevent an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from Tehran from landing, shattered the UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis, triggering the current escalation.
Mearsheimer gave credence to claims made earlier this month by the New York Times, which said Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman phoned Trump on multiple occasions in recent weeks, asking for military support against the Houthis. The president decided, however, not to intervene, according to the NYT. 
Trump was reportedly close to authorizing strikes on the Houthis last weekend, but reversed his decision at the last minute.
According to Mearsheimer, “the last thing [Trump] wants to do is get into a fight with [the Houthis] to try to rescue Saudi Arabia” – not least because of how badly America’s attempt to bomb the Houthis into submission went last year.
Less than two months into the campaign, Trump abruptly announced a ceasefire, declaring victory and saying the Houthis promised not to attack US ships.
“But in fact, the Houthis beat the United States. We did not defeat the Houthis,” Mearsheimer said.
Speaking to Al-Mayadeen on Saturday, the head of the National Security Committee in the Iranian Parliament, Ibrahim Azizi, warned neighboring Arab nations against cooperating with the US and allowing it to use their territory as a launchpad for attacks.
Azizi added that the US security umbrella in the Middle East has proven to be ineffective.

articles.title: Iran Claims to Have Seized Second U.S. Underwater Drone in Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has claimed to have seized a U.S. REMUS 600 UUV in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian media outlet IRIB reported this, citing a statement by the IRGC Navy.
According to the Iranian side, the UUV was detected while conducting a reconnaissance mission in the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC said the seizure operation was conducted using intelligence capabilities and electronic warfare systems.
After being seized, the REMUS 600 UUV was handed over to Iranian specialists, who are expected to examine the vehicle and attempt to retrieve information from its storage systems. The Iranian side also released video footage of the captured vehicle.
The United States has not officially confirmed the loss of this particular vehicle or disclosed the circumstances of its seizure.
The REMUS 600 is an autonomous uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV) developed in the United States. It was designed as a multipurpose platform for underwater missions, including reconnaissance, seafloor mapping, mine detection and classification, oceanographic data collection and the search for underwater objects.
The REMUS 600 can operate at depths of up to 600 meters. Underwater navigation is carried out autonomously using an inertial navigation system, Doppler velocity log and acoustic navigation, while GPS can be used after the vehicle surfaces.
According to Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, the REMUS 600 can remain operational for about 70 hours and has a range of up to 286 nautical miles.
The Iranian side said the vehicle’s recorded routes, sonar data, navigation parameters and other information that may have remained in its memory could be of particular value.
This is the second case in September in which Iran has claimed to have seized a U.S. UUV. On September 8, the IRGC Navy reported the seizure of a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle made by Anduril near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
The U.S. side then confirmed the loss of the vehicle, but said it had malfunctioned before falling into the hands of Iranian forces and did not contain classified equipment.
In July, U.S. Central Command used maritime kamikaze drones for the first time to strike Iranian military targets.
