articles.title: Men arrested in major incident at UK air base used by US
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Men arrested on explosives offences in major incident at UK air base used by US
British police said on Sunday they had arrested several men on suspicion of explosives offences and Army bomb disposal experts were examining a number of vehicles in a "major incident" near an air base used by the US in southwest England.
Police said nearby residents had been evacuated from their homes.
The British government gave authorisation to the US to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned in July that any base used in strikes would be a legitimate target.
A Reuters eyewitness said armed police had blocked access to the main gate of the base, while equipment had been positioned in front of access points and residents of a nearby village were evacuated to a leisure centre.
Around 30 emergency vehicles, including police cars, ambulances and fire engines, were stationed in the village of Fairford near the base.
"A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident. It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act," Gloucestershire police said in a statement, referring to a village near the air base.
"The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles."
Police said they believed the incident was now contained.
A spokesperson for the US Air Force declined to discuss specific force protection measures.
"The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families," the spokesperson said.
"We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families."
Britain said in July its armed forces were ready to protect the country from any attack after Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned the UK not to allow US bombers to fly from Fairford.
British ministers have also briefed providers of critical infrastructure on the threat posed by Russia, with the government increasingly concerned about possible sabotage operations and cyberattacks. Russia denies mounting hybrid attacks on Western nations.
(Reuters)

articles.title: Latvia moves to buy American long-range strike missiles
articles.body:
Latvia is moving to acquire Anduril Industries’ Barracuda family of long-range cruise missiles, a purchase that would make it the first Baltic state to field a strike weapon of that reach, following a visit by President Edgars Rinkēvičs to the American company’s California facilities on 25 September, the president stated in a post published after the visit.
Writing on X, Mr Rinkēvičs said: “It was great to visit Anduril to meet with Palmer Luckey and to witness signing of memoranda of cooperation with MOD of Latvia and Origin Robotics. Looking forward to complete acquisition of Barracuda long-range missiles and Latvian-US defense industry cooperation.”
Neither Latvia nor Anduril has disclosed which variant is wanted, how many missiles would be bought, the price or a delivery date.
The Barracuda-500M, the long-range member of the family, has a range of more than 500 nautical miles, or around 926 kilometres, which is roughly three times the reach of the ATACMS rounds Latvia has ordered for its HIMARS launchers. Given that the country operates no fast jets and has a limited helicopter fleet, a ground-launched configuration would be the obvious route for it to take.
Anduril offers the family as an answer to a shortfall in affordable, producible long-range precision weapons, claiming it requires half the production time, 95 per cent fewer tools and half the parts of comparable weapons. The variants can operate autonomously and collaboratively with one another, acting as decoys as well as conducting strikes, and can be launched from fighters, helicopters, cargo aircraft, ships and ground launchers.
Production is already being scaled up on both sides of the Atlantic. The American Department of War signed a framework agreement in May for at least 1,000 surface-launched Barracuda-500Ms a year over three years for the United States Army, starting in 2027, and in July the Polish state group PGZ agreed to assemble and later produce the same variant at its Military Aviation Works No. 2 plant at Bydgoszcz. PGZ has said European production could make the missile eligible for purchase by other EU member states under the bloc’s SAFE defence loan programme.
The second agreement signed during the visit concerns counter-drone work, and under it Origin Robotics, based in Riga, is to integrate its BLAZE autonomous interceptor into Anduril’s Lattice command and control system, giving a layered counter-uncrewed aircraft capability for Latvia and NATO’s eastern flank. BLAZE is a briefcase-sized interceptor using radar and camera guidance, while the company’s BEAK drone is already in service with Ukrainian forces.
Latvia has not said whether any Barracuda production, assembly or other industrial work would be carried out in the country however, though its Investment and Development Agency says the defence technology delegation now in the United States is seeking opportunities covering joint development, testing, manufacturing, system integration and supply chains.

articles.title: Araghchi says Iran ready for ‘doomsday war’ against US
articles.body:
NEW YORK, September 27. /TASS/. Iran is prepared to continue diplomatic efforts but intends to stand against any further US aggression even if the conflict escalates into a "doomsday war," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in an interview with NBC News.
"We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed. We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war," Araghchi said, adding, "At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose."
The minister stressed that Iran’s enrichment of uranium to 60% is conducted exclusively for peaceful purposes and is fully consistent with Tehran’s obligations under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT). "Enriching [uranium] up to 60% in not illegal. It is still withing the framework of the NPT and our peaceful program," he said.
At the same time, Araghchi noted that Iran could discuss a deal with the United States on its uranium enriched to 60%, but trust between the sides must first be strengthened before negotiations on the issue can take place.
"We offered a deal on our 60% [enriched nuclear] material in 2025 and 2026, and it is still something that could be considered if they prove their goodwill and their real determination for peace. We decided to put all nuclear issues to later stages and go for confidence building at this stage," he said.
Araghchi noted that Tehran’s proposed seven-day plan was specifically aimed at building trust with Washington.
The minister also talked about US claims that there are multiple centers of power in Iran and called them false, as decisions in the country are made on the basis of national consensus. "It is false to think that there are different sources of power inside Iran. We move based on national consensus," Araghchi said. According to him, Iran’s supreme leader is fine, and the country’s leadership continues to receive his comments, instructions, and views.
"We are all one front facing all challenges imposed on us by the United States, whether sanctions or military operations," he stressed.

articles.title: Poland wants a Patriot plant and a permanent U.S. military base - media
articles.body:
Poland wants a Patriot plant and a permanent U.S. military base - media
Kyiv • UNN
Poland has proposed establishing a U.S.-licensed Patriot missile plant. The country is also preparing legislation to accelerate the construction of a U.S. base.
Poland has proposed locating on its territory a plant producing missiles for Patriot air defense systems, if Ukraine receives the relevant license from the United States. This is reported by rmf24.pl, according to UNN.
Details
Deputy Minister of National Defense Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka noted that a special law would be adopted to accelerate the construction of a permanent U.S. military base in Poland.
She added that such a base could be located in western Poland, and that two possible locations are being considered.
Everything indicates that the Americans will not make a decision before the completion of the so-called strategic review initiated by Pete Hegseth. A report on the presence of Americans in Europe is currently being prepared. This report is to reach Secretary Hegseth's desk on November 1, and then President Trump's desk on December 1, and it is likely that only after that date can we expect a final decision
Responding to a question about the location of the base, she said that there are currently two proposals and that negotiations with the Americans are ongoing.
The American side has reviewed the locations we proposed and shared its assessment of these sites with us in Washington, and on this basis we will continue our work
The deputy minister also noted that the base could be located in western Poland, as this region "is considered by the Americans to be a safer place."
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka added that Poland's efforts to establish a service center and, subsequently, produce "Patriot" missiles are a process independent of Ukraine.
My interlocutors in Washington confirmed that even if such a decision is made regarding Ukraine, this will not change our efforts and will not cancel the approval for Poland
We remind you
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski stated that Ukraine had destroyed 30–40% of Russia's oil-refining capacity.

articles.title: ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky
articles.body:
The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter-of-fact: food had finally run out for the 2,000 or so civilians, including 50 children, remaining in the city and its surrounding villages.
“We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message from a woman in the besieged city who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces.
Before the war, she had weighed 110kg (17st); now she weighed just 67kg, she wrote. “At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.”
Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there.
This weekend, military authorities in Kherson carried out a large-scale airdrop of emergency food, water and medical supplies into the city and surrounding areas, using large drones, after Russia reportedly again rejected a ceasefire to evacuate civilians.
The military governor’s office in Kherson said an operation had dropped about four tonnes of food to 100 locations, but it was unclear how much the Russian military had intercepted.
The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York this week. A “Save Oleshky” banner was lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday.
In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”.
He said in an address during the general assembly: “Russia is deliberately making life there impossible. They are starving them to death.”
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents.
Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000. But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted.
Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops, who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save.
In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed.
“We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.”
On 1 September, a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops.
Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested.
Commenting on the airdrop over the weekend, Kherson’s military governor, Oleksandr Prokudin, described it as the largest operation of its kind so far.
“Food was delivered directly to 100 distribution points. And now I would like to address the Russians,” he said. “Civilians have absolutely nothing to do with the Ukrainian armed forces. Because of the conditions you have created in Oleshky, people simply have no choice but to take food. Do not deprive people of the chance to survive and avoid starvation.
“Russia, as the occupying power, is obliged to provide people with food, medicines and adequate conditions for healthcare and hygiene. If its own resources are insufficient, the occupying authorities must consent to humanitarian operations by international organisations and other states. Instead, we are seeing the opposite.”
He continued: “Russian occupying forces are obstructing the provision of aid to the civilian population. They are destroying vehicles attempting to deliver humanitarian supplies. And they are killing people trying to bring in food and medicines. They are also blocking all initiatives and agreements regarding the evacuation of people from Oleshky.”
According to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, problems began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult.
“The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult.
“And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning. People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson city. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.”
Hasanenko described a reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russia blew up the Kakhovka dam in 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers.
“Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said.
Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack.
Hasanenko said: “The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields.”
She added: “It’s an old city. It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.”
In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.”
Another messaged: “A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic.
“They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.”

articles.title: Andriy Rizol on How Cultural Diplomacy Advances Ukraine’s Interests
articles.body:
The Watch Ukrainian Association has organized more than 800 cultural events in 268 cities across 55 countries since March 2022, according to the organization. Its activities range from film screenings and photo exhibitions to concerts, lectures and international tours by Ukrainian artists.
The association says its projects, organized with partners and without state funding, have raised about Hr. 16 million for Ukraine’s armed forces, military intelligence and the rehabilitation of service members. It has held events at the Council of Europe, European Parliament, European External Action Service, UNESCO, US Congress, UN, UK Parliament and OSCE headquarters.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Its key initiatives include the CinemAid Film Marathon, Culture vs War, The Will to Win and Empowered. In 2024, Culture vs War became the umbrella brand for its cultural diplomacy projects.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Andriy Rizol, a producer and chairman of the association’s board, spoke to Kyiv Post about how culture can communicate Ukraine’s experience of war and build support abroad. Rizol is also CEO of Babylon and an honorary ambassador of Ukraine for cultural diplomacy.
What Germany’s Wingcopter 262 Means for Ukraine’s Drone War
“Be free to create”
Kyiv Post: How did Watch Ukrainian begin focusing on international cultural diplomacy?
Andriy Rizol: When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, we realized immediately that we had to act. On the fifth day of the war, we launched the CinemAid Charity Film Marathon. It brought together more than 70 events in 15 countries and helped us build a network of coordinators around the world while raising funds for the Armed Forces.
In April 2022, we launched the Culture vs War multimedia project. It combined documentaries, photo exhibitions and art books, with Ukrainian artists as protagonists.
We believed that international trust in artists was often higher than trust in politicians or the military — especially when artists were directly involved in the war. We wanted to tell the world about Russia’s war through their personal stories of resistance and their experiences.
What is the main message you want international audiences to take away?
Our slogan is “Be Free to Create.”
Ukrainians want victory, but we also need to explain why. We are fighting to preserve our freedom to create and to shape our own future.
The stories of our protagonists demonstrate this in different ways: members of the band Antytila through their service in a medical unit; Taras Kompanichenko through his moral support for the Armed Forces; Serhii Zhadan through his ability to inspire; and the first artists who volunteered to defend Ukraine, including Akhtem Seitablaiev, Serhii Mykhalchuk, Yaroslav Pilunskyi and Dmytro Linartovych.
How do you choose the protagonists?
The first criterion is a shared worldview. We look for prominent people who are known in Ukraine and internationally and who can serve as moral reference points.
But they cannot simply be made to speak from a script. Their stories have to reflect their genuine personal experience of the war.
This approach resulted in four feature-length documentaries, “Culture vs War,” “Palyanytsia,” “Empowered” and “Veterans’ Theater,” as well as seven short films focusing on individual artists.
Working with the government
How do you cooperate with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?
We began our dialogue with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs early in the full-scale war. It has always been based on equal partnership, and in some cases representatives of our organization also assist the MFA.
I have known Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha since his time as ambassador to Turkey, when we organized Ukrainian Film Days there. We have warm professional relations, and he understands the role culture can play in diplomacy.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Tetiana Sybiha has revitalized and brought together the Association of Wives of Ukrainian Diplomats, supporting humanitarian, cultural and charitable projects involving diplomatic and civic communities.
We also cooperate with the Diplomatic Academy of Ukraine and its head, Ihor Ostash, who has extensive diplomatic experience and a strong interest in culture and art. Together, we work with young diplomats on public and cultural diplomacy.
In August, we launched the School of Cultural Diplomacy together with the Institute for National Resilience and Security and the Diplomatic Academy. Its purpose is to strengthen joint efforts by increasing the expertise of professional diplomats.
We are gradually building an ecosystem that includes the MFA, diplomatic missions, the Association of Wives of Ukrainian Diplomats, the Diplomatic Academy and independent cultural institutions. The goal is to move from parallel efforts toward a coordinated system.
At the same time, Ukraine needs broader consolidation of cultural figures, specialized institutions, government and business to develop a comprehensive global cultural diplomacy strategy.
In 2024, the MFA granted me the status of Honorary Ambassador of Ukraine for Cultural Diplomacy. This has led to invitations to conferences, working meetings and panels where I can share our experience and develop joint initiatives.
Our goal is to make cultural diplomacy a priority and culture a national security priority.
For us, cultural diplomacy is not soft power. It is an effective tool for advancing Ukraine’s national interests and strengthening Ukraine’s ability to act internationally. In principle, it is an effective weapon.
That is why we focus on major political platforms and authoritative institutions capable of influencing decisions on support for Ukraine.
Why has the Veterans’ Theater resonated so strongly?
                                                                                                                                                                         
The idea emerged during a creative session of the Watch Ukrainian Association in April 2024. It was proposed by director, actor and civic activist Akhtem Seitablaiev.
We saw the project as a possible form of therapy through culture. At the same time, communicating the reality of the war to international audiences was becoming increasingly difficult as war fatigue grew.
We therefore created an art project that combined a stage production with a documentary featuring veterans as protagonists. It speaks about the war and its real consequences without necessarily putting the war itself “in the frame.”
The flagship production is “Eneida,” directed by Olha Semyoshkina, with Akhtem Seitablaiev as artistic director. It has attracted significant interest both in Ukraine and abroad.
The documentary “Veterans’ Theater” was screened in 19 countries as part of the Empowered UA film marathon.
For us, however, the motivation goes beyond the success of a particular project. We want to create trends, influence public discussion and help address real challenges.
Cultural diplomacy is essential to Ukraine’s future
What should Ukraine’s cultural presence in the world look like by 2030?
There are still remnants of an inferiority complex in Ukrainian society, but the situation has changed fundamentally.
Ukraine now has unique experience and significant achievements in military technologies, unmanned systems, IT, medicine, banking, logistics, e-document management, public services and volunteer practices, as well as in creative industries, documentary filmmaking, contemporary music and art. No other country has exactly the same experience.
Our next film is titled “Novators,” or “Innovators.”
By 2030, I want Ukraine to be respected and understood as a reliable and desirable partner of the democratic world. Cultural diplomacy can contribute to this.
We also need to change our perspective. We should not only learn from the world; we should also show what the world can learn from Ukraine.
That is the idea behind Empowered. We should no longer portray Ukrainians only as people who are poor, deprived or exhausted. We should show Ukrainians creating solutions, products, technologies, ideas and cultural phenomena that can be useful and interesting to the world.
The Empowered project was initiated by Watch Ukrainian with the support of the European Union and the MHP-Hromadi Foundation. It continues and develops the Culture vs War approach, seeking to strengthen the image of modern Ukraine as a strong country of talented people capable of enriching civilization across different areas of life.
We communicate this message through the personal stories of our protagonists.
I believe in large, ambitious, systemic and consolidated projects that produce concrete results. We simply do not have time for hesitation or delay.

articles.title: Russia's strike near Poland put Ukraine's railway lifeline in focus. But the bigger threat lies elsewhere
articles.body:
Russia's strike near Poland put Ukraine's railway lifeline in focus. But the bigger threat lies elsewhere
Passengers board their train after being evacuated due to an air raid alert near the border with Poland in Ukraine on Sept. 18, 2026. (Ania Tsoukanova / AFP via Getty Images)
On Sept. 13, a Russian drone struck the locomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw passenger train just 2 kilometers from the Polish border. The attack near Yahodyn caused no casualties, but it drew attention to one of Ukraine's most important links to the outside world amid the pressures of Russia's war — the railway.
Ukrainian state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said its monitoring team detected the threat early enough to evacuate the crew before the strike on the locomotive.
Russia has targeted Ukraine's railway throughout the full-scale invasion, but the intensity of attacks has risen sharply over 2026. At the same time, Ukraine increasingly depends on the railway for passengers, trade, diplomacy, and wartime logistics.
"The first goal is to disrupt logistics, both passenger traffic and the movement of goods," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told the Kyiv Independent.
"The second follows from that — weakening the economy, disrupting transport links with neighboring countries. Intimidating our partners may also be one of their goals."
While Moscow is unlikely to erode international support for Ukraine, he said, the immediate impact on transportation and trade is more serious.
read also
A lifeline
Ukraine historically developed around an extensive railway network, making it far more heavily dependent on rail than most European countries. Its road infrastructure, meanwhile, remains less developed.
Around 60% of the country's freight is transported by rail, and trains account for about 37% of domestic and international passenger transportation, according to Serhiy Vovk, director of the Centre for Transport Strategies.
In many European countries, he said, rail typically accounts for around 10% to 20% of passenger and freight transport.
"A passenger train may arrive six hours late after an attack, while five or six freight trains behind it can remain waiting for hours for capacity to reopen."
The dependence is even greater in foreign trade. About half of Ukrainian exports move by rail, Vovk estimates. For products such as iron ore, metals, and some agricultural goods, moving comparable volumes by road would be prohibitively expensive and place enormous pressure on highways.
Pressure on the railway could grow further if stable operations at Ukraine's Black Sea ports are not restored after another sustained Russian bombing campaign.
"If the issue of stable port operations is not resolved by November or December, domestic storage facilities may remain filled with grain and processed agricultural products that need to be exported," Vovk said.
The railway also became the backbone of Ukraine's "iron diplomacy," carrying foreign leaders and officials between the western border and Kyiv after the airspace closed in 2022.
Passengers increasingly feel the growing pressure on the railway. An attack hundreds of kilometers away can disrupt schedules for hours, and Russia's growing use of drones against trains and railway infrastructure means evacuations or emergency stops can become necessary along the route at any time.
But these visible delays are only one part of a wider disruption that can ripple through the network. Passenger trains operate on fixed schedules and are generally prioritized, while freight trains only move when capacity becomes available.
"A passenger train may arrive six hours late after an attack, while five or six freight trains behind it can remain waiting for hours for capacity to reopen. So the passenger sees the delay. But the larger hidden impact is felt by businesses and the economy," Vovk said.
read also
Real bottlenecks
Vovk does not see attacks on border crossings alone as a strategy capable of cutting Ukraine off from Europe. Western Ukraine has a relatively extensive railway network, so traffic can be rerouted when a route or junction is damaged.
But since the start of the full-scale invasion, Russian attacks have damaged or destroyed more than 500 Ukrainian locomotives, according to Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. More than half were hit this year alone.
"Without enough locomotives, the entire system can … grind to a halt."
Replacing the locomotives is difficult. Ukraine uses a 1,520-millimeter rail gauge, meaning most European locomotives cannot simply be transferred into service, and available compatible stocks abroad are limited.
"Without enough locomotives, the entire system can … grind to a halt," Vovk said.
Amid migration, mobilization, and losses among railway workers, Ukraine is also short of about 10% of the locomotive crews it needs, he said. Unlike a damaged track, that shortage cannot be fixed quickly.
"You cannot train a qualified driver in a year," Vovk said.
read also
A winter stress test
New rules allowing trains to continue operating under lower-level air threats rather than automatically stopping came into effect on Sept. 18. Under the highest threat level, boarding and disembarkation are suspended while passengers and staff move to shelters.
Decisions on trains already in motion are made on a case by case basis, using information from Ukrzaliznytsia's monitoring teams.
The company is also dispersing rolling stock and passenger flows, developing protected facilities for workers and passengers at major junctions, and exploring greater use of electronic warfare systems.
With winter approaching, preparedness becomes more urgent.
"A train that stops for hours in an open area in summer is an inconvenience. In freezing temperatures, particularly with children or elderly passengers on board, it can become a safety problem," Vovk said.
Protocols may increasingly need to ensure that trains stop near stations or populated areas where passengers can access shelter, electricity, and heat, he said.
Besides protecting tracks and stations under constant Russian threat across the country, Ukraine also needs to restore and procure locomotives, train new personnel, and build reserves.
"Otherwise, when passenger and freight volumes increase, the problem may no longer be whether the tracks are available, but whether there are enough locomotives — and enough people — to keep trains moving," Vovk said.

articles.title: A decade ago, Russian airline group S7 bet on a floating spaceport to break into the commercial launch market. Yet Sea Launch hasn’t launched a rocket in more than 12 years.
articles.body:
A decade ago, Russian airline group S7 bet on a floating spaceport to break into the commercial launch market. Yet Sea Launch hasn’t launched a rocket in more than 12 years.
On September 27, 2016, exactly 10 years ago, S7 struck one of the most ambitious deals in Russian spaceflight: the purchase of Sea Launch, a floating spaceport designed to send commercial payloads into space from the Pacific Ocean. S7 Group had ambitious plans to capture the commercial launch market, and its CEO, Vladislav Filyov, drew comparisons to Elon Musk. Science communicator Vitaly Yegorov explains what became of the project over the next decade and how the war affected its fate.
One project captures much of what went right and wrong in Russian spaceflight after the Soviet Union collapsed. Engineers from Russia and Ukraine built it from the remnants of the Soviet space program, with help from the United States and Norway. It saw successful launches and devastating accidents, lost out to commercial rivals, and fell victim to a political rift between former allies.
That project is Sea Launch, a floating spaceport for launching commercial satellites from equatorial waters in the Pacific Ocean. It now sits idle at a dock in Russia’s Primorye region, with no future in sight.
In the 1990s, Russia’s space industry was struggling to survive. State funding had fallen sharply, and the companies that had recently built the remarkable Energia rocket and Buran spacecraft had to scramble for money to pay their employees and keep their factories running. The international commercial market offered a lifeline. The United States and Europe needed relatively inexpensive launches, while Russian and Ukrainian companies needed foreign contracts. The U.S. interest was not purely economic; it also wanted former Soviet rocket technology to remain with those who already had it and not spread to countries Washington sought to keep it from.
Joint programs followed that would have seemed unthinkable just 10 years earlier. American space shuttles began flying to the Mir space station, Russian rocket engines went to the U.S., and Russian space companies formed joint ventures with European and American firms. One was the international Sea Launch consortium, established in 1995.
The engineering logic was elegant: put a spaceport on a vessel and take it to the most energy-efficient place to launch rockets. The equator is particularly well suited to launching commercial telecommunications satellites into geostationary orbit. There, Earth’s rotation gives a rocket up to 465 meters per second of extra speed at liftoff. More important, an equatorial launch avoids the need to adjust the orbit’s inclination relative to the equator. Together, these advantages increase a rocket’s payload capacity by about a quarter — a kind of gift from the planet. There is another benefit: in the middle of the Pacific, falling rocket stages pose less of a concern, reducing disposal costs.
The project began with a used, Japanese-built semi-submersible oil platform called Ocean Odyssey. It was converted for space launches and renamed Odyssey. The platform carried rockets to the launch site and served as the launchpad.
The second part of Sea Launch was Sea Launch Commander, an assembly and command ship built for the project. Rockets underwent final assembly and launch preparations aboard the ship while it was still in port. During a launch, the ship served as mission control and a tracking and command station. The original plan was to carry rockets to the launch site aboard Sea Launch Commander and transfer them to Odyssey at sea, allowing more than one launch per voyage. But the vessels’ motion at sea forced the consortium to abandon the idea.
The vessels were based in Long Beach, California, near Los Angeles. From there, they sailed to the equator, where the platform took up its launch position and the rocket was prepared for liftoff. The command ship then withdrew to a safe distance with all personnel aboard.
Boeing was the U.S. partner in the project, with a 40% stake. It handled overall management, financing, and commercial operations. On the technical side, Boeing was responsible for the rocket’s fairing and for preparing its payload section, allowing the project to comply with U.S. technology nonproliferation requirements. Personnel from Russia and Ukraine had almost no knowledge of what was beneath the fairing and had no contact with the payload. Russia’s RSC Energia developed the launch infrastructure and received a 25% stake. Norway’s Kvaerner received 20% for converting Odyssey and building the command ship. Ukraine’s Yuzhmash and Yuzhnoye Design Bureau, which worked on the rocket, received 10% and 5%, respectively.
The consortium chose the medium-lift Zenit-3SL rocket, derived from the Soviet Zenit-2. From the equator, it could launch satellites that would have required heavy-lift rockets from Baikonur or Cape Canaveral. Its first two stages were made by Ukraine’s Yuzhmash but contained many Russian components, including the RD-171 first-stage engine. Russia’s Energia also supplied the DM-SL upper stage — effectively the rocket’s third stage. Building the complete rocket therefore required contributions from three countries.
The first demonstration launch took place in 1999, followed by the first commercial launch. Sea Launch was in business, but it soon became clear that its finances were falling short of expectations.
Investment in Sea Launch totaled about $3.5 billion. In the 1990s, as the telecommunications market grew and Europe’s Ariane 4 was its only launch competitor, investors saw promise in the project. By the early 2000s, however, Russia’s heavy-lift Proton rockets, Europe’s Ariane 5, and the American Atlas V and Delta IV had entered the international market. Sea Launch struggled to attract orders, and its inability to launch several rockets on a single voyage erased the economic advantage of launching from the equator.
Zenit also proved far from the most reliable rocket. In 2000, a software error cost the project the ICO F-1 satellite. In 2004, Telstar 18 was delivered to an off-target orbit, though one that could be corrected. Then, on January 30, 2007, Sea Launch suffered its most dramatic accident. The rocket carrying the NSS-8 satellite exploded almost immediately after its engines ignited, engulfing the launchpad in a huge fireball. The platform needed repairs, though they were less extensive than the explosion had initially suggested. The year of downtime during those repairs dealt a much greater blow to the project’s finances.
In June 2009, Sea Launch declared bankruptcy.
In 2010, RSC Energia’s head, Vitaly Lopota, effectively decided on his own to save Sea Launch, and the Russian company took the lead in restructuring it. Through its subsidiary Energia Overseas, it gained control of 95% of Sea Launch’s shares. Boeing retained 3%, and the Norwegian side retained 2%. Bankruptcy, however, did not wipe out the old debts. Along with the spaceport, RSC Energia inherited a multimillion-dollar legal dispute with Boeing.
For Lopota, the effort to save Sea Launch ended in criminal prosecution. In 2014, investigators began examining RSC Energia’s financial transactions connected to the project. They believed the corporation’s management had signed deals that made little financial sense and spent substantial sums propping up a money-losing business. Lopota was convinced he had saved a unique project. In July 2025, the criminal case against him was closed because the statute of limitations had expired, after he agreed to end the proceedings on those grounds. It was not an acquittal, but neither did any court find him guilty.
Taking over the spaceport also meant that the Russian side had to pay to keep it running and remain responsible for Sea Launch’s existing financial obligations.
From 2011 through 2014, Sea Launch carried out six more launches, one of which again ended in failure. Over the project’s 15-year history, it conducted 36 launches: 32 successful, one partially successful, and three failures. SpaceX had emerged as another competitor by then, but Sea Launch was already facing a different set of problems.
In 2014, Russia annexed Crimea, and Moscow’s relations with Kyiv and Western countries deteriorated sharply. For Russia’s space industry, that meant sanctions and the collapse of cooperation with Ukraine on Zenit and other projects. Sea Launch was left with no orders, no rocket, debts to Boeing, and about $20 million per year in costs to maintain its U.S. infrastructure.
For a while, the project’s future was uncertain. There was talk of selling it to Israel or the United Arab Emirates, but in 2016, the possibility of a revival emerged from Russia’s private space sector. By then, Sea Launch was an asset of RSC Energia, part of the recently formed state corporation Roscosmos. The debt to Boeing for Sea Launch stood at about $373.5 million. Meanwhile, NASA was stuck: after the shuttle program ended in 2011, American astronauts could reach the International Space Station only aboard Russian spacecraft. After 2014, the prices NASA paid for seats began to rise, while American private companies had not yet completed spacecraft to replace the Russian ones.
Under a multilateral agreement, Boeing obtained rights to five seats aboard Russian crewed Soyuz spacecraft and then offered them to NASA. The bulk of the debt associated with Sea Launch was paid off, and Roscosmos was finally able to find a new investor for the floating spaceport.
In 2016, Vladislav Filyov, co-owner of the major Russian airline S7 Group, decided to try his hand at the space business. S7 Group finalized the deal in April 2018. The company acquired the Odyssey platform, the assembly-and-command ship, equipment, and the rights to the Sea Launch trademark.
S7 was counting on Roscosmos’s new Soyuz-5 rocket. It was effectively a Zenit redesigned to use Russian-made parts and carry heavier payloads. For launches from the equator, its projected performance and price were comparable to those of its main rival, the expendable 2015 version of the Falcon 9.
Filyov’s plans were ambitious: S7 was prepared to order 80 rockets from Roscosmos at once. While Soyuz-5 was still in development, S7 ordered 12 Zenit rockets from Ukraine’s Yuzhmash. Building them, however, required Russian components, whose delivery depended on permits from the Russian authorities.
For a time, it seemed that S7’s status as a private company might allow it to work around the political disputes between Russia, Ukraine, and the U.S. There was even a proposal to assemble the rocket from major components in the port of Long Beach, where the floating spaceport was still based. The “American” Antares was being built in the U.S. at the time in much the same way, using a Ukrainian rocket body and Russian engines, so the idea did not seem far-fetched. But the Russian authorities’ determination to deny Ukraine orders ruled out that option for Zenit. Filyov was left waiting for the delayed Soyuz-5.
In 2020, S7 moved Sea Launch from the U.S. to Russia to cut maintenance costs and avoid further political risks as relations between the countries worsened. The move came at a steep price: some of the American and Ukrainian equipment had to be removed, leaving the spaceport almost inoperable even if Zenit rockets became available again.
At the same time, S7 faced two crises. Vladislav Filyov’s wife, Natalya Filyova, who was also a co-owner of the company, died in 2019; then the economic fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic hit the airline in 2020. S7 had little capacity left to pursue its space ambitions, and 2022 effectively ended all of Sea Launch’s commercial prospects. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine brought a new wave of sanctions against its space industry, virtually shutting Russian rockets out of international competition.
Soyuz-5 did not make its first test launch from Baikonur until 2026, but that made no difference to Sea Launch. Even before the war, the cost of adapting the launchpad for the new rocket was estimated at $1 billion. Under current sanctions, the investment looks economically hopeless. What is more, the growth of low-Earth-orbit satellite constellations has diminished Sea Launch’s old advantage — launching from the equator — because those satellites instead need orbits closer to the poles.
As of September 2026, Sea Launch remains in the port of Slavyanka near Vladivostok. It has gone more than 12 years without a launch. The mothballed spaceport has yet to be scrapped, but a return to launches looks remote.
Perhaps Sea Launch’s only chance of revival today lies with Rassvet, a satellite internet project by the Russian company Bureau 1440. Competing projects Starlink and Amazon Leo are pursuing vertical integration, producing not only satellites but also rockets and launch facilities through SpaceX and Blue Origin. Bureau 1440 might be interested in launching satellites from a spaceport of its own, one beyond the reach of Ukrainian missiles. But that would take several more years and depend on many other factors — above all, the war.

articles.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said on Sunday it had seized a US Remus 600 autonomous underwater vehicle operating in the Strait of Hormuz, which it said was conducting espionage, according to state media.

The US could launch a renewed attack on Iran due to its bad regional situation, Iran's Army Spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia also said on Sunday, according to state media, adding that his country is ready for confrontation and to inflict greater damage on the US.

Iran Commander-in-Chief says war at decisive stage

articles.title: Investigation: Azov Optical and Mechanical Plant Involved in at Least Seven Russian Missile Programs
articles.body:
Investigators have found that the Azov Optical and Mechanical Plant (AOMZ), which was hit by missiles launched by the Defense Forces on the night of September 26, manufactures components for, among others, Kh-101 cruise missiles and Oreshnik ballistic missiles.
Private intelligence company Dallas Analytics reported this, citing documents from the Russian Azov Optical and Mechanical Plant that its analysts obtained.
The materials Dallas Analytics obtained include internal correspondence, state contract data, and production cooperation schedules from the Azov Optical and Mechanical Plant joint-stock company.
They cover the period between April 2023 and March 2025 and contain documents bearing the letterheads of four enterprises: AOMZ itself; Tactical Missiles Corporation (KTRV), which owns the plant and develops most of Russia’s tactical missiles; Michurinsk Plant Progress; and the Kurganpribor design bureau.
According to the company’s internal documents, the plant is part of the production chains for at least seven Russian missile programs.
The researchers found that AOMZ is involved in producing Kh-31P anti-radiation missiles, short-range R-74 and long-range R-37M air-to-air missiles, Kh-101 and Kh-35U cruise missiles, Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles, and Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missiles.
For the Kh-101 cruise missile, AOMZ manufactures the Otblesk navigation lidar and flight-control automation unit. The lidar helps the missile determine its position when satellite navigation is jammed, while the automation unit controls its systems and control surfaces. According to Dallas Analytics, no alternative suppliers exist for these components.
For the Kh-35U anti-ship missile and Kh-59/Kh-69 family of tactical air-launched missiles, the plant manufactures flight-control automation units. Internal documents also indicate AOMZ’s involvement in the production chain for the Oreshnik ballistic missile guidance system.
For the long-range R-37M missile, AOMZ is to supply switching units, power supply units, battery activation units, cable harnesses, assembly boards and housings.
In March 2025, the company was informed that the Russian Aerospace Forces required increased deliveries from 2026 of products containing the plant’s components. The company was given 72 hours to respond on whether it could supply 500 sets of electronic components and 1,000 housings annually starting in 2026.
The plant is also known to have worked on the Carthage-760 infrared seeker for the prospective short-range R-74 missile, developed by the Vympel design bureau to arm the Su-57 fighter jet.
According to Dallas Analytics, the Azov Optical and Mechanical Plant also manufactures seekers for the Kh-31P anti-radiation missile, which Russia uses against Ukrainian radars.
The company has also been linked to the 65SNL laser seeker for the Kh-38ML short-range air-to-surface missile and the 27NM-G seeker for the KAB-250L guided aerial bomb.

articles.title: South Korea demands apology from Zelensky
articles.body:
South Korea demands apology from Zelensky
South Korea has demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine over Vladimir Zelensky’s disclosure of a secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war captured in Russia, accusing Kiev of breaking a confidentiality agreement and then falsely denying that one existed.
Seoul’s presidential office escalated the diplomatic row in a statement on Sunday, expressing “strong regret” over Ukraine’s attempt to downplay Zelensky’s blunder at the UN General Assembly last week.
“We express strong regret over the Ukrainian government’s unilateral disclosure in violation of the confidentiality agreement, and its subsequent false public statement denying the existence of an agreement, and demand an official explanation and apology,” senior presidential secretary for public relations Seong Ghi-hong said. Seoul is also reviewing unspecified “further necessary measures,” he added.
According to Seong, the two governments had discussed the transfer through multiple channels, with Ukraine itself requesting that the arrangement remain secret. Kiev was reportedly concerned that publicizing the transfer could trigger criticism at home for giving up two North Korean soldiers who might otherwise have been exchanged for Ukrainian prisoners.
Zelensky bragged during his UN address on September 23 that Ukraine had recently sent the two men to South Korea, saying it was “not easy to capture them alive.” Pyongyang deployed troops to assist Russia in repelling a Ukrainian incursion into Russia’s Kursk Region in 2024-25.
The disclosure had drawn a sharp rebuke from South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, who said the transfer was an exceptionally sensitive matter affecting security on the Korean Peninsula. Lee accused Zelensky of putting short-term political interests ahead of national interests and said breaching the confidentiality arrangement was “deeply regrettable.”
Lee separately warned that people who jeopardize lives, national security and the national interest for political gain can be called “killers or traitors,” as he defended Seoul’s decision to keep the transfer secret.
Kiev subsequently denied that any secrecy agreement existed. Zelensky adviser Dmitry Litvin insisted that “there was no agreement to remain silent.” A source in the Ukrainian presidential office similarly told local media that Ukrainians had a right to know what happened to prisoners captured by their forces.
The dispute has also spilled into Ukrainian politics. Oksana Torop, a media adviser to Ukraine’s former top commander-turned-ambassador to Britain, Valery Zaluzhny, said a confidentiality agreement did exist and criticized Zelensky’s announcement as a “show” and “exaggerated publicity.”

Ukraine’s Retaliatory Drone Strikes Hit Russian Oil Refinery Supplying Moscow’s Forces
Ukrainian forces struck the Ilsky oil refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar region overnight on September 26 as part of retaliatory strikes in response to Russian aggression, triggering a fire at the facility.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed the strike on September 26, saying the refinery is involved in receiving, storing, and processing crude oil and producing petroleum products used to support the Russian Armed Forces.
The Ilsky refinery has an annual processing capacity of approximately 6.6 million metric tons of crude oil. The General Staff said strikes against facilities of this type are intended to reduce Russia’s military and economic capacity.
Reports of the attack began emerging around midnight, when residents in the area reported explosions and Russian air defense activity. Footage subsequently circulated by the Exilenova+ monitoring channel showed a fire at the refinery. ASTRA later geolocated eyewitness footage to the Ilsky facility in the Seversky district of Krasnodar region.
Krasnodar region Governor Veniamin Kondratyev confirmed that drones had targeted the Seversky district and said fires had broken out on the territory of two enterprises, though he did not identify the facilities.
The Ilsky refinery, located roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) from Krasnodar, has been targeted by Ukrainian drones multiple times. The previous reported strike occurred on August 8.
The Ilsky strike came one day after Russia’s Perm oil refinery halted operations following a Ukrainian drone attack. According to Reuters, it became the fourth Russian refinery to suspend operations in less than a week amid Ukraine’s continued strikes on Russia’s oil-processing infrastructure.

articles.title: No public mentions of Taiwan at official Xi and Trump meeting
articles.body:
Taiwan not openly discussed at Xi and Trump meeting
September 27, 2026
US President Donald Trump picked his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping up directly from the airport and in his welcoming remarks he praised the strong friendship between their two nations, as well as recalling how China and the US fought together as allies during World War II.
"Look at the greatness that we had together fighting in World War II," he said. "Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country," he said at the White House, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that fought alongside China against the Japanese between 1941 and 1942.
However, these pilots did not actually volunteer to fight with the People's Republic of China, whose leader was visiting Washington and which was not founded until 1949. The Americans were risking their lives for the former Republic of China, whose government relocated to Taiwan after communist victory in the Chinese Civil War in 1949.
"China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen," Trump said at a state dinner for Xi on Thursday evening. Sun Yat-sen was the founder of the Republic of China in 1912 and the Kuomintang, or KMT, which remains a major political party in Taiwan today.
Taiwan a major problem between US and China
Ever since the end of World War II, Taiwan has been a point of contention between Beijing and Washington. For decades, the US government ignored the communist regime in the People's Republic of China. But since 1972, Washington has acknowledged the "one China principle," according to which there is only one China, whose legal government is in Beijing and Taiwan belongs to it. Diplomatic relations between the US and China were only established in 1979.
The Taiwan Relations Act came into effect in 1979 too. The US law legalized arms exports to Taiwan. It also allowed the US government to take military action to prevent changes to the status quo in the Taiwan Strait.
A potential war between China and Taiwan would not only jeopardize stability in the Asia-Pacific region but also plunge the global economy into a prolonged recession, as supply chains would be severely disrupted.
During their high-profile meeting, Xi did not openly urge the US to respect the "one China" principle as he has done in the past, and Trump did not mention Taiwan in public either. In May, he put on hold a $14-billion arms deal that the US had concluded with the Taiwanese government late last year. The arms sales deal remains under review.
"Given the US' production capacity and its own military needs, it will take some time before approved arms can be delivered," said Ja Ian Chong, a political scientist and professor at the National University of Singapore. "It remains unclear what else the US can currently offer Taiwan."
Ahead of crucial midterm elections in November, Trump urgently needs some positive headlines. He and his Republican party rely on farmers for support so they need China to import US agricultural goods. In 2023, before their current trade war, China imported $43 billion worth of soy, beef, wood and other goods from the US. However Beijing has drastically reduced its imports since.
Taiwan mentioned behind closed doors
China used the meeting "to make clear to Trump its opposition to any US military support for Taiwan," said William Yang, an analyst with the International Crisis Group. "Xi wants to convey this message personally and behind closed doors, thereby influencing Trump's decision on arms sales to Taiwan."
China's Xinhua news agency said that Xi had addressed the issue behind closed doors. It reported that Xi had expressed hope that the US would take strong action against Taiwanese independence and said that China's position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity was clear. He reportedly added that "building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability is neither an expedient measure nor something that can be achieved overnight."
It will not have pleased Taiwanese politicians that the US president openly considered treating Taiwan as a bargaining chip in its negotiations with China, German sinologist Eberhard Sandschneider of the consultancy Berlin Global Advisers suggested during a political chatshow on German public television. "People living on the island of Taiwan do not take this lightly. This is an existential issue for Taiwan."
He added that he did not think China would take military action against Taiwan. That would be a move just as illogical as the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the US attack on Iran, he argued.
Nobody is playing poker in China, Sandschneider continued. "Clear strategic interests are pursued there. National sovereignty and winning back Taiwan are key concerns. At the same time, it is well known that any military attack on Taiwan would not only lead to a military disaster but also to an economic collapse. The resulting setback for the global economy would call into question the Communist Party's legitimacy," the expert said.
De Zheng contributed to this article, which has been translated from German.

articles.title: Ukraine Suspends Document Setting Limits Under Treaty on Conventional Armaments in CFE Flank Zone
articles.body:
Ukraine has suspended a 1996 document that established additional limits on the deployment of conventional weapons in the flank zone covered by the Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe (CFE Treaty).
The Office of the President of Ukraine published the relevant decree.
“To suspend the validity of the Document agreed by the States Parties to the Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe of November 19, 1990, concluded in Vienna on May 31, 1996, and approved by Decree No. 439/97 of the President of Ukraine dated May 14, 1997,” the decree says.
The 1996 document removed the Odesa region from the CFE Treaty’s original flank zone but established separate limits for it: no more than 400 tanks, 400 armored combat vehicles, and 350 artillery systems.
For Russian weapons in the original flank zone, the document established transitional limits through May 31, 1999: 1,897 tanks, 4,397 armored combat vehicles and 2,422 artillery systems. After that date, the limits were to be 1,800, 3,700 and 2,400, respectively. In approving the document, Ukraine stipulated that these provisions did not constitute its consent to the deployment of Russian military equipment on its territory.
At the end of the Cold War, NATO and the Warsaw Pact maintained large concentrations of troops and military equipment in Europe. In 1989, the sides began negotiations in Vienna on reducing conventional weapons, and the following year signed the Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe. Its purpose was to reduce the risk of a surprise attack and large-scale offensive.
The treaty established limits on tanks, armored combat vehicles, artillery, combat aircraft, and attack helicopters in the area from the Atlantic Ocean to the Urals. The participating states also agreed to exchange data on weapons and allow inspections.
NATO and the Warsaw Pact were assigned equal aggregate limits: each side could have no more than 20,000 tanks, 30,000 armored combat vehicles, 20,000 artillery systems, 6,800 combat aircraft and 2,000 attack helicopters. Of these, up to 16,500 tanks, 27,300 armored combat vehicles, and 17,000 artillery systems could be kept in active units.
After the Soviet Union collapsed, its share was distributed among the successor states under the 1992 Tashkent Agreement. Ukraine was assigned ceilings of 4,080 tanks, 5,050 armored combat vehicles, 4,040 artillery systems, 1,090 combat aircraft, and 330 attack helicopters.
For Russia, the Tashkent Agreement established limits of 6,400 tanks, 11,480 armored combat vehicles, 6,415 artillery systems, 3,450 combat aircraft and 890 attack helicopters. These quotas applied to Russian equipment in the treaty’s area of application, from the Atlantic Ocean to the Urals.
Under a separate Final Act adopted in July 1992, Ukraine was assigned a ceiling of 450,000 military personnel, and Russia a ceiling of 1.45 million personnel in the treaty’s area of application. The count included the personnel of land and air forces and land-based military formations specified in the act. It did not include, among others, naval personnel aboard ships or internal security forces.
In December 2007, Russia unilaterally suspended implementation of its obligations under the treaty. In response, some NATO member states that were parties to the treaty stopped implementing certain provisions concerning Russia in 2011, including providing Moscow with data on weapons and accepting Russian inspections. They continued to fulfill their obligations toward other participants.
On November 7, 2023, Russia formally withdrew from the treaty. That same day, NATO stated that continued compliance by the Allies, in the absence of such obligations for Russia, was unacceptable. NATO member states that were parties to the CFE Treaty announced their intention to suspend its implementation.

articles.title: American warship sunk by missiles off Scotland in live fire
articles.body:
The decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring has been sunk off the Hebrides during the joint US-UK live-fire exercise Atlantic Thunder 2026, in an engagement that drew in warships and aircraft from both navies, according to US Naval Forces Europe and Africa, which has released footage of the strike.
The video shows the American destroyer USS Paul Ignatius launching a missile and the frigate being hit. Other attackers took part alongside her, among them aircraft and further surface vessels, and the full order of battle has yet to be set out.
We will be bringing you an in-depth look tomorrow at what happened off the Hebrides, how the engagement was put together and which units and weapons were involved.
Paul Ignatius is an Arleigh Burke-class Flight IIA destroyer, hull number DDG-117, commissioned in July 2019 and named for the former Secretary of the Navy who held the post under Lyndon Johnson. She has been forward-deployed to Naval Station Rota in southern Spain since June 2022, one of the American destroyers held in Europe for ballistic missile defence and wider tasking across the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean.
Klakring was an Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigate, decommissioned in 2013 and laid up at the Philadelphia Naval Inactive Ship Maintenance Facility until she was towed down the Delaware River on 12 August ahead of the Atlantic crossing, making first for Campbeltown. The exercise itself was originally planned for a window in May before moving to the second half of September at the QinetiQ Hebrides range in north-west Scotland.
A Request for Information issued by the Ministry of Defence in August 2025, inviting industry to take part, described Atlantic Thunder 26 as “a US-UK multi-domain exercise designed to validate SUW kill chains, build resilient kill webs and deliver strategic messaging through kinetic demonstration.”
The strike was only one part of the exercise though, Klakring is expected to now settle at a depth of around 6,000 feet, where uncrewed underwater vehicles are to carry out battle damage assessment and seabed survey work, a phase the Ministry of Defence treated as central when it approached industry last year.
The precedent is Atlantic Thunder 22, held off the same range in September 2022, which ended with the sinking of the former USS Boone by HMS Diamond, USS Arleigh Burke, RAF Typhoons and US Navy P-8 Poseidons, and was billed at the time as the most complex multinational sinking exercise staged in UK waters.

articles.title: ADF neutralizes 147 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight

ADF neutralizes 147 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight

Hits were recorded at 18 locations, while falling debris from downed targets was reported at eight locations.

Saudi strike on Yemen's Taiz kills seven
A Saudi airstrike on Taiz in southwest Yemen killed seven people and wounded dozens more, Houthi media reported on Sunday.
The Iran-backed Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel said the strike killed seven and wounded 40 in a central marketplace in Taiz, minutes after reporting that a Saudi fighter jet had targeted the area.
Following years of relative calm, Yemen's war reignited in July, against the backdrop of the widening Middle East war.
Fighting intensified in September as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them seize Yemen's entire Red Sea coast, including the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping lane.
The Houthis have in parallel launched a blockade on Saudi energy exports, already choked off by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted two Houthi drones that were heading in the direction of the capital Riyadh.
Schools in Riyadh announced on Sunday that they would be shifting to remote learning for a week, without giving a reason, according to messages emailed to parents and seen by AFP.
Taiz, a major city controlled by the internationally recognised government, has been thrust to the frontlines of fighting between the Houthis and government forces.
Yemen's war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of vast swathes of the country's north.
Despite Saudi backing, Yemen's government forces have been unable to repel the latest Houthi offensive.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree nonetheless reported on Saturday that Saudi air forces launched 27 strikes targeting Taiz, Marib, Saada, Amran, Ibb and Hajjah provinces.

articles.title: Israeli regime nuclear arsenal cannot be ignored: Gharibabadi
articles.body:
Kazem Gharibabadi, deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, wrote on social media, "On the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons, a clear question faces the international community: how can one speak of disarmament while ignoring the nuclear arsenal of the Zionist regime?!"
He added, "Disarmament, peace and global security cannot be achieved with double standards and impunity for a particular regime."
